News.title: Yobs vandalise 4,000-year-old Bronze Age burial mound after removing rocks from protected historical site
News.content:
Next

A 4,000-year-old Bronze Age burial mound has been vandalised by yobs after removing rocks from the protected historical site.

The damage to Fire Beacon Cairn, near Crowcombe on the Quantock Hills National Landscape in Somerset, was spotted by a landowner on two occasions.



The shocking incidents were reported to local rangers and Historic England and marks the second time the monument has been vandalised in recent years.

Iain Porter, head ranger on the Quantock Hills, said he wanted visitors to grasp the historical importance of the ancient monuments.



He said: “It’s not a pile of stones – it’s a very important historic site… showing the ceremonial nature of that landscape historically.”

Fire Beacon Cairn is just one of around 50 scheduled monuments across the hills and it is a criminal offence to move the rocks or dig into the ground.

The cairn is a man-made mound, formed from a stack of stones marking a burial site – it is intended to measure around 4.9ft high and 82ft in diameter.

“Archaeologists and heritage officers are very concerned because if there are any finds or if there is any archaeological evidence of use and dating material, that’s where it’s going to be,” Mr Porter said.



He added that repairing the damage inflicted on the monument by vandals would likely come at a financial cost.

Dr Richard Brunning, senior historic environment officer at the South West Heritage Trust, said it was “especially worrying” when ancient monuments were damaged.

He said: “They’ve survived this long, it’d be terrible just to be destroyed on someone’s whim.”

Dr Brunning described the cairn as an “important relic of this very distant past”.

He added: “Archaeologically, they’re very important when they’re excavated because as they hold human remains that gives us a very good evidence for what past people were like.



“We can do all sorts of wonderful bits of science that you could never do in the past, such as looking at DNA from people buried that long ago.”

A Historic England spokesperson said the cairn had only recently been repaired after being vandalised two years ago.

They added: “We ask that the public remain vigilant and report any further vandalism to Historic England and the Quantock Hills National Landscape team.”

Quantock Hills National Landscape said the latest damage occurred “last week, and again over the weekend”.

A spokesperson added: “Information and evidence has been sent to Historic England.



“The pre-historic landscape is a key feature of the Quantock Hills with over 50 Scheduled Monuments and damage to a Scheduled Monument is a criminal offence.

“At these sites it is illegal to move rocks, stones or soil, to dig into or to cause any damage. It is also illegal to use metal detectors.”

Mr Porter, manager of the Quantock Hills National Landscape Team, said: “It is upsetting to see the level of damage caused to this Scheduled Monument.

RECOMMENDED STORIES

“These sites (there are over fifty Scheduled Monuments on the Quantock Hills), form a vast network allowing us to understand the ceremonial importance of the hills from the Neolithic, through the Bronze-Age and into the Iron Age.

“We are working with the landowner and partners from Historic England and the South West Heritage Trust to assess the damage and to repair the site.”

News.title: Andy Burnham doubles down on trying to reach Net Zero by 2050 despite soaring energy bills
News.content:
Next

ANDY Burnham has doubled down on trying to reach Net Zero by 2050.

The PM rejected demands to pull back on the eco dash to try to keep down energy bills.



He wrote in the Guardian: “The climate crisis presents us with an enormous challenge and possibility.

“In the coming years, we need to change the way we travel, build homes and produce energy.



“I have long seen the green transition as the best chance we will ever have to reindustrialise Britain.”

Energy Secretary Miatta Fahnbulleh confirmed that Labour would not grant new North Sea oil and gas licences.



But she is expected to approve the Jackdaw and Rosebank gas and oil fields.

Those fields already had licences but need her final sign-off.

She also dismissed rumours that a decision would not come before the Holborn and St Pancras by-election where the Greens are a threat.

But Reform’s Richard Tice said: “Burnham babbles on with Labour’s Net Stupid Zero zealotry whilst our bills soar.”

News.title: Andy Burnham’s ‘acting like Santa’ and must make tough cuts to get Britain back on track, blasts Iceland boss
News.content:
Next

ANDY Burnham has been told to stop acting like Santa and make the tough cuts Britain needs to get back on track.

Iceland boss Lord Walker, the Government’s former cost-of-living tsar, blasted the Prime Minister for piling promises on taxpayers while ducking unpopular decisions.



Since taking office, Mr Burnham has pledged to axe VAT on household electricity, keep the £2 bus fare cap, end rough sleeping and slash business rates for pubs, clubs and music venues.

But Lord Walker warned Britain can no longer borrow its way out of trouble – and said firms must not be treated like a “piggy bank”.



He told LBC: “Andy Burnham has been Father Christmas so far, and it would be great if he’d start to get a bit more unpopular.

“For the last 50 years, Chancellors on the Left or the Right haven’t been too dramatic on raising taxes or reducing spending because they’ve been able to borrow a little bit more.



“Borrowing, increasing borrowing, is now off the table as an option. The bond markets are teaching us that lesson. Therefore, tough choices are now needed.”

His broadside came as Mr Burnham warned that his first Budget next month would be “challenging”, with the war in Iran pushing up oil and gas prices.

Lord Walker said Britain must “stop focusing on the cost-of-living crisis and start focusing on the cost of getting Britain back to work”.

He added: “We cannot, for the sake of us all, keep taxing business and viewing it as a piggy bank that can constantly be raided, because only business creates growth.



“We must therefore start reducing spending – or at least slow the rate at which it is increasing.”

Former Bank of England economist Andy Haldane has also accused the Government of failing to rein in public spending.

But ministers insisted their priority remained helping squeezed families and making everyday life more affordable across the country.

News.title: Labour under pressure to save Freeview after millions of England fans hit by World Cup streaming chaos
News.content:
Next

LABOUR is under mounting pressure to protect Freeview TV after millions of England fans saw their World Cup streams buffer, freeze or stop altogether over the summer.

Almost one in two footie fans who streamed a Three Lions match experienced the game cutting out, new polling suggests.



It comes as Andy Burnham recently told MPs he was concerned about plans to stop free-to-air TV for good.

The Prime Minister told the Commons he was concerned about the proposals and wanted to have a “proper look” at them.



The Sun has launched a Save Our Sets campaign to protect free TV and has seen the MPs’ letter.

More than 40 per cent of footie fans had streaming problems with the World Cup final.



One in five Brits have had regular difficulties while trying to watch a big live event.

Meanwhile 34 per cent of people had problems during the FA Cup final and Eurovision.

Rotherham MP Sarah Champion said: “This polling shows the extent that free TV is still relied on including by many of my constituents in Rotherham and by over ten million homes across the UK, for some of those, the television connects them to the outside world.”

A Broadcast 2040+ spokesman added that nobody had voted to “have their telly switched off” and urged ministers to listen to people’s concerns.



They added: “Terrestrial TV is the one platform that never lets the nation down. It reaches almost every home, it’s free, and it doesn’t crash when 20 million people tune in at once.

Strand Partners surveyed 1000 members of the public in September.

Almost 70 per cent of punters have previously said they believe the PM will have broken his word if he goes ahead with the switch off.

News.title: Third person dies from malaria linked to Frankfurt Airport after ‘mosquito gets trapped on plane’ in rare outbreak
News.content:
FLYING FEVER Third person dies from malaria linked to Frankfurt Airport after ‘mosquito gets trapped on plane’ in rare outbreak







Next

A THIRD person has died of malaria after a single mosquito was reportedly trapped on a plane to Germany.

Several people were rushed to hospital following the rare outbreak of the tropical disease aboard a flight to Frankfurt.



Traps were set up around Germany‘s busiest transport hub in July as officials desperately tried to contain the outbreak.

But in August, one airport worker tragically died of the disease.



Now, an infected resident of Schwanheim, north of the airport, has passed away in hospital, city officials revealed on Thursday.

Shockingly, the victim was not an airport employee nor had they travelled to a malaria-riddled region.

Another resident of the area has also been struck down with malaria.

A statement from city officials confirmed: “Both individuals had become infected with the malaria-causing parasite, even though they had not travelled to a malaria-endemic region and had not worked at the airport”.

The terrifying phenomenon is known as “airport malaria” – and can strike anyone who comes into contact with the infected insect.

Parasites can be stowed away on flights from malaria regions – and then escape to bite people on the other side.



Malaria can only be contracted from the bite of an infected mosquito and cannot be spread human to human.

The disease can cause fever, chills and debilitating headaches.

Infections can even become life-threatening if they remain untreated, according to the World Health Organisation.

But public health officials said: “For the population of Frankfurt, the risk is considered very, very low.

Four employees were previously reported to have fallen ill with malaria between July 4 and 6.



News of the first infections was reported on July 16, with officials saying the employees were likely bitten earlier in the week.

An airport spokesperson said the victims worked in the airport’s baggage handling section.

It is unclear from where the plane had been flying.

RECOMMENDED STORIES

Between 1969 and 2024, 145 cases were reported – including nine in Germany.

The last known case of malaria at Frankfurt Airport happened in 2023.

News.title: Mystery death of Ukrainian Putin critic in Portugal being probed amid fears it was a Kremlin hit
News.content:
Next

THE death of a Vladimir Putin critic is being investigated amid fears it was a Kremlin hit.

Pavlo Sadokha, 56, was found dead at Quarteira, Algarve, on Sunday.



The Ukrainian had a history of heart disease and, at first, police cited natural causes.

But family said his health was “perfectly under control” — leading Portuguese prosecutors to investigate.



The family also want toxicology checks.

In June 2025 Sadokha claimed the Kremlin was using youth games to militarise children of Russian expats in Spain.



He lived in Portugal for two decades.

Putin’s FSB assassins are known to be hunting prominent Ukrainians across Europe.

Suspects are still at large over the 2024 gun murder of Russian defector Maxim Kuzminov near Benidorm.

The 28-year-old airman, who flew his Russian Mi-8 helicopter to Ukraine, was executed by six shots in a car park after starting a new life in Spain.



His killers – who fled in a car later found torched – have never been found.

News.title: Fury as ‘staggeringly naive’ Archbishop of Canterbury gives award to Bin Laden apologist on 25th anniversary of 9/11
News.content:
Next

THE Archbishop of Canterbury has been blasted as “staggeringly naive” for giving an Osama Bin Laden apologist an award — on last week’s 25th anniversary of September 11.

Dame Sarah Mullally presented the “reconciliation and interfaith co-operation” honour to Tahir Ashrafi, chairman of the Pakistan Ulema Council.



In 2007, Ashrafi sparked fury when he condemned the award of a knighthood to Satanic Verses author Sir Salman Rushdie. The bearded Muslim leader hit back further by announcing he would award Bin Laden the title of Saifullah, or “Sword of God” honour.

Ashrafi said at the time: “If a blasphemer can be given the title ‘Sir’ by the West then a mujahid who has been fighting for Islam against the Russians, Americans and British must be given the lofty title of Islam, Saifullah.



“We are pleased to award the title of Saifullah after the British Government’s decision to bestow the title of ‘Sir’ on blasphemer Rushdie. This is the highest title for a Muslim warrior.”

Left-leaning Dame Sarah beamed as she set aside Ashrafi’s views to salute him at Lambeth Palace.

Shadow Justice Secretary Nick Timothy MP said: “The naivety of the Archbishop in presenting an award to someone who openly praised Bin Laden is staggering — and on the anniversary of 9/11, too.

“Our leaders must face up to the reality not all cultures are based on the same foundations as ours, and not all share our desire for co-operation and freedom.



“Western political and religious leaders should stand up vigorously for our own values and achievements, rather than apologising for our history or celebrating those who seek to do us harm.”

Victim support campaigner Travis Frain OBE, a survivor of the 2017 Westminster Bridge attack, called the Archbishop’s move “a grave misjudgment by the Church”.

Tim Dieppe, at Christian Concern, added: “The absurdity of this beggars belief. Mullally is clearly uninformed about both Ashrafi and about Islam. There is no justification for giving him an award.”

However, last night a Church spokesman said: “Previous comments made by Imam Ashrafi have come to light . . . and we can now confirm the award has been withdrawn.”

News.title: Tributes to ‘beautiful and loving’ mum, 34, who died after being knocked down while waiting for bus – as man arrested
News.content:
BUS TRAGEDY Tributes to ‘beautiful and loving’ mum, 34, who died after being knocked down while waiting for bus – as man arrested







Next

TRIBUTES have been paid to a “beautiful and loving” mum who died after she was knocked down while waiting for a bus.

Danielle Sharpe, 34, was pronounced dead at the scene following the horror crash in Corby, Northamptonshire, on September 11.



Northamptonshire Police said a black Vauxhall Insignia smashed into a bus stop at around 7.30am.

The force said a 55-year-old man from Corby was arrested on suspicion of causing death by dangerous driving and driving a vehicle while unfit through drugs.



He has been released on bail pending further enquiries.

Now, Danielle’s family has released a heartbreaking tribute, describing her as a “loving mother, daughter, granddaughter, sister and aunty”.

It read: “Danielle was such a beautiful and loving mother, daughter, granddaughter, sister and aunty and was loved by so many.

“We are just beyond heartbroken and cannot believe that she has gone.

“In her short life she left a remarkable stamp on this world, and we cannot put into words just how much we are going to miss her.

“We are so thankful for everybody’s love and support during this difficult time, but while we try to come to terms with the loss of Danielle, we would appreciate some time and space to grieve in private.



“We would also ask that people do not speculate about what happened on social media and please allow the police to investigate the collision.”

Cops say the black Vauxhall was travelling along Willow Brook Road and “appeared to be turning left into Fotheringhay Road, when the vehicle left its intended path and collided with a bus stop”.

A teenage boy was also left with minor injuries following the incident.

A police spokesperson said: “Detectives from the Serious Collision Investigation Unit would still like to hear from anyone who may have dash-cam footage which captured any part of the collision.”

News.title: Toys ‘R’ Us to open 120 stores in US as part of 'biggest expansion in years'
News.content:
Toys ‘R’ Us to open 120 stores in US as part of 'biggest expansion in years'

Toys 'R' Us is set to open more than a hundred new stores in the coming weeks across America as part of its biggest expansion in nearly a decade, driven by a surge in toy sales to adults

View 3 Images Pictured is the former Toys R Us building at the Wyvern Retail Park, Derby (Image: Derby Telegraph)

While numerous major High Street retailers are shutting their doors, children's retail giant Toys "R" Us is launching its biggest expansion in almost ten years.

‌



The ambitious project will see 120 physical shops open their doors across the US in the coming weeks and months.

‌



The resurgence stems from increased interest among adult shoppers, the firm revealed on Thursday, having secured fresh agreements for numerous one-year leases throughout the US.

‌



Data from consumer tracking firm Circana shows toy sales have experienced their most significant growth since 2020. During the first six months of 2026, toy sales jumped by an impressive 17 per cent - marking the strongest first-half showing in six years for the retailer.

This growth is predominantly driven by "kidults", or grown-ups purchasing trading cards and collectables. Circana's research indicates that adults now account for 55% of total toy purchases.

View 3 Images Bunch of Barbie Fashon Dolls (Image: Getty)

‌



The new outlets opening across America will stock major brands including LEGO, Barbie, Hot Wheels, Pokémon and KPop Demon Hunters. Selected branches will additionally house their own cafés and confectionery sections, the business confirmed.

Approximately 40 stores have already launched throughout the US, featuring a 20,000-square-foot flagship branch in New Jersey and another in Minnesota.

A Toys "R" Us representative stated that the expansion initiative began last month when Go! Retail Group - which specialises in operating pop-up stores and discreetly began the Toys "R" Us revival last year - has started rolling out outlets spanning between 3,500 and 7,500 square feet.

‌



View 3 Images The former Toys R Us building in Derby (Image: Derby Telegraph)

The total number of branches is anticipated to hit 160 within the next few weeks.

While the brand may be flourishing once again, 160 sites represents merely a small proportion of the 750 stores the chain operated before filing for bankruptcy in 2017 and shuttering all its American locations.

‌



The firm's demise dealt a devastating blow to the toy retail industry, which had depended on Toys "R" Us to drive sales and launch new products.

In the years since, American retailers Walmart, Amazon and Target have predominantly stepped in to fill the void.

Yet, according to Jamie Uitdenhowen - a former Toys "R" Us veteran who now serves as WHP Global executive vice president - "the toy industry is incredibly strong."

Article continues below

This might well signal a comeback for the toy retail giant in the coming years.

News.title: Hospital horrors as patients died and others deteriorated during sweltering 44C heatwave
News.content:
Hospital horrors as patients died and others deteriorated during sweltering 44C heatwave

One nurse described the situation as "horrendous" and said patients were left "suffering more from the actual heat than the actual reason they are in hospital"

View 4 Images Nurses described "suffocating atmospheres" in British hospitals (Image: Getty Images)

Patients died — and nurses witnessed maggots in wounds — as temperatures hit 44C highs over the summer, hospital staff claim.

‌



Nurses reported seeing patients die and others deteriorate in what they have described as "suffocating atmospheres" due to the sweltering heat on NHS wards, a Royal College of Nursing (RCN) survey found. The concerning finds also include accounts of nurses witnessing cancer patients dripping with sweat during chemotherapy sessions with one claiming to have seen maggots in wounds.

‌



Record-breaking heat meant patients came to harm, according to the RCN. It has since called for more Government investment so hospitals can better cope in warm weather. The survey of 2,471 nursing staff during the summer heatwaves found high temperatures affected care, with examples of poorer outcomes for patients.

‌



One children's ward in Yorkshire reached a scorching 44C, according to one nurse, while another in the North West of England called the situation was "horrendous" with patients "suffering more from the actual heat than the actual reason they are in hospital." The damning claims come after nurses ended up fainting in swelteringly hot hospital wards which were condemned as "not fit for humans."

Are you affected by this story? Contact webnews@mirror.co.uk

View 4 Images The UK was hit by multiple heatwaves over the summer (Image: Getty Images)

‌



Nurse shaved head daily to fake cancer in brazen scam that paid for Dubai holiday READ MORE :

'Maggots in his wounds'

Campaigners and unions have slammed that there are no maximum temperature workplace temperatures, even though there is a minimum standard. It comes after Britain was hit by five heatwaves during a record-breaking summer which made work in hospitals more challenging.

Another nurse said patients fainted, and other patients suffered dehydration, particularly older people. One common theme in the survey was the effect on people with heart failure and respiratory conditions, who seemed to fare worse because of the heat.

A nurse in Wales said: "We had two frail patients for whom the extreme heat directly impacted their deaths. Whilst it was not the only cause, if you are in respiratory failure, the heat is a death sentence."

‌



A palliative care nurse working in a hospital in the South West of England said: "We had a palliative patient with chronic ulcers on the ward. In the hospital's care, during the last heatwave, the wounds festered enough that they attracted flies and were found to have maggots. Some of his and his relatives' last memories will be knowing of and, in his case feeling, maggots in his wounds."

View 4 Images Staff complained of horrendous conditions in the summer (Image: Anadolu via Getty Images)

‌



'This feels like a safety concern'

A nurse treating cancer patients in London said: "I've seen patients sweating and dripping due to the heat during chemotherapy. There is no air conditioning running in the unit. During one particularly hot period, patients were visibly sweating throughout their treatment. This feels like a safety concern, not just a comfort issue."

Paramedics also spoke of "unbearable" shifts and crews being sent out in ambulances in stifling heat with faulty or no air conditioning. Multiple nurses also reported mental health patients becoming more challenging, leading to further assaults on staff.

Some 74 per cent of those polled said they had little or no confidence that the Government was taking sufficient action to reduce the impact of climate change on the NHS and social care. Freedom of Information figures released earlier this month suggested more than 1,000 operations at NHS hospitals were cancelled because of the heat during record-breaking heatwaves in May and June.

‌



View 4 Images Thousands of nurses took part in the survey (Image: PA)

Tim Lane, president of the Royal College of Surgeons of England, said surgeons reported extreme heat as well as old ventilation systems as making it more difficult to keep operating theatres open. He added: "When an operation is cancelled, patients face extra pain, anxiety and uncertainty as they wait for a new date.

"Many will have already arranged time off work and care responsibilities. Cancellations also put further pressure on NHS services, with lost theatre time and delays that can affect waiting lists for months."

‌



Temperatures in the UK reached 35C during May, June, July and August, the first time this has happened. RCN chief executive Professor Nicola Ranger said: "This testimony reveals the devastating impact of extreme heat on patients, with increased death, deterioration, and conditions in services which, frankly, are an assault on people's right to dignified, safe care.

"The reality is that climate change is here, but long-term underinvestment in our health and care services has left them so unprepared. Staff did everything they could in record-breaking temperatures to keep patients safe and comfortable, but they were fighting a losing battle in buildings which often lack even the most basic cooling facilities. It's been incredibly traumatic.

"We are all aware of the pressures that winter brings, but extreme heat is here to stay, and the clock is now ticking to accelerate investment in hospitals, care homes and other settings to ensure they are prepared. This summer was our warning. By next, we need everywhere to have effective cooling facilities in place, or patients will suffer shocking harm once again."

Article continues below

A Department of Health and Social Care spokesperson said:

“These harrowing testimonies reinforce the importance of the action announced last week by the Health Secretary to prepare the NHS better for future heatwaves, as well as the tribute she paid to every nurse who continued delivering the highest standards of care this summer despite the pressures placed on them.

“In her statement last week, the Health Secretary announced a significant package of funding to improve the safety of hospitals across the country, including an initial £32 million to improve cooling and ventilation systems and strengthen hospitals’ resilience to extreme heat. She also announced the launch of a new Heat Taskforce, which will future heatwave planning is placed on the same footing as planning for the pressures of winter.”

News.title: 'Diana’s wounds ripped open again – but William and Harry must not pay the price'
News.content:
'Diana’s wounds ripped open again – but William and Harry must not pay the price'

Excerpts from Earl Spencer's book, Swan Song: Diana, My Sister – Earl Spencer, have been published — and have sparked an "unprecedented" response from Buckingham Palace

View Image Voice of the Mirror has its say...

Nearly 30 years after Princess Diana’s death, the wounds surrounding her tragic life and marriage are being torn open once again.

‌



Earl Spencer’s claims about King Charles are extraordinary and deeply damaging. He alleges the then-Prince sounded “giddily elated like a lottery winner” when telling him Diana had died. Buckingham Palace strongly disputes his account. Only those involved know exactly what was said in those dreadful days of grief and turmoil. Spencer is entitled to give his account of what happened to the sister he adored. But amid these painful revelations, he must spare a thought for nephews William and Harry. They lost their mother when they were just 15 and 12. Now they must absorb allegations suggesting their father responded to her death with something approaching relief. Diana remains loved and remembered by millions, while William and Harry have borne the consequences of this tragedy for almost three decades. Whatever truths still need telling, their grief must be treated with care. They should not be made to pay, yet again, for the mistakes and bitterness of an older generation.

‌



We must modernise NHS hospitals

It is shameful that patients went into NHS hospitals for treatment and ended up being put at greater risk by the wards themselves. Nurses describe suffocating temperatures, frail patients deteriorating, newborn babies struggling to breathe and cancer patients dripping with sweat during chemotherapy. Most appalling is the account of a dying patient whose wounds became infested with maggots. If true, it is a disgrace in a modern health service. Nurses should be caring for the sick, not desperately trying to stop hospital wards becoming unbearable heat traps. The warnings have been there for years. Hotter summers are no longer some distant threat, yet too many hospitals remain woefully unprepared when temperatures soar. That failure now has a human cost. Ministers must treat safe hospital temperatures as a matter of patient safety and launch a properly funded programme to modernise NHS wards.

Article continues below

Coleen’s hairdryer treatment

Wayne Rooney spent years at Manchester United getting Sir Alex Ferguson’s legendary hairdryer treatment. But years of headlines about wayward, boozy nights mean Wazza knows wife Coleen’s heat is far fiercer. Now reality TV cameras are inside Rooney Towers - a place where Wayne admits to battling to stay out of the doghouse.

News.title: Dead newborn baby found dumped in bin as mum, 24, charged by Australian police
News.content:
Dead newborn baby found dumped in bin as mum, 24, charged by Australian police

Warning: Distressing content A young mother has been charged weeks after dead newborn baby boy was found dead and dumped in a rubbish bin in Auburn, Australia

View 3 Images The baby was a newborn boy but no further information has been released at this stage (Image: 7News)

A 24-year-old mum has been charged by police after her newborn baby boy was found dead and dumped in a rubbish bin.

The mum, who has not been named, was found by police at a nearby address and taken to hospital for assessment. Upon release from hospital she was arrested and taken to Auburn Police Station where she was then charged with mother alone conceal birth by disposing body.

Police received reports that the body of a baby had been located in a rubbish bin in Harrow Road, Auburn, on Monday Augist 31 at around 11.20am.

View 3 Images Police at the scene (Image: ABC News)

Following weeks of extensive inquiries investigators executed a crime scene warrant at a unit on Harrow Road yesterday where they found who they believed to be the mother of the child.

She has since been charged and is awaiting a court hearing on October 27.

A New South Wales Police spokesperson said: "A woman has been charged after the body of an infant was located in Sydney’s south west last month. About 11.20am on Monday 31 August 2026, emergency services were called to Harrow Road, Auburn, following reports the body of a baby had been located in a garbage bin.

"Officers attached to Auburn Police Area Command attended and located the body of a newborn boy. Police established a crime scene, and detectives commenced an investigation into the incident under Strike Force Alenor.

View 3 Images The police investigation lasted several weeks (Image: 7News)

"Following extensive inquiries, about 6.45am today (Thursday 17 September 2026), investigators executed a crime scene warrant at a unit on Harrow Road, Auburn. A short time later, police spoke with a 24-year-old woman – who is believed to be the mother of the infant – at another address in Auburn before she was taken to hospital for assessment.

"Upon release from hospital, the woman was arrested and taken to Auburn Police Station. The 24-year-old was charged with mother alone conceal birth by disposing body. She was granted conditional bail to appear before Downing Centre Local Court (John Maddison Tower) on Tuesday 27 October 2026."

News.title: Major update after UK airline plunged into administration – 'We are delighted'
News.content:
Major update after UK airline plunged into administration – 'We are delighted'

British freight airline European Cargo Limited entered administration on June 3, but its fleet of 16 Airbus A340-600 aircraft has since been rescued

View 2 Images European Cargo's aircraft have been acquired by European Aviation Group (Image: European Cargo Limited)

A huge fleet of cargo aircraft has been acquired after a British airline set up during the Covid-19 pandemic collapsed into administration.

‌



European Cargo Limited (ECL) - a freight airline based at Bournemouth International Airport - entered administration on June 3, with Stuart Morris, Robert Fishman and David Soden, of Teneo Financial Advisory Limited, appointed as joint administrators.

‌



Teneo Financial Advisory said the appointment followed a "period of significant financial pressure on the business, driven by reduced flying activity and working capital and fuel cost pressures". The administrators confirmed that ECL had ceased trading and that 178 employees had been made redundant.

‌



View 2 Images European Cargo Limited entered administration on June 3 (Image: European Cargo Limited)

EES delays update over 9 UK tourist destinations - key details READ MORE :

Flight to Manchester declares mid-air medical emergency after entering UK airspace READ MORE :

However, all of European Cargo's assets have since been acquired by European Aviation Group, which is led by Paul Stoddart, the former boss of the Minardi Formula One team.

The deal, announced in late August, includes ECL's fleet of 16 Airbus A340-600 aircraft, seven of which are understood to be flight-ready, as well as its Rolls-Royce Trent 553 and Trent 556 spare engines.

‌



Stoddart, chairman and chief executive of European Aviation Group, said: "We are delighted to have concluded our acquisition of all of the assets of ECL with the joint administrators.

"Whilst this is a massive investment from EAL, I feel totally confident that we can keep this excellent fleet of cargo aircraft flying for the foreseeable future."

Despite the sale of its assets, ECL remains in administration, according to Companies House.

Article continues below

European Aviation Group has not confirmed whether any of the 178 former European Cargo employees will be offered jobs as a result of the acquisition.

European Cargo began operations in April 2020 after its parent company at the time, European Aviation, responded to an urgent request from the UK Government to transport personal protective equipment (PPE) from Malaysia.

The carrier subsequently operated more than 400 charter flights carrying PPE and Covid-19 testing kits. Its aircraft were also painted in commemorative liveries paying tribute to the NHS.

News.title: Woman died in horror wall collapse at home eight years after alarm first raised
News.content:
Woman died in horror wall collapse at home eight years after alarm first raised

Clarice Berry, 77, died when a 3,800kg wall collapsed on top of her at the rented property in Wigan - eight years after her husband first raised concerns over the state of the building

View 2 Images Clarice Berry, 77, died when a wall collapsed at her home (Image: Facebook)

A woman died in a horror wall collapse at her home nearly eight years after her husband first raised the alarm about the rented property, a coroner found.

‌



Clarice Berry, 77, died from chest injuries "incompatible with life" after the 3,800kg gable wall of her home collapsed onto her on July 18, 2021, trapping her beneath the rubble.

‌



Eyewitnesses described a frantic scene as neighbours desperately attempted to rescue her from the wreckage.

‌



She suffered a severe fracture of the sternum and fractures to all her ribs, and was pronounced dead at 4.10pm at Royal Albert Edward Infirmary in Wigan.

View 2 Images Ms Berry was in the lean-to carport beneath the gable end of the property (Image: MEN Media)

Noah Woods confirmed dead as police say body pulled from pond is tragic 3-year-old READ MORE :

Assistant coroner for Manchester West, Bronia Hartley, ruled her death could have been prevented if action was taken - finding concerns about the wall were repeatedly raised in the years leading up to the incident.

‌



In a prevention of future deaths report published today, Ms Hartley said Mrs Berry’s husband reported the bowing wall nearly eight years before her death. The home was an end-of-terrace rental property owned by landlord S&G Properties (No 2) Limited, and overseen by property management company KMPM.

The property showed signs of cavity wall tie erosion as early as 2013, Ms Hartley’s report said. Mr Berry reported concerns to the property’s previous managing agent, but his report “fell by the wayside” when a new managing agent, Kaye Mackenzie, took over. A property manager from Kaye Mackenzie visited the property in August 2013, and recorded in his notes: “Gable wall big bulge in wall - needs urgent repointing/+rebuild.” The same manager visited the property again in March 2016, and noted that the gable “needs repointing”. The manager retired when Kaye Mackenzie was wound up in January 2020.

One of the former partners continued the property management side of the business as the company KMPM. The bulge in the gable wall was pointed out again in around February or March 2021 to a gas engineer who was at the property to install a new boiler, but no works were carried out, Ms Hartley wrote. She said in her report: “There was no monitoring of, and no structural engineer or quantity surveyor was instructed to investigate, the defective brickwork.” After Mrs Berry’s death, investigations revealed the bowing had been caused by “the complete failure” of a series of wall ties in the upper part of the cavity wall below the gable wall. The inquest heard evidence that the wall’s eventual collapse was “inevitable” without the necessary repairs, and that it was unlikely to have lasted another winter had it not collapsed when it did, the report said.

Article continues below

Ms Hartley wrote: “I found that any reasonably competent property management company and/or responsible landlord would, at the very least, have ensured that the wall was monitored for any signs of progression and, by no later than 2018, would have ensured that a structural survey was performed.” She added that had such investigations happened, the collapse which caused Mrs Berry’s death would have been prevented. The coroner found neither the landlord not the property management company followed government guidance designed to minimise potential hazards. Ms Hartley said no clear systems were in place to prevent a similar incident from happening again, “namely the development of a serious hazard during a tenancy which, as in the deceased’s case, is reported but is not appropriately or timeously responded to, or which is not identified by the tenant”. Neither company carried out a post-incident evaluation to assess whether their properties were free from serious, outstanding hazards which have not come to the attention of the local authority, she added. In their response, a director of S&G Properties (No 2) Limited, whose name has been redacted, said Mrs Berry’s death was “a terrible tragedy and one which has caused me considerable sadness”.

The company said it had made ”significant changes” since the incident, including arrangements for independent inspections to be carried out for all its residential properties.

In its response, KMPM said: “KMPM has undertaken a comprehensive review of its property management procedures and has introduced a number of significant changes to its inspection, hazard identification, escalation, compliance monitoring and project management procedures.”

News.title: Abducted British mum, 47, found in daring Malawi rescue as police officer shot
News.content:
Abducted British mum, 47, found in daring Malawi rescue as police officer shot

Nusrat Osman, from Leicester, was abducted from a neighbourhood in Blantyre, Malawi, as African police said the motive for the kidnapping was unclear

View 2 Images Nusrat Osman has been found

A British mum who was kidnapped in Malawi, Africa, has been rescued.

‌



Nusrat Osman, 47 and from Leicester, was abducted on September 11 at lunchtime in the southern city of Blantyre, with Malawi police saying they were looking for four men who had used a grey car to kidnap her.

‌



The motive was not clear and the suspects made no contact with the woman's family. She was taken in broad daylight after the school run.

‌



Inspector General Richard Luhanga, the head of the Malawi police, told The Associated Press that the mother was safe but declined to give more details.

Ms Osman's brother, Shobi Jiwa, said she was rescued in an operation during which police officer Dr Noel Kayira was shot and wounded.

View 2 Images Nusrat Osman - Brit mum abducted after school run in Malawi as devastated family beg for her return

‌



Noah Woods confirmed dead as police say body pulled from pond is tragic 3-year-old READ MORE :

Speaking to the Sun, Mr Jiwa said: "He is the hero of our family. He’s the hero of the country. He’s the hero of the world, actually, for putting his life at risk and taking a bullet into himself for my sister."

Mr Luhanga said a statement on the rescue operation will be issued in due course. It's unclear if any arrests have been made at this stage.

Ms Osman, who has two young children and works as an auditor, is said to not be "too shaken" after the events, her brother added. He described her as a "humble soul and a beautiful person".

Article continues below

Nusrat, originally from Leicester, works as an auditor in Malawi after moving to the African country when her husband set up a business there.

Speaking to Nyasa Times, he said: "I don’t know where she is or how she is. My wife is an auditor and I have no issues with anyone."

Malawi authorities put out a reward of more than £12,700 for information that could lead to the mum's rescue and the arrest and conviction of the kidnappers.

News.title: Greater Manchester school sends warning to parents as man seen recording pupil
News.content:
Greater Manchester school sends warning to parents as man seen recording pupil

A man described as 'bald and in his fifties or sixties' was reportedly spotted recording a pupil on Clover Road in Timperley, Greater Manchester, outside Wellington School

View Image The incident took place in the vicinity of Wellington School in Timperley (Image: Google Street View)

Parents of students at a school in Greater Manchester have been asked to be vigilant after a man was reportedly seen following and recording a pupil.

‌



The incident allegedly took place outside Wellington School, a mixed secondary and sixth form in Timperley.

‌



An email sent to parents described the man as "a bald male in his fifties or sixties".

‌



The warning added that he appeared to be recording the student in question on his phone.

It read: "We want to make all parents and carers aware of a report that an adult male in the area was seen on Clover Road yesterday appearing to follow a student and record them with his phone.

Couple jailed over ‘depraved’ plans to sexually abuse young girl in Wales READ MORE :

Met Office names areas facing heavy rain on Friday with 19 counties at risk READ MORE :

"He has been described as a bald male in his fifties or sixties, wearing glasses and a dark tracksuit."

‌



The school added that the incident has been reported to the police, Manchester Evening News reports.

The message continued: "Staff on the school gates have been alerted to this report so that they can remain vigilant as students are leaving site."

Parents have also been urged to contact the school should they have any further concerns and report any similar incidents to the police.

Article continues below

The concerning incident quickly attracted reaction from parents on social media, as the email was shared in an Altrincham Facebook group. The poster urged: "Please make your children aware."

One user replied: "These warnings feel far too frequent these days, so worrying."

Mirror Online has approached Greater Manchester Police for comment.

News.title: Remains found after wildfire identified as mother-of-three missing since 2019
News.content:
Human remains discovered in woodland in south-west London following a wildfire have been identified as a woman who has been missing since 2019.

Mother-of-three Joanne Sheen, then aged 44, was last seen when she travelled from Fareham to Southampton with a friend on 5 December 2019.

Metropolitan Police officers were called to Padstow Walk in Feltham on 12 August after bones were discovered in an area of shrubland damaged by a fire the previous week.

A 56-year-old man from Southampton has been arrested on suspicion of conspiracy to commit murder and he remains in police custody.

Detectives in London have now handed the investigation over to Hampshire Police after the remains were identified as those of Sheen.

Sheen's disappearance sparked a major police investigation, which the force described as "long and complex".

News.title: Charles 'sounded giddily elated' after Diana died, Earl Spencer claims
News.content:
Earl Spencer, brother of Diana, Princess of Wales, has claimed King Charles "sounded giddily elated" when he called him after her death in 1997.

In a controversial book about Diana, he alleged the then-Prince Charles sounded like a "lottery winner" after the news.

Buckingham Palace strongly pushed back on Wednesday against the credibility of the book after an initial extract claimed Charles had said of Diana: "We'll forget her soon enough."

A spokesperson said: "While we do not comment on books as a matter of principle, His Majesty is mindful that the pain of fraternal grief can cloud reason, affect judgment and colour memory in ways others do not recognise, even many years after such a loss."

The latest claims are once again highly personal in their attacks on King Charles and the royals, interpreting their motives in a very harsh light.

The evidence is Earl Spencer's own recollection of conversations about that emotional time around his sister's death, almost 30 years ago.

What remains to be seen is how the public might respond to the allegations, whether they might support this book as a new and different Spencer perspective, or whether they might feel it to be inappropriate to be sharing such private disputes.

Representatives of Prince Harry have said they do not want to comment on the book and Buckingham Palace has pointed back to its response from Wednesday, when it rejected the account of Prince Charles in the wake of Diana's death in Paris.

News.title: War may be coming. Are we psychologically ready?
News.content:
If the UK suddenly found itself at war, would you know what to do? Do you know what would be expected of you?

The Government wants us all to start preparing for severe disruption to our lives. It wants us to stockpile canned food and drinking water, strengthen our civic resilience, and plan for the possibility of war.

Work has begun on the government's so-called "war book", which hasn't been updated in decades.

The UK's most senior soldier has sounded the alarm. The Chief of the Defence Staff Sir Richard Knighton this week said the threat from Russia meant Britain was living through the "most dangerous" period of his 35-year career in the armed forces.

But what is the threat? In 1940 the danger of a German invasion of the UK was very real. But the chances of Russian tanks rolling up Whitehall are surely negligible.

"It's not the tanks you need to worry about," says historian Margaret MacMillan, author of War: How Conflict Shaped Us.

"It's the cutting of cables on the ocean floor. It's the hacking into systems on which so many things depend. The possibility for asymmetric war, for cyber war, is growing by leaps and bounds."

But are we ready? After 80 years without war on our own soil, are we, as a society, psychologically prepared for it? Are we ready to approve large increases in defence spending, and for the sacrifices that that might entail in other areas of our national life? Or does the threat seem too far-fetched to be real?

News.title: New wild cat species discovered - with only one known living member
News.content:
A spotted cat from the forests of Bolivia has been confirmed as a new species.

The small feline, about the size of a domestic moggy, went under the radar because it was confused with other wild cats that share similar spots and stripes.

But DNA studies show the cat is actually in a class of its own, highlighting how much remains unknown about some of the world's most elusive mammals.

Scientists hope the discovery will draw attention to the conservation of tiger cats, a group of small wild cats found in South and Central America that receives far less public attention than their larger cousins like lions, leopards and tigers.

News.title: US fans with Ed Sheeran tickets are left 'torn' by Macklemore controversy
News.content:
The snowballing controversy over pro-Palestinian rapper Macklemore being dropped as a support act for Ed Sheeran has plunged the tour into crisis and left concert-goers in the middle of the fraught Israel-Gaza debate.

Fans who spoke to the BBC - including those who have tickets to see Sheeran's next show - have been split since Macklemore was dropped from the Loop Tour this week after his "free Palestine" protest on stage.

All of Sheeran's opening acts have since quit in solidarity.

"I'm still torn," Damien Given told the BBC on whether he would attend Sheeran's show on Saturday, calling the artist's response disingenuous. Another fan called it a "no-win situation".

Since the controversy blew up earlier this week, ticket prices, external for his remaining shows in the US, Mexico and South America have dropped, as calls for boycotts spread.

Sheeran has responded, saying he's been "appalled by the conflict between Israel and Palestine", but would not be drawn into a political debate.

News.title: Watch: Can humpback whales experience grief?
News.content:
Humpback whale mothers may experience grief when their calves die, a rare observation led by Griffith University and Sea World Foundation has found.

The BBC's Tiffanie Turnbull explains everything you need to know about the sighting off Australia's Gold Coast, and why it's so rare.

News.title: Badenoch says she is bringing in lawyers to challenge government after Tory-run council's 94% tax hike
News.content:
Conservative leader Kemi Badenoch has said she has brought in lawyers to challenge the government over local funding cuts, after a record council tax rise in one of her party's flagship local authorities.

She told BBC Newsnight the proposed 94% hike in Wandsworth, a south-west London borough run by the Tories, was "outrageous".

Badenoch said the Conservative Party had "instructed lawyers" to explore if an Â£84m-a-year government funding cut, which Wandsworth Council has blamed for the increase, can be blocked.

The government has insisted it needs to reform the "outdated" council funding system to move money to where it is most needed.

Wandsworth has long had one of the lowest council tax rates in the country, with an average Band D property currently paying just over Â£1,000, compared to above Â£2,000 in an increasing number of London boroughs.

But this would nearly double with the planned Â£958 rise - half of which is set by the council and the other half the mayor of London.

There has been heavy criticism since the move was announced in a council meeting on Tuesday. A final decision is to be made early next year.

Commenting for the first time on the row, Badenoch accused ministers of seemingly "taking money from areas that don't vote Labour and giving it to places that do vote Labour".

"I think it is outrageous that Wandsworth Council is having to put up council tax.

"But they're not doing it because they want to. It is because the government has taken away 40% of their funding.

"So we have actually instructed lawyers, as the Conservative Party, to see if we can challenge the government on this decision."

News.title: Father's tribute to 'sweetest little boy' Noah Woods
News.content:
People from as far afield as Birmingham and Hampshire turned up to help with the search for Noah, who was from nearby East Bergholt.

Helicopters, dog units and members of the public had been scouring the area, close to the River Stour on the Suffolk-Essex border.

Reflecting on the community response, Woods wrote in his Facebook post: "It seems he has made an impact across the whole nation.

"You have all taken Noah into your own hearts, with all the overwhelming help, we were all just trying to bring him home to us safe and sound."

He thanked everyone who came together to search for "our boy" - listing emergency services, businesses and venues in the village - and "all of the people who gave up their time in their busy schedules to help us when we most needed it".

"The compassion shown by all of you will never be forgotten by us, and brought us comfort and strength at the darkest time of our lives."

He finished the post by addressing his son.

"It has been a privilege to be your parents and be able to have packed so much love in the short three years you were with us."

Suffolk Police said his death was not being treated as suspicious, but that officers still had inquiries to complete before submitting a file for the coroner.

Supt Tom Pearse thanked the family for their "patience and understanding throughout the searches".

"It was clear from the media coverage we saw that they not only had all of Suffolk behind them, but an outpouring of goodwill from across the entire country and beyond.

"I know how grateful Noah's family are for all the support and kind messages they have received, but would reiterate our plea to now allow them the time, space and privacy they need at this deeply distressing time."

News.title: Not just 'Nice Guy Eddie': Lib Dems eager for leader to show radical side at party conference
News.content:
Discontent bubbles not far from the surface as the Liberal Democrats gather for their conference this weekend.

Two years on from their best ever general election result, conversations with those on the party's frontbench, its MPs, and backroom staff reveal a frustration at what many see as a failure to capitalise on that success.

Polling by YouGov in the build up to the conference highlighted the Lib Dems "have seen no real growth in support since the last general election" and if anything have slipped back.

"We lack the ability to say something new or interesting," said one senior Lib Dem MP.

"There is no energy, no excitement."

A frontbencher said: "With the possible exception of our position on Trump, you could characterise most of our press lines as 'a Lib Dem spokesperson said, steady on now, gently does it'."

Others describe the party's approach as "boring" and are spooked by the rise of the Green Party under Zack Polanski.

The party's leadership are aware of the anger. They insist this conference will be a "gear shift".

Daisy Cooper, the deputy leader, told me it would be "a gloves-off kind of conference".

"You'll see a bit of fighting talk," she said.

Some of the caution until now has been deliberate. The party's leadership met over the last few months and discussed whether to copy Polanski's punchy, social media-focused style but decided it wouldn't appeal to the well-heeled areas of southern England that form the Lib Dem heartlands.

Those involved in that decision point to Polanski's recent struggles and feel vindicated.

But at all levels of the party there is an acknowledgement they lag behind other parties on grabbing attention on social media, highlighted by Andy Burnham's "social first" approach.

The party has only recently rolled out training for its MPs on making social videos, something senior figures despair at.

"When we have a success we're very good at getting a leaflet sent out to supporters straight away," one senior MP said. "But we don't do that for socials."

Digital and social media will be a focus of at least 17 fringe events at conference, as the party tries to improve its online communications.

But others worry that social media is just the medium and the problem is with the message.

News.title: Sunshine to return to parts of UK with warmer and drier weather on way
News.content:
Don't pack away your summer clothes just yet as warmer and drier weather could be set to return to the UK next week.

Temperatures could reach as high as 25C in parts of England and Wales - several degrees above the average for the time of year.

Forecasts for early next week show an area of high pressure building near the UK. This will largely block Atlantic weather systems, which often bring wind and rain, from reaching the country.

North-west Scotland will see some rain but these systems are not expected to push across the rest of the UK, so this would mean drier weather with lighter winds and higher daytime temperatures for most.

The last few weeks have been very changeable with rain and strong winds in most parts of the UK.

Despite this, the whole of Wales and most of England are still in drought.

After stronger south-westerly winds are due to blow cloud and outbreaks of rain across from the west on Friday, the weather will start to settle down over the weekend.

The northern half of the UK will see a return to sunshine and blustery showers on Saturday, with most of the showers being in Scotland.

The southern half of the UK is likely to be more cloudy and have a muggy feel with the chance of light rain and drizzle.

News.title: Ukrainian guilty of vandalism at mosques linked to Russian network behind Starmer arson attack
News.content:
A Ukrainian man has pleaded guilty to spraying abusive graffiti on mosques in east London, in a case linked to the Russian state network behind arson attacks against the former prime minister Sir Keir Starmer.

Illia Bilyk, 21, entered guilty pleas at Thames Magistrates' Court to five counts of racially and religiously aggravated criminal damage.

Bilyk sprayed graffiti on the Stratford Islamic Association, Al-Birr Mosque and Leyton Jamia Masjid on 23 January 2025. Two days later he targeted Noor Ul Islam Primary School and the Islamic Shariah Council.

The BBC has learned that Bilyk told police he was recruited into spraying the graffiti by a Russian speaker after being approached on the messaging app Telegram.

Bilyk said the Russian speaker told him where to target and paid him afterwards.

In June this year two Ukrainians - Roman Lavrynovych and Stanislav Carpiuc - were jailed for conspiring to carry out arson attacks targeting a property and a car connected to prime minister Sir Keir Starmer.

An investigation by the BBC and Hope not Hate revealed that Russia was behind the arson attacks and had also generated Islamophobic vandalism throughout London, including on the east London venues which Biluyk has now admitted vandalising.

News.title: Archbishop of Canterbury withdraws award from Muslim cleric who praised Osama bin Laden
News.content:
The Archbishop of Canterbury has withdrawn an award given to a Muslim cleric who praised Osama Bin Laden.

Hafiz Muhammad Tahir Mehmood Ashrafi received the award for reconciliation and interfaith cooperation from Dame Sarah Mullally last week, on the 25th anniversary of the 9/11 attacks.

Lambeth Palace faced a backlash after it emerged Ashrafi praised Bin Laden - the architect of the 2001 attacks - as someone who had "been fighting for Islam against the Russians, Americans and British", in comments from 2007.

Ashrafi also reportedly said he would give Bin Laden the title Saifullah, which means "Sword of God". He told the BBC his remarks had been "totally taken out of context".

Lambeth Palace now says "comments made by Imam Ashrafi have come to light that have led (us) to reconsider this award and we can now confirm that the award has been withdrawn".

In presenting the award last week, the Archbishop's office said Ashrafi was being honoured for "his outstanding work as an ambassador of interfaith harmony in Pakistan, known for his commitment to promoting religious tolerance".

His award was presented by Dame Sarah in a ceremony that coincided with the 25th anniversary of the 9/11 attacks in the US in which nearly 3,000 people were killed.

Ashrafi told the BBC that his remarks had been "totally taken out of context" and the backlash had been "an unfair campaign" against him.

He said that he was only speaking about Bin Laden in 2007 in response to "the hurt felt by many Muslims" over a knighthood being awarded to the Satanic Verses author Sir Salman Rushdie.

But he defended the comparison he made between an author and a man who was behind the deaths of thousands of people.

Criticism of Ashrafi has gone beyond his comments about Bin Laden.

In giving him his award for promoting interfaith harmony last week, Lambeth Palace had cited the fact that Ashrafi had intervened in the 2012 case of Rimsha Masih, a young Christian girl in Pakistan falsely accused of blasphemy.

But Ashrafi has otherwise been supportive of Pakistan's blasphemy laws that have led to an estimated 2000 people being prosecuted since the late 1980s.

They include a disproportionately high number of Pakistan's minority Christians and Ahmadis in particular, but many majority Sunni Muslims too.

Ashrafi claimed the blasphemy laws actually "save lives", stopping people taking matters into their own hands.

But Human Rights Watch said last year that "the laws perpetuate religious discrimination and are used to target the poor and minorities in unlawful evictions and land grabs".

The organisation has called on the Pakistani government to urgently reform the laws to prevent them "being weaponised to [...] attack marginalised communities".

News.title: Healey to ask EU finance ministers to let UK into 'Made in Europe' industry scheme
News.content:
The chancellor is to warn the European Union (EU) not to lock the UK out of its scheme to protect industries from unfair Chinese competition.

John Healey will push for closer UK-EU partnerships on tech, defence, and manufacturing at a meeting of EU finance ministers in Dublin on Friday.

But he will call on the EU to design its "Made in Europe" programme in a way that deepens ties with the UK "rather than erecting new barriers", Treasury sources told the BBC.

Officials said Healey will tell European finance ministers it is important to "learn lessons" after talks collapsed last year for Britain to join an EU defence loans scheme.

That dispute centred on how much money the UK would pay to join.

The "Made in Europe" policy, officially called the Industrial Accelerator Act (IAA), is currently being considered by the bloc and aims to protect EU manufacturing with restrictions on goods from outside countries.

There is concern in government the scheme could lock British firms out of European supply chains.

Treasury officials said Healey wanted to reduce the economic impact of Brexit and build closer ties with the EU, but not at any cost to the UK.

Healey said: "The next chapter of Britain's growth story will be written in more places.

"To me, closer ties with the EU means British businesses â wherever they are based across the UK â get better access to both the supply chains and the customers they need to grow."

Healey will use the meeting in Dublin to focus on tech firms, defence companies, and manufacturing.

"The chancellor wants to make sure nothing holds them back," a Treasury source said.

It comes after a reset summit with the EU was delayed after Sir Keir Starmer's resignation as prime minister.

Treasury sources now expect that to take place in November.

Healey's meeting in Dublin comes after it emerged earlier this week that he is in discussions about joining a global investment bank aimed at raising more money for defence spending.

He is considering a bid to join the Defence, Security and Resilience Bank (DSRB), not long after his predecessor Rachel Reeves rejected the idea.

Canada has been leading efforts to establish the bank, which supporters say would enable governments to borrow at lower costs to increase military spending.

Paying for the UK's growing defence commitments is one of Healey's biggest headaches as he prepares for the Budget in October and next year's spending review.

News.title: UK Youth Parliament looks set to be axed
News.content:
The UK Youth Parliament is at risk of being axed within months, BBC News has learned, as the government is not committing to funding it any longer.

The parliament was launched in 2000 to boost interest in politics among young people and has more than 300 elected members aged between 11 and 18.

Once a year, the young politicians are allowed to hold debates in the House of Commons chamber, on a day when MPs are not sitting.

Some MPs and young people say axing it would be a blow for youth democracy, while others say it is not providing value for money.

The Department of Culture, Media and Sport (DCMS), which funds the parliament each year with taxpayer cash, is not committing to giving any more grants to it.

A spokesperson for the DCMS praised the youth parliament's "important legacy... giving elected young people a national platform to represent their peers, engage with decision-makers and develop confidence, leadership and skills for life and work".

It received Â£453,000 in taxpayer funding in the last year alone with about Â£2.4m public money spent on it among other youth initiatives between 2017 and 2024.

While no final decision has been made on funding beyond March 2027, a government source said: "The government has not committed to continuing the programme in its current form."

UK Youth Parliament insiders told the BBC that without government funding, it is likely to close.

It follows a government review, external published in October last year, which concluded that while the parliament was delivering on its intended goals, only a quarter of young people know about it - and some schools felt "excluded from the process".

The government says it is working with young people and youth organisations to design a new scheme that increases their involvement in democracy and decision-making, with further announcements to be made this autumn.

Any new scheme will have a "particular focus on under-represented groups", a government source said.

Bobby Forbes, the recently departed chair of the UK Youth Parliament's Youth Select Committee, which works with officials in Westminster, said it gives teenagers "a direct way to scrutinise government and hold decision-makers to account".

News.title: King Charles warns of 'existential danger' of AI falling into wrong hands
News.content:
King Charles has warned AI executives of the "existential dangers" posed by the technology falling into the wrong hands.

He made the comments at a summit he had convened at Dumfries House in Ayrshire to discuss how the tech can be used to benefit society.

Those gathered at the meeting also included Kanishka Narayan, the UK's AI Minister, the Pope's advisor, and participants from AI giants such as Nvidia, OpenAI and Anthropic.

It comes amid a series of recent warnings from people inside the industry about the rapidly evolving capabilities of advanced or "frontier" AI models and the regulation needed to keep them in check.

"Those who have created these technologies are now increasingly warning that AI risks developing darker capacities - perhaps even to take life," the King told the executives.

He said there seemed to be an "urgency" in "adequately considering the existential dangers of such technologies falling into the wrong hands, and being used in potentially catastrophic ways".

"The task before you is not merely to advance technology, but to ensure that it remains firmly in the service of humanity, community and the natural world," he told the group.

The summit has been called to consider whether a "shared set of principles" can be developed to "help guide the future application" of AI.

News.title: Interest rates held but Bank signals rise if energy prices stay high
News.content:
The Bank of England has held interest rates at their current rate of 3.75% for the sixth time in a row but said they were likely to rise if high energy prices persist.

The US-Israel war with Iran has disrupted global energy supplies leading to a sharp increase in petrol and diesel prices and an uptick in inflation.

But Bank of England governor Andrew Bailey said energy price volatility made it more likely that interest rates would rise.

The Bank also announced it was slowing its sales of UK government debt, prompting an easing in the UK's long-term borrowing costs.

The Bank of England's main interest rate is a crucial benchmark for banks and other lenders in setting interest rates for individuals and businesses who want to borrow or save money. Higher rates can help dampen inflationary pressures, while lower rates can help boost spending and investment.

The UK's central bank aims to keep inflation at a target of 2%, but it has been above that rate for nearly two years, with inflation hitting 3.1% in August.

On Thursday the Bank of England raised its forecast for inflation predicting it would be "slightly above 4%" at the start of next year. It warned that the price cap on household gas and electricity bills for January was "now expected to rise substantially further".

Speaking after the Bank's decision, Bailey said the direct impact of higher energy prices was clear, but officials were still assessing how far those costs would feed through into wider inflation across the economy.

News.title: AI-assisted air traffic control is coming to some of the nation’s busiest skies
News.content:

Whether it's investigating the financials of Elon Musk's pro-Trump PAC or producing our latest documentary, 'The A Word', which shines a light on the American women fighting for reproductive rights, we know how important it is to parse out the facts from the messaging. At such a critical moment in US history, we need reporters on the ground. Your donation allows us to keep sending journalists to speak to both sides of the story. We believe quality journalism should be available to everyone, paid for by those who can afford it. Your support makes all the difference. Read more

Federal officials plan to launch an artificial intelligence-powered system in the Washington, D.C., area as early as Monday, the first step in a broader push to modernize U.S. air traffic management.

The software — known as Smart, or Strategic Management of Airspace, Routes and Trajectories — is designed to analyze flight schedules, weather forecasts, airport runway capacity and operational limits to predict traffic flows and spot potential bottlenecks ahead of time.

Developed by Air Space Intelligence under an $875 million, 12-year government contract awarded earlier this year, the tool is intended to function as a central intelligence center for the nation’s airspace once fully operational, as reported by The Wall Street Journal. The primary goal is to help the Federal Aviation Administration and major carriers navigate schedule disruptions, cutting down on delays and cancellations.

Though industry insiders previously anticipated a broader initial release after months of planning, government officials told the publication that the rollout was always meant to begin on a limited scale.

In its current phase, Smart will serve as a decision-support tool during operational disruptions. Future iterations are expected to handle complex tasks, such as managing flight arrival intervals and mapping out routes days in advance.

open image in gallery Federal officials are set to launch an artificial intelligence-powered system in the Washington, DC, area as early as Monday, marking the initial phase of a broader effort to modernize US air traffic management ( Getty Images )

As part of the launch, federal authorities plan to open a centralized office for the program at the Transportation Department’s headquarters on Monday.

The initiative comes amid a broader push by the Trump administration to modernize the country’s aging aviation infrastructure through multi-billion-dollar technology investments and expanded controller hiring to address persistent staffing shortages.

However, the transition presents coordination challenges. The FAA has been holding talks with commercial carriers regarding schedule alignment, though industry representatives have raised concerns over how the automated system will operate amid intense market competition for peak flight slots.

open image in gallery Federal officials are set to launch an artificial intelligence-powered system in the Washington, DC, area as early as Monday, marking the initial phase of a broader effort to modernize US air traffic management ( Getty )

During Senate testimony earlier this year, FAA Administrator Bryan Bedford addressed the need for structural change in airspace management.

“The way we manage traffic today is chaotic, and we can do better,” Bedford said. “We need to manage that at the FAA, rather than rely on commercial airlines to simply schedule however they want.”

Despite operational questions, industry advocates have welcomed the technology. Airlines for America, a trade association representing major domestic carriers, told The Wall Street Journal that the software offered significant potential to boost safety, expand airspace capacity and enhance overall efficiency.

The organization described the project as “one of the most exciting and bold initiatives taken on by the FAA in decades.”

News.content:

A majority of independent voters in Texas have said the Republican midterm convention in Dallas last week made no impact on their excitement to cast their ballot, despite President Donald Trump calling the event a “winner.”

The Republican Party, like the Democratic Party, typically holds a convention every four years where it announces its nominees for president and their running mate. But in an unusual move, Trump headlined a two-day conference to drum up support for GOP candidates ahead of November’s midterms.

Trump raved about the event’s success, saying it was “a solidly sold out winner for Republicans” — despite reports of many empty seats — in a Truth Social post Monday. “Should have a big impact on November 3rd,” he predicted.

But 68 percent of independent voters in Texas — a key target for Republicans and Democrats in general elections — said the convention made no impact on their excitement to vote, according to a new The Hill/Emerson poll.

The convention did galvanize Trump’s own party, with 59 percent of Texas Republican voters saying that the event made them more excited to vote. Fifty-three percent of Texas Democratic voters, however, were also more eager to cast their ballot following the convention — presumably against GOP candidates.

open image in gallery A majority of independent voters in Texas have said the Republican midterm convention in Dallas last week made no impact on their excitement to cast their ballot, despite President Donald Trump calling it a 'winner' ( AFP via Getty Images )

There’s a particularly competitive race in Texas as the state’s Republican Attorney General Ken Paxton and his Democratic opponent James Talarico vie for a U.S. Senate seat.

While the convention was meant to boost support for candidates like Paxton, Trump insulted the Republican during his speech for two nights in a row.

The president took issue with Paxton’s fashion sense, telling the crowd Wednesday night, “He may not dress right. He may not talk exactly perfectly, and he may not be the best-looking guy I've ever seen, but you know what he is? He's the greatest Attorney General in America, and he deserves to be your next senator.”

Paxton and Talarico remained neck and neck in the new poll taken after the convention. Talarico had 47 percent of support from Texas voters and Paxton had 46 percent.

open image in gallery Sixty-eight percent of independent voters in Texas — a key target for Republicans and Democrats in general elections — said the convention made no impact on their excitement to vote ( Getty Images )

During his Wednesday night address, Trump also promised that his administration would pay a “Trump Dividend” to each American adult if voters helped Republicans keep the majority in Congress.

“So if the Republicans win, you win with us, and you get $5,000,” Trump said.

Critics accused the president of bribery while others questioned where the money would come from.

Treasury Secretary Scott Bessent said he believed the Trump administration can find a way to pay for the $5,000 checks without adding to the nation’s $40 trillion debt, but remained tight-lipped about the details.

“I’m not ready to discuss it at present, but at Treasury we’ve been working on it for quite a while,” Bessent said.

open image in gallery There were concerns ahead of the convention that Trump, with low approval ratings, would hurt GOP candidates' campaigns more than help them ( AFP via Getty Images )

There were concerns ahead of the convention that Trump, with low approval ratings, would hurt GOP candidates' campaigns more than help them.

Trump had a net approval rating of negative 18 percent in a new The Economist/YouGov poll.

His administration has been dogged by an unpopular war in Iran that has raised gas prices for Americans and a massive immigration crackdown that has been criticized as too aggressive.

Fifty-two percent of Americans disapproved of Trump’s handling of immigration compared to 45 percent who approved, according to the survey from The Economist and YouGov.

His approval rating for his handling of Iran was even bleaker, with 60 percent disapproving of his job on the issue and 33 percent backing it.
