World.title: Virginia Governor Abigail Spanberger quietly rolls back Youngkin's plans to protect girls' sports
World.content:
Virginia Gov. Abigail Spanberger's administration quietly rolled back proposed protections for girls' sports in the state, without announcing it to the public.

Spanberger’s administration withdrew a proposed regulation that would have prevented biological males from competing on female-only athletic teams and entering certain female-designated spaces, including locker rooms and bathrooms.

The withdrawal occurred July 30, 2026, but received little public attention until September. The administration did not issue a news release or publicly announce the decision.

THE STATES THAT STILL ALLOW TRANS ATHLETES IN WOMEN'S SPORTS FACE QUESTIONS AFTER SUPREME COURT RULING

The change appeared instead on the Virginia Regulatory Town Hall website, which lists the proposed regulations as having been "withdrawn on 07/30/2026 after the comment period had ended."

OutKick has reached out to Spanberger's office for an explanation, but has not received a response.

The proposal had not yet become a finalized regulation. Its withdrawal ended the rulemaking process initiated under former Republican Gov. Glenn Youngkin.

The effort began with a petition filed in April 2025 by female athletes Réka György, Lily Mullens and Carter Satterfield. The petition asked the Virginia State Board of Health to adopt regulations barring biological males from female-only athletic teams and competitions, as well as female spaces in which women and girls could be undressed.

The Virginia High School League changed its eligibility policy in February 2025 to restrict participation in girls’ sports to students whose biological sex is female. The organization oversees most public high school athletic competitions in Virginia.

Virginia’s Department of Education also issued model policies under Youngkin in 2023 directing public schools to generally separate athletic teams and intimate facilities on the basis of biological sex. Those policies state that school divisions should provide reasonable accommodations to students while preserving the availability of sex-separated bathrooms, locker rooms and other facilities.



Implementation of the state’s model policies has varied among local school divisions, contributing to a prolonged dispute over transgender policies in Virginia schools. The issue has been especially contentious in Northern Virginia, where disagreements over bathrooms, locker rooms, pronouns and parental notification have prompted clashes between state officials and local school boards.

The withdrawn Board of Health action would have established a separate regulatory framework reaching organized female sports and sex-separated spaces across Virginia. With the July 30 withdrawal, there are no remaining actions listed under the proposed regulatory chapter. The athletes argued that the participation of biological males in women’s sports and their access to female-designated facilities created physical and psychological harms for women and girls.

In August 2025, the Board of Health unanimously approved the petition by a 14-0 vote and authorized the state to begin developing the regulations.

According to the state’s regulatory website, the proposed rules were intended to "prevent biological males from participating in organized female-only athletic teams and competitions in Virginia" and from entering designated female spaces where women and girls were likely to be in a state of undress.

FROM AUSCHWITZ, HOLOCAUST SURVIVOR ISSUES URGENT WARNING OVER RISING ANTISEMITISM IN CANADA

Huckabee referenced a letter sent to Trump by the National Association of Christian Lawmakers earlier this month calling on the administration to allow Jewish Canadians to more easily obtain visas to enter the U.S.

"I think we've all seen and, frankly, been quite alarmed at some of the extraordinary Jew hatred that is taking place in Canada, and many Canadian Jewish people are really concerned and afraid for their lives," Huckabee said.

"And they fear that they might be the subject of some violent attack or a terror attack. The rhetoric in the country has gotten very, very harsh, and President Trump, as you may remember, took the letter from the NACL, and he published it and said that he would certainly look into it."

BILL MAHER RIPS MACKLEMORE'S GAZA STANCE, SAYS CELEBRITY 'MORAL CONFUSION' IS FUELING ANTISEMITISM

The ambassador also addressed the latest developments in the conflict with Iran, namely the Iran-backed Houthi offensive against Saudi-backed government forces in Yemen.

Asked whether Israel may be interested in assisting Saudi forces in the conflict, Huckabee said Israel has made it clear it wants to improve relations with all of its close neighbors in the Middle East.

"Would Israel be willing to bring some assistance? I think they would. Whether they have been asked? That's something to ask the Saudis or to ask the Israelis. Wouldn't be for me to say what has been done or what has been requested. But there is a growing sense that Israel isn't the problem over here. Israel isn't trying to take anybody else's land," he said.

World.title: Rubio takes behind-the-scenes role on Iran war while keeping his options open for the future
World.content:
WASHINGTON — The talks to end the Iran war had hit a snag.

Vice President JD Vance had flown to Pakistan for negotiations with the Iranians, a sign that the two sides had narrowed their differences and the White House might be poised to announce a breakthrough.

As the marathon April meeting unfolded, though, U.S. negotiators began to worry: It looked like the Iranians were changing the terms of a potential deal. So, during a pause, they phoned Secretary of State Marco Rubio to get a “steer” on what they should do next, an administration official with direct knowledge of the matter said in an interview.

Rubio agreed that they couldn’t accept Iran’s offer, the official said. There would be no deal.

Rubio isn’t the face of the Iran negotiations. He’s kept a discreet public distance as the unpopular war grinds on. Donald Trump’s son-in-law Jared Kushner and the president’s longtime friend and special envoy Steve Witkoff are the main protagonists in the push to end both the Iran and Russia-Ukraine conflicts.

The arrangement is an unusual one. Past secretaries of state commanded the spotlight when it came to war and peace. Henry Kissinger won a Nobel Peace Prize in 1973 for negotiating a ceasefire in the Vietnam War during the Nixon administration. John Kerry, in the Obama administration, flew back and forth between Washington and the Middle East as he tried in vain to broker a peace deal between the Israelis and Palestinians.

Still, Rubio has been a hidden hand throughout, helping craft the Trump administration’s strategy while privately advising the officials who play a more public role in the peace talks.

He holds a unique place in the Cabinet, one of the most expansive in the modern presidency. Rubio doubles as national security adviser — first in an acting capacity, now permanent — meaning he has a spacious office in the West Wing and gets more face time with Trump than most Cabinet members.

This account is based on interviews with 12 present and former administration officials and others close to Rubio and the White House. Many spoke on condition of anonymity to talk freely about internal policy and political dynamics.

“The reason that the American people perhaps don’t see Secretary Rubio as front and center on Iran is because he really does have the rest of the world to worry about and pays enormous attention to the Western Hemisphere and our European allies,” White House chief of staff Susie Wiles told NBC News. “President Trump is so busy and active around the world, it takes more than one person. So, Secretary Rubio is leading the other efforts around the world that are so important to America’s stability and future promise.”

Trump has given Rubio wide latitude, allowing America’s top diplomat to be selective when it comes to the public parts of the job. Rubio was more visible in the early phase of the Iran war than in the later stages. That could prove advantageous down the road.

Polls show widespread American disenchantment with the conflict. As public opinion hardens, Rubio may be better positioned to sidestep any political backlash than Vance, who has attended futile rounds of peace talks in far-flung locales.

Rubio has said publicly that he currently has no plans to run in 2028, and two people familiar with the matter have told NBC News he has also said that privately. He has acknowledged behind closed doors that the landscape may be tough for Republicans in 2028 and suggested that a presidential run in 2032 or 2036 may be more promising, a person close to him said.

But Rubio’s comments don’t close the door completely. A second person close to him said that he has not ruled out a potential 2028 presidential run, but he is not discussing his future plans.

“Nobody knows what he’s going to do,” the source said. “Political calculation does not factor into literally anything that he’s doing right now.”

Another consideration is personal. Rubio has also said privately that after nearly three decades in public office he may want to take a job in the private sector when Trump’s term ends, two people familiar with the matter told NBC News.

His financial disclosure form shows his net worth to be no more than $240,000 apart from his house, listed in a range between $1 million and $5 million. Those are modest sums in an administration packed with officials worth $100 million or more.

Rubio could readily land a lucrative job that would be a boon to himself, his wife and their four children if he sat out the race, and at 55, he is young enough to mount a campaign later on.

Relationship with Trump

Once angry rivals, Rubio and Trump have developed a good rapport. Rubio may be in and out of the Oval Office five or six times a day, a White House official told NBC News. Both love sports, and they’ve been overheard jawing about baseball batting averages or a knockout punch in the latest mixed martial arts match, the official said.

Olivia Wales, a White House spokesperson, said in a prepared statement: “As President Trump says, Marco Rubio will go down as one of the greatest Secretaries of State in history. The president and Secretary Rubio have successfully restored American dominance on the world stage and are relentlessly working to advance our foreign policy interests.”

After spending 14 years in the Senate, Rubio grasps the politics and legislative tactics needed to pass bills into law and will advise the president on ways to push his agenda through Congress, the official said.

“I can think of many times in which we’re talking about whatever he [Trump] is focused on that day and he’ll say, ‘What do you think, Marco?’ I’ve heard that more times than I can count,” a person close to the White House said. “They jell well together. I’ve seen people who don’t jell well with the president, and Marco is not one of those people.”

Rubio gets more face time with President Donald Trump than most Cabinet members. Kent Nishimura / AFP via Getty Images

Rubio’s influence in the peace talks is largely behind the scenes. Witkoff checks in with him before agreeing to attend negotiating sessions, takes guidance before meetings and briefs him afterward, the administration official said.

Last weekend, the two men spoke by phone multiple times about an escalating conflict involving Iran and Yemen. On Saturday, Witkoff reached Rubio while the secretary of state was at the University of Florida football stadium in Gainesville, watching his son play for the Gators, the official said.

Leaving the Senate last year to work for Trump was a gamble for Rubio. The two faced off in the 2016 Republican presidential primaries, where they one-upped each other in schoolyard taunts. Trump derided the Florida lawmaker as “Little Marco.” Rubio mocked the New York businessman’s hand size.

Time and pragmatic politics have transformed the rivalry into a partnership. The Senate confirmed Rubio by a vote of 99-0, a feat that has impressed even Trump.

“It’s not an easy job to be both the secretary of state and the national security adviser, but Secretary Rubio has managed it beautifully,” Wiles said. “He is an experienced, smart and intuitive adviser to the president and the rest of the team, be it national security or foreign affairs.”

Venezuela and a legacy

Other Cabinet secretaries have flamed out since Trump began his second term. Attorney General Pam Bondi is gone, as are Homeland Security Secretary Kristi Noem, Labor Secretary Lori Chavez-DeRemer and Director of National Intelligence Tulsi Gabbard.

Rubio, by contrast, has thrived in a job that aligns with his political and policy interests. One of his main priorities is building American clout in the Western Hemisphere, where he is leaving an imprint.

He helped forge an oil deal with Venezuela this summer that the Trump administration believes will buoy both the U.S. and Venezuelan economies.

Earlier this month, Rubio met with heads of state in Latin America as he sought to combat illegal immigration and drug trafficking.

The son of Cuban émigrés, he is also driving the administration’s effort to transform Cuba and bring an end to the regime in Havana.

If he can nudge Venezuela and Cuba toward democratic governance, that could be an enviable legacy for a secretary of state who is nursing presidential ambitions.

Rubio’s statement to a Colombian radio station earlier this month that he currently has “no plans” to mount another campaign was not a hard-and-fast denial. Even if it was, it might not matter. When Rubio first ran for president, he made clear he was done with the Senate. And he sounded adamant.

“I have only said like 10000 times I will be a private citizen in January,” he wrote on social media in May 2016, two months after he dropped out of the presidential contest. The following month, he did an about-face, ran for re-election and won.

If Vance enters the race and falters in the Republican primaries, Rubio might jump in the contest, the second person close to Rubio said.

Another possibility would be for Rubio to become Vance’s running mate, something he would be inclined to do if asked, this person said. Trump himself has suggested the two men pair up in 2028, and his opinion counts given his grip on the Republican base.

Trump likes to ask people privately who they think should be the GOP nominee.

“Whoever the Republican nominee is in 2028, Donald Trump will decide,” the White House official said. “Of course, the primary process will run. But the president will have such an outsized influence in it, and I think he does wish they would run together.”

After the midterm elections in November, attention will turn to 2028 and the post-Trump era. Rubio won’t have much time to decide his future.

“If he’s serious about running, he would have to say so reasonably soon,” the White House official said. “Once you’re elected, you never really get rid of that bug. Ultimately, if there’s an opportunity and an opening, you’d be almost fighting your instincts not to do it.”

World.title: ‘Godfather of AI’ warns Congress has ‘maybe a year’ left to regulate AI
World.content:
WASHINGTON — Geoffrey Hinton, a Nobel laureate known as the “Godfather of AI,” issued an ominous warning to lawmakers: Congress may have only one year left to implement safeguards on artificial intelligence before it loses control of it.

“Maybe a year, but not much more than a year,” Hinton said Wednesday evening after he and other AI experts huddled with Senate and House lawmakers behind closed doors. “If you look at predictions for when we’ll get superintelligence,” he continued, “it used to be maybe 30 years, maybe 50 years. Then it came down to maybe 10 years, maybe 20 years. Now people are saying, a lot of the researchers are saying only a few years.”

Hinton and other experts came to Capitol Hill at the invitation of Sen. Bernie Sanders, I-Vt., one of the chamber’s chief critics of AI, who invited lawmakers of both parties to the private briefing. Louisiana Sen. John Kennedy was the only Republican to attend.

01:31 'Godfather of AI': Congress has about a year to get ahead of AI 00:00 00:00

Hinton’s dire warning came as the House departed Washington for the last time before the November midterm elections. And there appeared to be lots of conversations but little sign of progress on any substantial AI regulation in the Senate.

“This is bats--- crazy, insane science fiction stuff that literally happened recently,” Rep. Ted Lieu, D-Calif., a member of House Democratic leadership, told NBC News after Wednesday’s briefing.

Lieu was referring to the Hugging Face incident, when a swarm of OpenAI agents accessed the internet, hacked the platform Hugging Face and tried to cover their tracks to deceive humans about their actions. Hinton, who resigned as a vice president and engineering fellow at Google in 2023 over concerns about AI safety and went on to win the Nobel Prize in physics the following year, called the hack a “little Chernobyl.”

House and Senate lawmakers in both parties, including Sens. Ted Cruz, R-Texas, and Maria Cantwell, D-Wash., have rolled out legislation seeking to halt or slow down AI development in the last few years, though none has gone anywhere to date. Al Drago / Bloomberg via Getty Imagesfile

“AI has now reached the point where AI is designing better AI,” Hinton told reporters after the briefing. “That’s called recursive self-improvement. ... It is going to get out of control unless we do something. We need to slow down.”

In response to the Hugging Face breach, Lieu teamed up with Rep. Nathaniel Moran, R-Texas, to introduce the AI Kill Switch Act to require AI developers of powerful models to preserve technical powers to suspend or shut down their systems. It would also create a framework to empower the government to trigger such a shutdown if needed.

“I hope it comes up this year,” Lieu said. “We still have a lame-duck session, and there’s also interest on the Senate side. It is a very simple, commonsense bill. At a very basic level, humans must be in control of AI, not the other way around.”

The Hinton briefing capped a flurry of activity on Capitol Hill this week after AI researcher Jacob Coxon resigned from Claude-maker Anthropic and took to social media to warn that the people building AI systems believe it could “kill us all by the end of the decade.”

House and Senate lawmakers in both parties have rolled out legislation seeking to halt or slow down AI development in the last few years, though none has gone anywhere to date.

But the national interest in the issue has revived talks over past proposed AI regulations among Senate Majority Leader John Thune, R-S.D.; Sen. Amy Klobuchar, D-Minn.; Senate Commerce Committee Chairman Ted Cruz, R-Texas; and the panel’s ranking member, Sen. Maria Cantwell, D-Wash.

“Look, my hope is that we can mark up legislation, in particular on catastrophic risk. I’ve been working closely with Amy Klobuchar and John Thune. It’s still not clear if we’re going to get bipartisan agreement,” Cruz told NBC News this week. “We’ve got to have bipartisan agreement before we have something that can move forward. And I would say those talks are ongoing.”

After hearing from Hinton, Sen. Elizabeth Warren, D-Mass., said she believes “we are in the last minutes of being able to get some meaningful control over these agents that are beginning to replicate themselves.”

For years, Sanders has been sounding the alarm that AI will erase millions of jobs in America, harm children and young people who become overreliant on it and concentrate power in a “handful of oligarchs.”

“There is now growing alarm about the future of humanity and creating a technology that human beings cannot control,” Sanders said. “And I’m happy to tell you that I think there is a growing sense of urgency upon members of Congress that this has to be dealt with.”

Kennedy, the sole Republican attendee, said that the experts discussed the “larger risk” of “what happens when AI no longer is a tool controlled by humans, but AI through recursive self-improvement becomes an independent species.”

“If you have fire ants in your kitchen, you’re probably going to step on them,” he said. “What would happen if we created an independent species that became superior to a human species? Would they step on us? Would they create a virus or a bacteria that can spread as quickly as the common cold to kill all of us? Now, if there’s a 1% chance of that, we have to take it seriously. And I don’t think the United States Congress is ready yet to try to reach a global solution.”

Moments later, his suspicions appeared to be confirmed as Sen. Rand Paul, R-Ky., blocked Kennedy’s request for unanimous consent to pass his own “kill switch” bill, aimed at preventing AI agents from slipping out of human control.

“Right now, Congress can’t pass gas,” Kennedy quipped.

World.title: Former ‘Alligator Alcatraz’ detainee says he was placed in phone booth-sized cage for 15 hours
World.content:
For around 15 hours, immigration detention officers kept Raúl Suárez Herrero confined in a cage slightly larger than a phone booth, where he feared snakes and endured mosquitoes in the middle of Florida swampland, the former detainee alleged.

Suárez, 59, told José Díaz-Balart in an interview for Noticias Telemundo’s “Ahora 360” that he was forced into the cage, measuring 7 feet, 9 inches high and 4 feet, 3 inches square, for praying out loud for an ill young man at “Alligator Alcatraz,” an ICE detention site.

“I feel like I was in hell,” Suárez later told NBC News in a phone interview from Mexico, where he was deported.

Suárez spoke days after a Department of Homeland Security watchdog confirmed the use of the phone booth-sized cages at the now-shuttered Florida detention camp in a Sept. 11 report.

“The use of such restrictive spaces is highly unconventional and does not align with standards for humane treatment,” the report said.

The DHS Office of Inspector General report documented its inspectors’ findings during an unannounced January visit to the Ochopee, Florida, site.

In December, Amnesty International issued its own report on conditions at the detention site based on interviews with detainees and its own tour of the facility. The organization detailed the use of the small cages and said it amounted to torture.

The facility staff told inspectors that the cages were “calming areas” where immigrants could de-escalate and have time alone and that no one spent more than two hours inside them.

But Suárez told Noticias Telemundo that “they took me there and I spent more than 15 hours inside in that little hole,” referring to the small cage. He said he was forced in around 1 p.m. and taken out at about 5 a.m. “when morning was breaking.” According to Suárez, the cage was in a recreation area where detainees took exercise time. Suárez said he couldn’t stretch out on the cage floor and got little sleep for fear of what might slither into the cage.

“I had to be careful because on the ground there were snakes and you don’t see them. You can’t fall asleep because they can come into the cage,” Suárez said in a video interview.

DHS did not directly address Suárez’s allegations or case in response to questions from NBC News. But a spokesperson rejected “claims that there were ‘inhumane’ conditions” at the immigrant detention center. Those claims are “categorically false” and any allegations of excessive use of force are “FALSE,” the spokesperson said in an email.

“No detainees were being beaten or abused,” the DHS spokesperson said. DHS provides long-standing medical, dental and mental health services, three meals a day that are evaluated by certified dietitians, clean water, clothing, bedding and hygiene products and access to phones to talk with family and lawyers, the spokesperson stated.

Alligator Alcatraz’s standards were consistent with those under other administrations, the spokesperson also said. Further questions were referred to the state of Florida, “as this facility was managed by the State of Florida through the Division of Emergency Management.”

"Alligator Alcatraz" shut down in June. Alon Skuy / Getty Images file

The facility in the heart of the Everglades was built by Florida Gov. Ron DeSantis as part of the state’s push to support President Donald Trump’s aggressive immigration crackdown.

Alex Lafranconi, a spokesman for DeSantis, has dismissed criticism of the small cages. Lafranconi has described the small cages as a confinement area for “violent criminal aliens who have proven they cannot remain peaceful,” and said “we’d make them smaller, if we could.”

Although DHS said the inspector general “indicated” all recommendations have been administratively closed, the OIG said in its report that the administration did not address its 10 recommendations, including that it “discontinue the use of the small metal enclosures to hold detainees for any reason or amount of time.”

The OIG also said that at the time of the inspection, all the detainees were ICE detainees and there was evidence that ICE had some degree of oversight authority and engagement at the facility.

President Donald Trump and then-Homeland Security Secretary Kristi Noem tour the facility in July 2025. Andrew Caballero-Reynolds / AFP - Getty Images

Originally from Cuba and in the U.S. since he was 12, Suárez was detained by ICE in July 2025 during an ICE check-in.

Before it was recently ordered closed, Alligator Alcatraz had been denounced by multiple detainees and legal and immigrant advocates for its conditions.

The detention facility’s records state the average time people were placed in the smaller cages with metal fencing was 59 minutes and 27 seconds, according to the OIG report. But the OIG said it could not confirm or refute ICE officials’ assertions regarding use of the enclosures or detainees’ allegations they had been denied food or other abuses.

The small cages at the facility were supposed to be a “safe and secure place” where people could “reflect on their behavior choices, manage their emotions, reduce stress, and practice self-directed behavior,” according to the detention camp’s policies, the report stated.

According to detention center records cited by the OIG, 79 people were held in the small cages during the period of July 17, 2025, to Jan. 18, and none were held more than two hours. Detainees in the small cage “may leave at any time by detainee request or per staff directive,” according to the report.

But Suárez was adamant that his confinement was not voluntary and lasted far more than two hours.

“Everybody lied” about the small cages, Suárez said, disputing that he could have gotten out or requested to be let out.

He said he was forced into the cage after praying out loud for a man who had an epileptic seizure as they were waiting to get registered at the detention camp.

Help for the man was taking “too long,” according to Suárez. That’s when he said he started praying aloud, as he used to do at the evangelical church he attended before his arrest.

“I asked God for the young man’s life,” he said.

Suárez alleged two guards then forced him to stand up, asked where he was from and then grabbed him and dragged him “all the way back to where that little cell was.” He said he was kicked in the leg so hard he thought they broke it. “My leg was so big and black.”

“They just dropped me over there and locked the doors,” he said. He said he got no medical treatment for his leg or a medical evaluation after the confinement.

Suárez said his experience has left him psychologically “shattered.”

Suárez was removed to Mexico in February after more than four decades of living in the United States. He was detained on July 16, 2025, when he went to an immigration check-in.

Suárez had been ordered removed from the U.S. in 2000 after serving a prison sentence stemming from a plea agreement on a drug charge. Because Cuba was not accepting U.S. deportees then, Suárez was released and told to check in with ICE annually, a court document states. Cuba has allowed few of its citizens to return after U.S. deportation.

An attorney attempted to get Suárez released from detention. The federal judge had given DHS until late January to remove him or release him, but the judge then extended the government’s time for two weeks. On the deadline date, Feb. 11, DHS deported Suárez to Mexico and the judge closed the case.

“Forty-seven years. They took me to the U.S. as a 12-year-old, when I was a child,” Suárez said. “I was raised my whole life there [in the U.S.]. I’m bilingual and everything. I went to school there and everything. And everything happened from one moment to the next. I still can’t absorb what happened.”

Suárez said he had been a truck driver since he was 17 and had built his own truck driving business with his brother, an American citizen, who died in 2021 from Covid. His father had died in Cuba when he was 3 and his mother, who became a U.S. citizen, died about a decade ago.

When immigration laws were toughened in 1996, making legal residents deportable for certain crimes, he could no longer seek U.S. citizenship, he said.

His mother had urged him to get citizenship, but he didn’t do it, he said.

“I was pretty young. When you are pretty young, you don’t listen to anybody,” he said. He had no other encounters with law enforcement, he said. He said he’d been living a normal life, preparing to buy a house and had a girlfriend.

“Life is changed. I don’t know what is going to happen here in Mexico.”

World.title: White House withdraws Trump’s nominee to lead ICE
World.content:
he White House withdrew President Donald Trump’s nominee to lead ICE, former Oklahoma state trooper Lance Schroyer, according to a notice published Thursday.

The White House did not say in the notice why Schroyer’s nomination was withdrawn.

Immigration and Customs Enforcement did not immediately provide a response about the withdrawal, but a spokesperson said a statement from the agency is forthcoming.

Schroyer’s nomination was blocked by Sen. Rand Paul, R-Ky., the chair of the Senate Homeland Security Committee, according to a person familiar with the decision, because Paul was unsatisfied with how much information he obtained from the White House about the shootings of two U.S. citizens in Minnesota by federal agents.

The White House has not responded to a request for comment. ICE has not responded to a request for comment about Paul.

Schroyer is a senior adviser to Homeland Security Secretary Markwayne Mullin, and he was the secretary’s top pick to take over as director of ICE after Todd Lyons’ exit from the position in April.

Lance Schroyer. Department of Homeland Security

Mullin was previously a U.S. senator for Oklahoma and knew Schroyer from that time.

Schroyer has decades of experience working in local law enforcement in the state, but not specifically with ICE.

Trump announced Schroyer’s nomination in a Truth Social post in June, saying, “Lance has firsthand experience getting Illegal Aliens OFF our streets and, just like ME and our Secretary of Homeland Security Markwayne Mullin, he LOVES the men and women of ICE.”

Acting ICE Director David Venturella is expected to remain in his role leading the agency for the time being, according to an ICE spokesperson.

World.title: Salvadorans with TPS don’t know how long their protections will last
World.content:
HOUSTON — José Palma’s face lights up when he remembers leaving El Salvador in 1998 at the age of 23 for the U.S., with the dream of working, learning English and building a family.

Twenty-eight years later, his life is divided between paperwork, community hearings, and a family full of love and varying immigration statuses: Palma, who lives in Houston, has U.S. citizen children — two of whom are still young — and a wife who’s a legal permanent resident, and he’s a beneficiary of Temporary Protected Status, which allows eligible immigrants from certain countries to live and work in the U.S. without fear of deportation.

As the national coordinator of the National TPS Alliance, Palma has been answering a lot of questions from Salvadorans with TPS: Their immigration protections were set to expire last week, but the Department of Homeland Security announced that Salvadorans will retain TPS protections — including work authorization — for now until an announcement is made at a later date.

But there’s uncertainty among Salvadoran TPS holders about what could come next and what happens now with work permits or driver’s licenses that have expired or are about to expire. Immigrants from countries that have lost their TPS designation, including Haiti and Nicaragua, have lost their work permits and ability to be in the U.S. legally, and they face deportation.

Palma has lived under TPS protection since 2001.

“Everything we’ve built is in danger of collapsing,” he said. “Twenty-five years is not a short time. It’s a lifetime.”

Palma said that amid the uncertainty, Salvadoran TPS holders and their families have been dealing with real consequences: People are being asked not to return to work by their employers, families fear the loss of their health insurance and parents are unsure if they will be able to continue driving vehicles in the United States.

Advising caution

Palma recommended one thing to Salvadoran TPS beneficiaries: “Don’t panic or make decisions based on rumors,” he said.

The Trump administration has said that until it announces a decision, Salvadorans with TPS still have protection, so Palma’s advice is “to rely only on official sources, credible community organizations and established media” for accurate information.

One of the biggest points of confusion, Palma acknowledged, is whether Salvadoran TPS holders can continue working.

“DHS has said that people retain protection, but USCIS guidance for employers indicated that certain automatic work permit extensions were valid until Sept. 9,” Palma said, referring to U.S. Citizenship and Immigration Services. “People should keep their USCIS letters, check their myUSCIS account and seek accredited legal advice before assuming which document applies to their case or employment.”

Palma has lived under TPS protection since 2001. Albinson Linares / Telemundo News

For those who have already received warnings from employers, Palma had this advice: “Do not resign or sign any documents you do not understand. Bring any official notifications you receive from USCIS to your employer and ask human resources to check the agency for updates regarding Form I-9. No one should decide the future of your immigration case based on an unverified comment, social media post or phone call.”

Unfortunately, some Salvadoran TPS holders have already been affected. Palma said that people who applied between January and March 2025 to renew their work permits haven’t received them. Some employers have told them not to return to work, and others have told them they can only work until a certain date.

“Driver’s licenses depend on immigration status, health insurance can be cut off and loans can be denied — the consequences go far beyond losing immigration protection or a work permit,” he said.

If the Trump administration decides to end TPS protections for Salvadorans, people don’t have to leave the country within 60 days, Palma emphasized.

“That period is the minimum protection period before a decision can take effect,” he said. “After that, each person must evaluate their case: There may be a family petition, asylum, another legal process or an immigration defense. The recommendation is to seek legal evaluation now and not wait for an emergency.”

What to do in the meantime

Salvadoran TPS holders should be gathering copies of their work permit, TPS certificate, passport, driver’s license, USCIS receipts, birth and marriage certificates, children’s medical and school records, proof of employment, and tax returns, Palma said.

The National TPS Alliance estimates that 170,000 Salvadorans are directly protected by TPS. Albinson Linares / Telemundo News

He also said it’s important to identify a licensed immigration attorney or accredited organization. He urged people not to lie on any forms or submit applications for which they don’t qualify or give money to people who promise to “fix” their immigration status.

Palma also warned against signing documents without understanding them, giving access to bank accounts or personal information to strangers, or trusting a notary as if they were an immigration lawyer.

TPS holders should also avoid any legal problems or issues such as driving under the influence of alcohol, using false documents or committing acts that could jeopardize any future immigration status.

When asked what TPS holders should do if they’re stopped or approached by authorities, Palma said the important thing to do is “stay calm.”

“Bringing a copy of your identification or immigration documents can be helpful. If it’s an immigration officer, don’t sign any papers without knowing what they contain or without speaking to a lawyer,” he said. “Every case is different, but a signature obtained under duress can have serious immigration consequences.”

Temporary status for decades becomes a ‘whole life’

The National TPS Alliance estimates that 170,000 Salvadorans are directly protected by TPS. However, Palma explained that the actual number of people affected is much higher when one includes U.S. citizen children, spouses, employers, churches, businesses and entire communities.

If TPS for Salvadorans is ended, “the impact would be immediate in cleaning, hotels, restaurants, kitchens and construction; there are also Salvadorans with TPS working in transportation, healthcare and professional occupations,” he said.

Palma was asked what he tells people who say that TPS is temporary and beneficiaries should return to their countries.

He said it’s important to understand the history of the program.

“It’s been renewed every 18 months, under both Democratic and Republican administrations, for 25 years. After all this time, we haven’t been given an opportunity to apply for permanent status,” he said. “So, the question is legal, but also moral: If someone has lived in the United States for 25 years with immigration status, is that really temporary? For many, 25 years is a whole life.”

“The least we deserve is the opportunity to continue our lives, as we have done all these years, but with permanent immigration status,” Palma said. “I want Democrats and Republicans to take this issue seriously, reach an agreement and find a permanent solution.”

An earlier version of this story was first published in Noticias Telemundo.

World.title: New wild cat species is identified for first time in 100 years, researchers say
World.content:
Tiger cats — small, wild cats in the Leopardus genus native to South and Central America — face stiff conservation challenges as development and agriculture expand.

The new study says there are five tiger cat species in South America.

“All of them are in habitats that are vanishing fast,” said Tadeu de Oliveira, another co-author of the study and an ecologist at the State University of Maranhão in Brazil.

Leopardus tilcayo might have continued to escape notice if not for Nogales-Ascarrunz’s sharp eyes. She volunteers at a wildlife rehabilitation center near La Paz called the Senda Verde Wildlife Sanctuary.

“I saw this cat. It was really, really small, and I couldn’t believe how small it was,” Nogales-Ascarrunz said. “I thought it was a kitten.”

The tilcayo tiger cat is smaller than a house cat. Fernando Faciole / National Geographic

The cat had been brought in by a man living in a community in the forest near La Paz who had mistaken the cat for a domestic kitten, according to details recorded by the sanctuary. He had fed the animal noodles, rice and eggs, only to realize it was wild and that he could not take care of it. So he brought it to the sanctuary.

Initially, colleagues at the sanctuary thought the animal might be a known tiger cat species from Brazil, but Nogales-Ascarrunz wasn’t convinced.

“If you look at the spots or the tail, they really don’t match,” she said.

Nogales-Ascarrunz did genetic testing, using tissue from the tiger cat and a second animal that also turned up at Senda Verde. The results from those specimens revealed that the two cats were unique and from the same species, which had diverged from other tiger cat lineages about 1.4 million years ago. That’s enough genetic distance to consider it a new species.

Nogales-Ascarrunz said, however, that local communities in Bolivia have been aware of the species’ presence for generations.

“This cat, they call it tilcayo. And when you ask, ‘Does it have some meaning in Quechua or Almyra and other Indigenous languages?’ they say, ‘No, my grandpa told me that’s the tilcayo,’” Nogales-Ascarrunz said. “This is a traditional knowledge that they have in the community. We want to preserve that knowledge and we didn’t want to give it another name.”

Nogales-Ascarrunz is working to install camera traps in the Yungas forest in Bolivia to search for more signs of Leopardus tilcayo. Fernando Faciole / National Geographic

It’s not rare for scientists to add a mammal species to the taxonomy — they do so about 65 times a year, according to a study released last year. But many of those new species — including some recently named wild cats — are the result of a split. That’s when scientists realize what was once considered a single species has sufficient genetic distinctions to become two.

For example, the Sunda clouded leopard found on the island of Borneo — called Neofelis diardi — was first recognized in 2006 when its genome was distinguished from its mainland counterparts. But examples of the Sunda clouded leopard were already in museums at that point.

The tilcayo, on the other hand, was completely novel to scientists.

“We didn’t have specimens in museums,” de Oliveira said. “It had never been collected before.”

Nogales-Ascarrunz said this new species is likely in danger. She views the discovery as yet another argument in favor of conservation.

“It’s a new reason to protect the world,” she said.

World.title: Driver charged with 2nd-degree murder in L.A. bus crash that news helicopter was covering
World.content:
LOS ANGELES — The woman accused of ramming into a Los Angeles city bus Tuesday has been charged with second-degree murder in the deadly crash, officials announced Thursday.

Bailee Lynn Rios, 36, was arrested Wednesday in connection with the crash, which killed two passengers. While it was covering the tragedy, a news helicopter crashed nearby, killing the reporter and the pilot on board and a pedestrian on the ground.

“What is particularly tragic about this case is that this is a preventable tragedy,” Los Angeles County District Attorney Nathan Hochman told reporters.

In addition to the two counts of second-degree murder, Rios has also been charged with driving under the influence of a drug and reckless driving, according to a complaint.

“She will be looking at a maximum sentence of life in prison,” Hochman said.

It was not immediately clear whether Rios had an attorney who could speak on her behalf.

According to police, Rios drove her 2004 Ford Expedition the wrong way down a busy street, ran a red light and hit a car before she slammed into the bus. She was rescued by first responders and taken to a local hospital.

Investigators found drugs in Rios’ car following the wreck, and prosecutors suspect she was driving under the influence, Hochman said.

“She was driving well beyond the speed limit, she entered into opposing traffic because she was approaching a red light where cars were stopped, and she didn’t stop,” he said.

One passenger was fully ejected from the bus and another was partially ejected, police said. Video from the scene in Chatsworth, a neighborhood in Los Angeles’ San Fernando Valley, showed Rios’ SUV partially wedged into the middle of the bus.

In a helicopter high above, reporter Eliana Moreno described the crash as “horrific” on live television.

“This is terrifying,” she said in what would become one of her final broadcasts.

Moreno and pilot George Marciniw were killed when the chopper, providing coverage for NBC Los Angeles and Telemundo 52, suddenly lost altitude and plummeted toward two storage containers.

A person on the ground, Edy Gutierrez Mejia, also died.

NewsChopper 4 was owned and operated by Angel City Air.

The aftermath of a news helicopter crash in Chatsworth, a neighborhood in Los Angeles, on Wednesday. Ethan Swope / AP

The deaths left Chatsworth and the greater Los Angeles community in shock and mourning. Rios’ loved ones said they never could have imagined she would be involved in something so horrific.

“It’s so awful,” her mother, Cindy Rios, told NBC News in a brief phone call Thursday.

Rios’ longtime friend Brad Aragon told the California Post that Rios had struggled with addiction in the past and went to rehab at least once. He confirmed the Post’s reporting to NBC News.

On social media, Rios occasionally posted about being in recovery and battling addictions. Friends left encouraging words and offered help if she needed it.

Hours before the crash, Aragon and Rios had texted each other about planning a visit in October. She seemed shaken by recent events in her life and said she was hanging around with people she knew were toxic, Aragon told the Post.

According to court records, Rios was convicted in 2022 of driving with a suspended license. Previous charges of driving under the influence, drug possession and carrying drug paraphernalia were dismissed.

Hochman said his office is still examining her criminal record. Rios is expected to be arraigned Friday, he said.

She is being held on $4 million bail.

Asked whether the three helicopter-related deaths would be rolled into Rios’ case, Hochman declined to speculate.

“We’ll wait to see what the investigation reveals, and then we’ll make the call at that time,” he said.

World.title: 1 in 3 Americans with health insurance have medical debt, survey finds
World.content:
Even Americans with health insurance are piling up medical debt, according to a new analysis.

One in three Americans with health coverage through their employer, the Affordable Care Act marketplace or the private market say they have medical debt that they are paying off over time, the Commonwealth Fund, a nonpartisan health policy research group, said in a report on Thursday.

Hospital visits are the primary source of medical debt, with nearly two-thirds of U.S. adults reporting carrying debt related to such care. Patients also carry debt stemming from obtaining routine medical care, such as doctor's office visits or getting lab or diagnostic tests, the study found.

"The primary reason why these people have debt is about the extent to which their insurance covers their out-of-pocket costs," Sara Collins, the study's lead author and a health economist at the Commonwealth Fund, told CBS News.

"Unable to pay"

Almost half of Americans with medical debt, which amounts to about 15% of all working-age, privately insured adults, owe at least $2,000, according to the survey. To pay those bills, 37% said they drained their savings, while 30% reported cutting back on essentials like food, heat or rent, according to the Commonwealth Fund. Thirty percent also reported delaying or forgoing medical care.

"Most Americans don't have a lot of extra cash lying around, and when they are hit with an unexpected expense in a month when their income is allocated across all necessities of life, it can push people into medical debt they are unable to pay," Collins said. "Especially among people who are low-income, they are on pretty regimented household budgets, and medical bills can really tip that budget over into the realm of not being able to pay for certain things and having to cut back."

The findings were based on a telephone and online survey with a nationally representative sample of 6,353 adults.

There are some steps people with heavy medical debt can take to seek relief, Collins told CBS News. For example, healthcare providers may send a bill with erroneous charges, which the consumer should dispute if they believe the charges were a mistake.

Some consumers are hesitant to do so, for fear that failing to pay will hurt their credit scores, Collins noted. "It's a tough situation to be in, but it's important to make sure what you are being asked to pay is correct."

When coverage for medical services is denied, people can also contact their insurers and healthcare providers to negotiate a payment plan that lowers their out-of-pocket expenses.

World.title: Trump photo shows him viewing "Kennedy Center demolished" document
World.content:
A federal judge on Thursday ordered the Trump administration to give 30 days' notice before any "demolition" occurs at the Kennedy Center, an order that came less than 24 hours after President Trump said that the performing arts center could be "ripped down," and photos showed him looking at a document that said "Kennedy Center Demolished."

Before Mr. Trump's comments, a spokesperson for the Kennedy Center insisted Wednesday that "nothing is being demolished" at the performing arts center.

U.S. District Judge Christopher Cooper on Thursday issued an order requiring a detailed report from the Justice Department by next Wednesday on the current "temporary closure" of the center and emergency repairs described in court filings by the center's executive director, Matt Floca.

The Justice Department said in court documents Thursday that the duration of the closure will be for one week, "unless extended" to address safety hazards.

In a declaration submitted by the Justice Department prior to Cooper's ruling, Floca said that "acute risks to public safety resulting from continued structural deterioration ... necessitated a temporary closure of most public spaces in the main building." In an email to Kennedy Center staff that was also submitted to the court, Floca said that any extensions of the closure would be evaluated on a week-to-week basis.

"To be clear, this is not a decision to effectuate the Board's separate vote to close the building for renovation," Floca wrote in the email. "It is a distinct decision by management to address imminent life-safety risks pending the Court's ruling on that vote."

Cooper on Thursday also denied a request from Rep. Joyce Beatty, an ex officio board member who sued last year to halt Mr. Trump's changes to the Kennedy Center, for an emergency hearing on what she called the "unlawful closure of the Kennedy Center."

Beatty, in court documents filed Wednesday, argued, "Given the unexplained and unlawful closure, it is possible Defendants intend to undertake immediate steps in order to make public access practically impossible for the foreseeable future, including by demolishing public avenues of access to the building, and thereby evade the Court's order by fait accompli."

Beatty also noted in the filing that a witness said they saw a "forklift run into and hit the pillars on the building several times."

Fencing was also erected around the Kennedy Center on Wednesday.

Roma Davari, the Kennedy Center's vice president of public relations, told "Real America's Voice" Wednesday night that "nothing is being demolished" and that people should ignore "the media that is saying that because no one has ever said that coming from the institution."

Thursday's ruling marks the latest in the ongoing fight over Mr. Trump's vision for renovations to the performing arts center.

Cooper ruled Tuesday that Mr. Trump's name cannot be put on the building, following a second attempt by the center's board to add it, saying: "Defendants cannot install memorials for President Trump or anyone or anything else at the Kennedy Center without Congress's blessing. The board resolution bucks a federal court order and a statute Congress enacted."

Shortly afterward, the board, which is filled with allies of Mr. Trump's, voted to close the center for renovations, a source said. Congress last year appropriated more than $250 million for the restoration. Cooper, who has been overseeing the case, must approve the board's decision, but he has not yet determined whether the vote was lawful.

Mr. Trump on Wednesday night reiterated that if he were to raise money for the Kennedy Center's restoration, his administration should be recognized — or the site's future would be in question.

"So for the Trump administration, for me, to get involved and to take that on long term and to carry it, or to raise money to carry it, I think that the Trump administration should certainly have recognition," Mr. Trump said. "Because frankly, if we don't do that, it's going to close. It'll end up being ripped down."

On Air Force One Wednesday night, Mr. Trump could be seen looking at a document that said "Kennedy Center Demolished" as he was returning from a rally in North Carolina. The photo was entered as evidence in the emergency motion.

President Trump is seen aboard Air Force One checking a Kennedy Center large printout after landing at Joint Base Andrews, Maryland on Sept. 16, 2026. Brendan Smialowski /AFP via Getty Images

The Kennedy Center, which opened in 1971, is a national cultural center and is the official "living memorial" to President John F. Kennedy.

World.title: F-16 from Texas crashes in Michigan, evacuation order issued
World.content:
An F-16 fighter jet crashed in Grand Traverse County, Michigan, on Thursday, and an evacuation order is in effect along part of County Road 633, the county's emergency management said.

A spokesperson with the 149th Fighter Wing of the Texas National Guard confirmed that the pilot ejected and is in stable condition. They are currently receiving medical treatment. Michigan State Police, which is assisting the Grand Traverse County Sheriff's Office, says no other injuries were reported.

"A 149th Fighter Wing, Texas Air National Guard F-16 Fighting Falcon was on a routine training mission from the Air National Guard's Combat Readiness Training Center, in Alpena, when it experienced an incident earlier this afternoon," the Texas Military Department said in a statement.

The crash is under investigation.

Emergency management initially issued a shelter-in-place order covering County Road 633 from Jefferson Place to Blair Townhall Road. Officials had instructed those in the area to stay indoors, close their windows and vents, and follow instructions from emergency personnel.

Now, an evacuation order is in effect within 1 mile of the site. Anyone in that area is urged to evacuate away from the intersection of County Road 633 and Jefferson Place. Shelter is available at Kensington Church (6880 Secor Road in Traverse City, Michigan). Emergency management says Kensington Church and the American Red Cross are assisting impacted residents.

Grand Traverse officials said the plane went down near County Road 633 and Blair Townhall Road and that traffic in the area is shut down. Responders were headed to the scene, and the agency asked people to stay away.

Blair Township Supervisor Nicole Blonshine said she does not believe anyone on the ground was hurt or that any homes were damaged.

Blonshine did not say what caused the crash, who operated the aircraft or whether anyone else was on board.
