World.title: Greetings from Beijing, where baozi are worth the wait in line
World.content:
Greetings from Beijing, where baozi are worth the wait in line

Jennifer Pak/NPR

To get the best food in China, I'm told you have to stand in line.

That's true for baozi — a fluffy steamed bun with filling. My go-to in Shanghai is dried tofu and veg.

I don't eat it often because I hate waiting.

But when I was assigned a story about Chinese breakfasts, I dutifully queued at a bun shop outside a Beijing park. I snagged baozi stuffed with their bestseller — soy sauce pork — also an eggplant and green pepper, plus one with pickled veg.

Juice from the fillings stained the buns. That's an indicator of a good bun, Beijing resident Samantha Zhao told me as she took part in a baozi-making workshop at a trendy shop called Bao Er Jiu. She was making the Beijing classic, juicy fennel pork baozi.

Sponsor Message

Bao Er Jiu also serves eye-catching pineapple-shaped buns, though the signature flavor is chocolate red bean — tasty and not too sweet.

If I pass this shop again — and if the line moves fast — maybe I will wait for baozi.

For more Far-Flung Postcards, click here.

World.title: U.N.-backed experts cite possible U.S. war crimes in Iran, including a school attack
World.content:
U.N.-backed experts cite possible U.S. war crimes in Iran, including a school attack

toggle caption Vahid Salemi/AP

GENEVA — Experts commissioned by the U.N.'s top human rights body say they have found "reasonable grounds" to believe the United States committed war crimes in two strikes in Iran, including on a school in the southern city of Minab. They also accuse Iran's theocratic government of carrying out crimes against humanity against its own people in a report published Thursday.

The report, while not binding, adds to international evidence gathered about crimes in the war in Iran, and could eventually be used in efforts to reach justice in international courts.

The fact-finding mission on Iran, chaired by jurist Sara Hossain of Bangladesh, is made up of independent experts and was created in 2022 by the Human Rights Council, the U.N.'s top human rights body, which is based in Geneva.

Sponsor Message

The experts were expected to present their findings on Monday to the council, which is made up of 47 U.N. member countries.

The White House issued a scathing statement in response, with spokeswoman Anna Kelly saying the human rights body has "accomplished nothing for human rights while spouting unserious nonsense for decades."

"The only party in this conflict that has committed war crimes is the Iranian regime, which has murdered thousands of its own people, killed Americans overseas, executed acts of terrorism in the Strait of Hormuz, and launched indiscriminate attacks against its neighbors in the region," Kelly said Thursday.

The team says the U.S. launched "indiscriminate" attacks

The international fact-finding mission says its findings on U.S. war crimes center on a pair of U.S. airstrikes that killed at least 178 civilians, including women and children.

At the start of the U.S.-Israeli war against Iran in February, at least one U.S. missile hit the Shajareh Tayyebeh school in Minab, according to an Associated Press investigation. There has been no final accounting of what happened.

Iranian state media have said 168 people were killed in the strike, most of them children.

"Following the United States and Israeli attacks on 28 February, the mission found reasonable grounds to believe the United States committed the war crime of launching indiscriminate attacks resulting in the loss of life or injury to civilians or damage to civilian objects," a U.N. statement about the team's findings said.

Sponsor Message

The U.S. State Department did not immediately respond to a request from The Associated Press seeking comment.

In their report, the experts concluded that "the building of the school was the intended point of impact" and the resulting damage wasn't the result of an errant strike or collateral damage from an attack on a compound of Iran's Revolutionary Guard next to the school.

The Trump administration has yet to directly accept responsibility or release the findings of a Pentagon investigation into the school bombing.

The U.N.-backed team based its allegations on two strikes — one involving Tomahawk missiles that hit the "clearly identifiable" school, and another in which Precision Strike Missiles dispersed tungsten pellets over a "clearly identifiable sports complex and residential area" in the southern city of Lamerd, also on Feb. 28.

The U.N.-backed team said 22 civilian men and women were killed. U.S. Central Command has denied responsibility for the strike on Lamerd.

Experts cite "crimes against humanity" by Iran's government

The team found that killings by state security forces in Iran have occurred on a "staggering scale," and civilians faced "gross human rights violations and crimes against humanity committed by their own government."

Iranian security forces carried out "violent repression" over the last two years by firing assault rifles into crowds, beating protesters and arresting healthcare workers, among other things, the team said. Detainees faced torture, and were deprived of legal counsel, leaving their families "in the dark" about their whereabouts, the experts said.

The Tehran government intensified the use of the death penalty, and said more than 70 people – including five women and three boys – remain at "imminent risk of execution," they added.

"The report concluded that many of these gross violations amount to crimes against humanity — including murder, imprisonment, torture, and other inhumane acts committed as part of a widespread and systematic attack on civilians," the statement said.

Sponsor Message

Both U.S. and Iran should provide reparations, they say

The experts said the United States and Iran should halt all rights violations and crimes, and provide "full reparations to victims."

The report, built on a "victims-centered approach," was based on interviews with 73 people both inside and outside Iran, along with documentation, satellite imagery, photographic and video material and information from "credible" organizations and experts, the experts wrote.

The ongoing conflict that has driven people from their homes in Iran as well as an internet shutdown and a lack of full cooperation from the two governments partially impeded the team's efforts to get information.

Nearly three dozen requests from the experts for information from Iran's government went unanswered, they said, as have requests in June to the U.S. government for information and meetings with officials.

World.title: Carney wants Canada to join Europe's Erasmus+ program. What is it?
World.content:
The audio version of this article is generated by AI-based technology. Mispronunciations can occur. We are working with our partners to continually review and improve the results.

As Canada and the EU court closer ties, Prime Minister Mark Carney signalled clear interest in joining Erasmus+, a popular European exchange program.

While many details of the suggested new partnership are left to be ironed out — like what it would mean to be the EU's first "associate member" — Carney specifically pitched Canadian involvement in Erasmus+ when he delivered a speech at the European Parliament in Strasbourg, France, on Thursday.

"Canadian membership of Erasmus+ would give your students and ours more opportunity to learn at some of the world's top universities, to broaden their horizons and to build those lasting ties that will sustain our alliance for the future," Carney said.

Carney has been clear that Canada is not seeking full EU membership and that the possible new partnership requires a different framework.

He also expressed interest in getting involved in the next iteration of Horizon, Europe's research and innovation funding program in which Canada already participates. The current Horizon framework for 2021-2027 has over $140 billion in funding.

WATCH | Carney's full speech in Strasbourg: FULL SPEECH | Carney calls for 'alliance for the future' in speech at European Parliament | Duration closed caption 22:52 Prime Minister Mark Carney delivered remarks about Canada-Europe ties a day after European Commission President Ursula von der Leyen opened the door to Canada becoming an 'associate' member of the EU.

Speaking to reporters alongside Carney, European Parliament President Roberta Metsola said the EU is optimistic for new opportunities with allies like Canada.

"If you ask our young people what they associate the European Union with, I would tell you Erasmus is the first thing they mention," Metsola said. "Horizon is the second thing they mention in terms of opportunities that with Canada could only get bigger."

"Just think of the opportunity young people in Europe, in Canada, to study in our two jurisdictions, to live and work in those jurisdictions, to learn from each other, build the bonds that will strengthen our ties," Carney said.

While there were no concrete details of what Canada's involvement in Erasmus+ would entail, the U.K.'s recent agreement to join the exchange program could serve as a possible roadmap, given they aren't an EU member either.

The U.K. signed a temporary deal to join Erasmus+ in April. The deal currently only lasts for one year where the U.K. is expected to contribute 570 million pounds (over $1 billion Cdn) to the program in 2027.

What is the exchange program?

First established in 1987 as Erasmus, the flagship EU program allows people to study and train at institutions across Europe for up to a year.

The initial program focused on university exchanges, but has since expanded to include exchanges for work experience, apprenticeships and sport.

Over 16 million people have taken part in the program since its inception, according to the program's 2024 report.

In 2014, the program expanded under a new name, Erasmus+, to include a number of separate initiatives and cover new areas like European competence and sport, receiving €14.7 billion (over $23 billion Cdn) in funding from the EU for 2014 to 2020.

What questions do you have about the proposed partnership between Canada and the EU? Send them to ask@cbc.ca.

The EU's budget is composed of member states' contributions, which are based on their respective gross national incomes.

The program's total funding doubled for the current period of 2021-2027 to an estimated €28.5 billion — roughly $45 billion Cdn — according to its 2024 report.

The report shows 60 per cent of its budget supports learning mobility. The remainder of the program's funding supports its other goals, namely co-operation projects and policy development activities.

Erasmus+ includes all 27 EU member states and also Norway, Iceland, Liechtenstein, Serbia, Turkey, North Macedonia and the U.K.

World.title: Frank Stronach will not face jail time for indecent assault conviction, judge says
World.content:
The audio version of this article is generated by AI-based technology. Mispronunciations can occur. We are working with our partners to continually review and improve the results.

WARNING: This story refers to sexual assault allegations and may affect those who have experienced​ ​​​sexual violence or know someone affected by it.

Canadian billionaire Frank Stronach will not serve any time in jail for his conviction of indecent assault, an Ontario judge said on Thursday.

Ontario Crown prosecutors had been asking that the 94-year-old founder of auto-parts giant Magna International be sentenced to six months in jail for that conviction.

But at the end of the sentencing hearing on Thursday, Ontario Superior Court Justice Anne Molloy said while she hadn't yet decided the sentence she would impose, jail time would not be part of her decision.

Molloy said she had "very firmly" decided that, based on the circumstances of the case, she would not be sentencing someone who is 94 to a jail term. Court will return on Dec. 11 for that decision.

Assistant Crown attorney Jelena Vlacic had also asked for a Sex Offender Information Registration Act (SOIRA) order and that Stronach be placed on Canada’s National Sex Offender Registry for 10 years.

Molloy asked Vlacic what she would consider to be a reasonable conditional sentence for Stronach. Vlacic said six months house arrest with exceptions for medical appointments and court appearances.

When his judge-alone trial began in a Toronto courtroom in February, Stronach was facing 12 charges related to allegations of sexual assault from seven women dating back almost 50 years.

But at his sentencing hearing on Thursday, the 94-year-old founder of auto-parts giant Magna International is facing sentencing on just one of those charges — indecent assault.

Court hears victim impact statement

On that charge, one of the women had told the court that Stronach invited her to a midtown Toronto apartment sometime in the fall of 1977, and while there, he bent her over the arm of a chair, lifted up her skirt and tried to rape her.

In a victim impact statement on Thursday, the woman told court that she had felt ambushed and overpowered by Stronach and that her physical privacy had been violated without her consent.

The woman, whose identity is protected by a court-ordered publication ban, said the assault had destroyed her sense of safety in social settings and that her feeling of apprehension is ongoing.

"I felt that I deserved an apology. I was upset when none was forthcoming," she told the court.

"The impact of an assault is not limited to the physical. It can also jolt one's identity and personality," she said. "Recovering one's comfort with people requires time and resilience, and it may never be complete."

Crown, defence make submissions

Vlacic, the Crown prosecutor, argued that the passage of time since the assault occurred is a consideration but that people need to be held to account for their conduct.

She said those found guilty must pay for their crimes and that to do otherwise would encourage people to lie low and bring the administration of justice into disrepute.

But Stronach's lawyer, Leora Shemesh, countered that her client, instead of any jail time, should receive an absolute discharge — meaning the finding of guilty would remain but no conviction would be registered and Stronach would not have a criminal record. The finding of guilt would still come up in a background check but only for a year.

She also argued that Stronach should not be registered as a sex offender.

Shemesh went through a list of Stronach's accomplishments and contributions to society, stressing as well that until these charges, he had had no brushes with the law.

She told the court that Stronach faces only one charge from the initial 12 and that this particular offence of indecent assault, "on the continuum of sexual or indecent assault, is on the least serious end of the spectrum."

"The Crown's position is manifestly excessive, ... unreasonable and seems quite un-Canadian," Shemesh said, noting how Stronach's honours have been revoked, his name has been stripped from various centres and "dragged through the mud," and he has suffered and been punished enough.

Stronach had been charged with attempted rape and indecent assault for that particular incident. But during the course of the trial, the Crown dropped the attempted rape charge.

Ontario Superior Court Justice Anne Molloy presided over Stronach's judge-alone trial. (Alexandra Newbould/CBC)

In her decision, Molloy agreed that much of what the witness described had happened, but also agreed with the Crown's decision to withdraw the attempted rape charge because it was unclear whether Stronach would have been able to penetrate the woman based on her state of dress at the time.

Still, Molloy referred to it as "gross and disgusting conduct," which is why she found him guilty of indecent assault. The offence is a historical charge, having been repealed from the Criminal Code in 1983. That means anyone charged similarly today would face a sexual assault charge.

In June, Molloy also found Stronach guilty of sexual assault related to another woman who said Stronach groped her in his Toronto Harbourfront condo sometime in 1983 or 1984. The woman said she had gone to meet him for dinner to discuss why she had been fired as a waitress at his then restaurant, Rooney's. She said Stronach invited her to his condo, which is where he groped her.

Molloy said she was "completely convinced" by the woman's evidence. Molloy did, however, "with considerable trepidation," describe it as a minor sexual assault, saying that the conduct was at the "low end" of the spectrum of sexual assault.

2nd conviction granted mistrial

However, weeks after the decision, emails were presented in court from the woman's lawyer in a separate civil complaint. Stronach's lawyer Leora Shemesh alleged those emails told a story inconsistent with the woman's testimony in the criminal trial.

Molloy then granted a mistrial on the sexual assault conviction. The Crown is appealing that decision.

Throughout the trial, which lasted more than two months, the Crown withdrew a number of charges following the testimony and cross-examination of some of the complainants, saying there was not sufficient evidence to sustain findings of guilt beyond a reasonable doubt on those particular counts.

By the time Molloy was set to render her decision in June, Stronach was facing five counts related to three women.

All of the initial seven complainants, whose allegations span the period between 1977 and 1990, testified in court, offering an emotional account of the sexual offences they say they experienced at the hands of Stronach.

Stronach, who was in court every day but never took the witness box in his own defence, had denied the allegations and pleaded not guilty to all charges.

Meanwhile, Stronach is set to face another trial in Newmarket, Ont., next year. When Stronach was initially arrested in June 2024, he was charged with 18 offences involving 13 complainants. But the case was split into two trials later that year.

World.title: Far-right German politician heckles Carney with 'U.S.A.' chant before EU address
World.content:
The audio version of this article is generated by AI-based technology. Mispronunciations can occur. We are working with our partners to continually review and improve the results.

As Prime Minister Mark Carney approached the podium at the European Parliament in Strasbourg, he was met by a lone heckler with an unexpected chant for a Canadian leader speaking to the EU in France.

"U.S.A.! U.S.A.!" German MEP Siegbert Droese called out.

Some in the crowd groaned, then Carney chuckled and carried on with his speech where he called for closer ties between Canada and the EU and an "alliance for the future."

In a statement provided to CBC News, Droese said the chant was his way of "addressing the geopolitical elephant in the room."

WATCH | German MEP chants 'U.S.A.': ‘U.S.A., U.S.A.': German politician chants as Carney speaks to EU Parliament | Duration 0:06 Siegbert Droese, a member of the European Parliament from the far-right Alternative for Germany party, chanted 'U.S.A., U.S.A.' before a speech from Canadian Prime Minister Mark Carney Thursday. Carney addressed the Parliament in Strasbourg, France, calling for an alliance between Canada and the European Union.

Droese said Carney's reaction to his callout shows the prime minister "clearly has a sense of humor."

Carney's address to the Parliament in Strasbourg is just another step in a bilateral push for a tightened relationship with the EU and comes just a day after European Commission President Ursula von der Leyen said she wants Canada to become the bloc's first "associate member" — a new, and as of yet, undefined title.

"It was an absurd and unrealistic knee-jerk reaction for Ms. von der Leyen to propose an 'associate EU membership' for Canada: a status not provided for in any of the European treaties," Droese wrote in his statement.

Droese is a member of the far-right Alternative for Germany (AfD), which has been surging in popularity among German voters.

A 'Make America Great Again' hat sits on the desk of the German Member of European Parliament Siegbert Frank Droese in 2024. (Virginia Mayo/The Associated Press)

The AfD's domestic policies include proposing large-scale deportations of anyone of non-German heritage and a push for what the party calls a patriotic cultural policy to cut funding for projects not deemed suitably national — such as some Holocaust remembrance programs.

In his statement, Droese called the European Commission president corrupt and suggested she's seeking an agreement with Canada to bypass her "abysmal" relations with the U.S.

Droese ended his statement by saying there is a "certain irony in the fact that the six letters 'USA! USA!' were enough" to trigger a reaction.

World.title: Manitoba adopts permanent daylight time after survey suggested overwhelming opposition to clock changes
World.content:
The audio version of this article is generated by AI-based technology. Mispronunciations can occur. We are working with our partners to continually review and improve the results.

Manitobans no longer need to remember to spring forward or fall back one hour on their clocks, as Premier Wab Kinew says the province will adopt permanent daylight time.

The change means clocks will not revert to standard time on Nov. 1, the province said in a news release Thursday.

Manitoba joins several other provinces and territories that have adopted or are moving toward a permanent time, including British Columbia, Yukon, the Northwest Territories, Alberta and Saskatchewan.

Just six months ago, Kinew said his government was too busy with more important matters to consider changes to the clocks. He was asked about it in early March, shortly after B.C. announced it intended to remain on daylight time permanently.

WATCH | Manitobans split on permanent daylight time: Manitobans split on permanent daylight time | Duration closed caption 2:13 The province's announcement on Thursday that Manitoba will remain on daylight time, rather than changing clocks twice a year, has been welcomed by some, who say it will help businesses and keep life more consistent. But one doctor says sunnier evenings will be harmful in the long run.

He later softened his stance, suggesting it may be time to revisit the issue for Manitoba.

In April, Alberta announced plans to table legislation to cement a move to permanent daylight time. Days later, the Northwest Territories said it will also end time changes. Yukon has been on permanent time since 2020 and Saskatchewan since 1966.

Had Manitoba opted for standard time year-round, it would have synced up with the other Prairie provinces. Kinew previously pitched a "Prairie time zone" in April, saying permanent standard time could benefit interprovincial trade.

In May, Manitoba launched a survey to ask the public to weigh in the issue. For those who did want to see the twice-annual changes halted, the survey asked if they preferred to stay on standard or daylight time.

On Thursday, the province said nearly 72,000 votes were submitted in its survey, with 92 per cent of respondents saying they wanted to see an end to seasonal time changes. Among respondents, 58 per cent preferred permanent daylight time and 34 per cent sided with standard time.

In its news release at the time the survey launched, the province included a link to an analysis by Manitoba Health, which concluded that eliminating the time change would be better for population health.

The report says loss of sleep is the "most immediate consequence" of the spring clock change, when clocks have moved forward an hour. The amount of time a person spends sleeping drops slightly in the week following, with adolescents particularly vulnerable, the report says.

Disruption of sleep and circadian rhythm following the spring shift have been linked to short-term increases in cardiovascular events, injuries and traffic collisions, as well as reduced well-being, according to the report.

Historical data from Manitoba Public Insurance shows a 20 per cent increase in collisions on the province's roadways following the spring change when compared to all other Mondays, with loss of sleep and biological clock disruption being contributing factors, according to Manitoba Health.

'Should have chosen standard time'

Moving to a permanent time "would remove the acute risks" that come from switching twice a year, the report says.

One researcher says the province should have adopted permanent standard time rather than daylight time.

Inna Rabinovich-Nikitin, an assistant professor with the University of Manitoba's department of physiology and pathophysiology, says moving to permanent daylight is not the right decision for people's health.

"Our body has an internal circadian clock … and when we're moving to daylight savings time, it doesn't align with the light and dark cycles outside, and that basically makes us feel like we're always jet-lagged," she said.

"It's better not to change the time twice a year, but between daylight savings time and standard time, we should have chosen standard time."

However, a doctors' advocacy group said it supports the move to permanent daylight time.

Although permanent standard time might offer the closest alignment to natural circadian rhythms, permanent daylight time provides other health and societal benefits, particularly more usable sunlight in the late afternoon and evening for people to get outside and get active, Doctors Manitoba said in a written statement Thursday.

WATCH | Here's how ending clock changes will impact Manitoba: Sunrise at 3 a.m.? How ending time changes would affect Manitobans | Duration closed caption 3:11 Premier Wab Kinew says the days of Manitoba changing the clocks twice a year are numbered. How would adopting permanent daylight time or permanent standard time change things in Manitoba? CBC weather specialist Riley Laychuk explains.

Manitoba's Progressive Conservative caucus said the move to end seasonal time changes could have happened after the party's former government passed legislation to do so in 2023, but it did not come into law by way of proclamation once the NDP came into power later that year.

While the province could have been a leader in western Canada by ditching seasonal time changes had the NDP "put their politics aside," it's now "lagging behind" every other western province and territory, the caucus said in a news release.

Manitoba enacted the Official Time Act, bringing provincewide daylight time into effect on May 12, 1963. It set the start of daylight time as the first Sunday in April, continuing until the last Sunday in October, when clocks fell back to standard time.

Daylight time was extended in 2007, starting the second Sunday in March and continuing until the first Sunday in November, to match U.S. changes.

Concern in northern Manitoba

Marilyn Strukoff, who's lived in Winnipeg for over five years, says she's never noticed the difference between the time changes.

"I think I'll be relieved not to have to change the clocks," she said.

But Strukoff is waiting to see how the change affects her before cementing a stance on it.

"It's just an adjustment we have to make."

Matthew Klassen says he thinks the province "jumped the gun" and shouldn't have made the change.

Working-class people and farmers appreciate sunlight early in the morning, he told CBC News in Winnipeg.

"I work construction, and lots of sites have poor lighting in the morning."

Winnipegger Declan Shroeder, who runs Winnipeg Daylight Tracker — a "novelty account" on X — said changing clocks twice a year is "just something that's become archaic."

He supports the province's move, saying he appreciates daylight more in the evening than in the morning.

"The winters are so long and crushing in Manitoba that I really relish the idea of having the sun up till 9:30 or 10 p.m. in the summer."

But Joe Stover, who lives in Churchill, said parents in northern Manitoba are worried about their kids getting to school, now that the sun will rise there after 10 a.m. in the winter.

"Kids will be going to school when it's pitch black," he said, though he's not surprised by the support for the change.

"I'm all for democracy. It's what the people wanted, and so we'll reap what we sow either way," he said.

He hopes the province will review the change in about a year.

"I just hope that people aren't stubborn about it [and] have an open mind, whether you're for this or against this."

World.title: Great Dane gets stretcher ride down B.C. mountain after injuring paws
World.content:
The audio version of this article is generated by AI-based technology. Mispronunciations can occur. We are working with our partners to continually review and improve the results.

A rough excursion for a very large dog and her two owners ended on a positive note last weekend, with a full-service stretcher ride down a mountain near Revelstoke, B.C.

The 10-year-old, 120-pound Great Dane was out for a hike with her owners on Mount Macpherson on Sept. 13 when she tore her paw pads, according to Revelstoke Search and Rescue manager Ren Bassette.

"She was an angel," she said. "A 100 per cent good girl."

Bassette said the dog's owners didn't want to make the injuries worse and knew they couldn't carry their large pooch all the way out, so they activated the emergency SOS function on one of their phones.

Typically, Bassette said, the provincial government won't reimburse search and rescue teams for non-human rescues, but she said temperatures on the mountain were dropping rapidly and the owners needed urgent help too.

Bassette said the two weren't prepared to spend the night outside, and weren't willing to leave their dog behind.

Revelstoke Search and Rescue said the dog's owners needed a little extra horsepower to get their injured pup down the mountain. (Revelstoke Search and Rescue)

Thankfully, another hiker stopped and lit a small fire for the owners and dog to keep warm as they waited for assistance, said Bassette.

"They were in good shape when we arrived."

Basette said their team bandaged the dog's paws and loaded her into a wheeled basket stretcher.

"She was so calm," said Bassette. "And she looks like she enjoyed the ride."

The owners walked out behind their chariot-riding dog, wearing extra clothes the search team had brought in.

Bassette said the team finally loaded the dog into her owners' vehicle around 1 a.m., and that all three are doing well.

World.title: Judge denies Tamara Lich's request to take Caribbean cruise and visit the White House under house arrest
World.content:
The audio version of this article is generated by AI-based technology. Mispronunciations can occur. We are working with our partners to continually review and improve the results.

Tamara Lich had been seeking permission to visit the White House and go on a Caribbean cruise while serving house arrest for her role in the 2022 Ottawa convoy protest, a request an Ontario judge has now rejected. The CBC's David Fraser reports.

A judge has denied Tamara Lich's request to travel internationally while she serves a house arrest sentence, including going on a Caribbean cruise and to the White House.

Lich was found guilty in April 2025 of mischief and other offences for her role in organizing and sustaining the 2022 convoy protest that paralyzed downtown Ottawa for nearly a month.

She was handed a conditional sentence last October that included 12 months under house arrest.

A month after being sentenced, Lich asked for and received permission to leave her home in Medicine Hat, Alta., to attend her grandchildren's school. Since then, she has travelled to other provinces for her job with Rebel News.

In July, Lich asked for permission to travel internationally.

Lich appeared virtually in court from the passenger seat of a vehicle on Thursday, wearing a Rebel News hoodie as the ruling was read.

"The fact that an activity can be described as work does not compel permission to leave the jurisdiction," said Justice Heather Perkins-McVey, spending around 45 minutes sharing her reasons for the decision.

Lich was also told there must be "legitimate circumstances" for temporary travel outside of Alberta. Perkins-McVey instructed Lich to make individual requests to do so.

Against principle of sentence

In her initial request to travel abroad, Lich didn't offer the court a detailed itinerary, but her request mention ed attending press events at the White House, going on a seven-day Caribbean cruise with Rebel News, and travelling to Arizona to speak with Rob Schneider, a right-wing comedian whose controversial content prompted his removal from a Saskatchewan stage in 2024.

Crown prosecutors said the additional exemptions would give her a "blank cheque" to travel internationally. They opposed the request, arguing that granting it was unnecessary and would diminish the impact of her sentence "to an unacceptable extent."

Her defence said in July she had " abided by the terms of her conditional sentence to the letter."

In Perkins-McVey's ruling Thursday, she said there was not enough evidence to show Lich's request is needed, including to maintain employment, and it would go against the principle of her sentence.

The judge characterized the Rebel-sponsored Caribbean cruise as a "commercial event" and "fundraiser." She said the Arizona trip was "promotional" and much of the proposed international work could be completed from Canada.

Speaking after court, Lich's lawyer Lawrence Greenspon said the judge's decision was "very considered"

"There's nothing in what the judge said today, or in the sentence itself, that prevents (Lich) in any way from speaking freely, and associating freely and working to the extent that she can by the conditions that were imposed."

Other legal matters

Fellow 2022 convoy leader Chris Barber, who was convicted and sentenced alongside Lich, travels south of the border through his work as a commercial truck driver.

Sentenced Oct. 7, 2025, the two have already served the bulk of their sentences; but they are far from being done with Ontario courtrooms.

Crown prosecutors are appealing the judge's findings and sentencing, arguing both should have been found guilty of more crimes than they were as well as given harsher sentences. Barber and Lich have accepted their sentences, but are appealing the judge's initial decision.

The Ontario Court of Appeal isn't likely to hear those arguements until early 2027.

Lich and Barber are also involved in civil court matters.

World.title: Barenaked Ladies sing O Canada at Buffalo Bills home opener
World.content:
The audio version of this article is generated by AI-based technology. Mispronunciations can occur. We are working with our partners to continually review and improve the results.

The Barenaked Ladies drew cheers from thousands of football fans in Buffalo, N.Y., on Thursday as they sang O Canada ahead of the Bills' home opener.

In the midst of ongoing trade tensions between Washignton and Ottawa, the Toronto-based band was invited to sing by the team, which has about 10,000 Canadian season ticket-holders.

Ahead of the game, Kate Hussmann, Buffalo Bills chief strategy officer, said in a statement, the team was "thrilled to be part of such a unique event and to celebrate the connection we share with Bills fans across southern Ontario. The passion and support we feel from our Canadian fans is incredible, and we look forward to continuing to deepen those relationships and create memorable experiences together for years to come."

One day before the game, the White House said U.S. President ‌Donald Trump ​signed a presidential ​memorandum to ⁠identify ⁠Canadian-origin goods ‌in federal ⁠civil government procurement for the purpose of removing them, and the Bills celebrated their Canadian fans with a game of cross-border catch, from boat to boat, floating along the Niagara River.

Trump's memorandum signed Wednesday is the latest move in the escalating trade war between Canada and the U.S. after talks fell apart last month. It came a week after he banned the import of Canadian alcohol, motorcycles and various other products into the U.S.

For the Bills, it was the latest effort to celebrate their Canadian fans in advance of their home opener, the first ever regular-season game at the team's new Highmark Stadium in Orchard Park, New York.

"The Canadian fan base for the Buffalo Bills has always been very important to them," said Sal Capaccio, a sports talk host and reporter who follows the Bills.

"It's a very important relationship, because Buffalo isn't New York, it's not Chicago, it's not LA. It's a small market," Capaccio added. "The further they can expand their footprint, going into southern Ontario, going into Toronto... that really matters to the Buffalo Bills. They're a team that wants to make sure they have all their bases covered for people to be welcomed in."

On Wednesday, the team posted a video on social media platform X showing retired Bills quarterback Ryan Fitzpatrick and retired wide receiver Stevie Johnson complete a few cross-border catches along the Niagara River, tossing to each other from aboard distant ferries.

Niagara Parks, the Ontario agency that manages the Canadian side of the Niagara River, said in a news release on Wednesday that the successful boat to boat passes "will be aired during NFL on Prime’s broadcast of the Buffalo Bills first 2026 home game on Thursday, September 17."

Former Buffalo Bills quarterback Ryan Fitzpatrick, now retired, played a game of catch across the border with former Bills wide receiver Stevie Johnson on Wednesday, Sept. 16, 2026, a day before the team plays its first home game of the 2026 season. (Niagara Parks)

Last week, the team said on social media platform X that both O Canada and The Star-Spangled Banner would be performed before Thursday's home opener against the Detroit Lions and that the team "will celebrate the American and Canadian anthems during pregame." Actress and singer Auliʻi Cravalho performed the American anthem.

The Canadian national anthem is rarely heard before NFL games, but it's commonly played before National Hockey League games in Buffalo, even when the Sabres are up against American opponents. In April, fans at KeyBank Center in Buffalo sang O Canada after a microphone failed before the Sabres' playoff game against the Boston Bruins.

World.title: 'Blood is on our hands': Haitian honour student's death sparks outcry over ICE ankle monitors
World.content:
The audio version of this article is generated by AI-based technology. Mispronunciations can occur. We are working with our partners to continually review and improve the results.

The family of a Haitian college student in Ohio says they believe the humiliation of being forced to wear an ICE-ordered ankle monitor, combined with the fear of deportation, led to his suicide after temporary protected status for 300,000 Haitians was revoked in July.

Warning: This story contains descriptions of suicide.

Decorated with academic and athletic awards, Pierre Damas Bel was well on his way to fulfilling his dream of becoming a neurosurgeon.

Described by teachers as a " student of the highest calibre " and a " deeply dedicated " member of his community, Bel was an honour student, captain of the varsity soccer team and volunteer at a food bank in Springfield, Ohio.

But this summer, Bel lost the protected immigration status that allowed him to legally live in the U.S. after fleeing the ongoing instability in Hait i in 2024.

U.S. Immigration and Customs Enforcement (ICE) fitted the 20-year-old Wright State University student with an ankle monitor in late July as an "alternative to detention." But the device prevented him from playing soccer, and he reportedly began to be bullied by classmates and felt he was " treated like an animal ."

"I came here to study, to build my future … not to be treated like [a] criminal," he wrote in a post.

A proud member of the Junior Reserve Officers' Training Corps at Springfield High School, Pierre Damas Bel was an aspiring doctor and neuroscience student at Wright State University. After U.S. Immigration and Customs Enforcement fitted him with an ankle monitor in July, he walked into highway traffic in what his family believes was a suicide. (scsdoh/Instagram)

Bel was one of about 350,000 Haitians living and working in the U.S. who lost temporary protected status (TPS) after a U.S. Supreme Court ruling allowed the Trump administration to revoke the humanitarian protection.

Homeland Security's deportation campaign began immediately.

"Those with terminated TPS are in our nation illegally," it posted alongside a video showing Haitian migrants in chains , escorted onto a repatriation flight on Aug. 27.

Once a lieutenant in his high school's Junior Reserve Officers' Training Corps (JROTC) program and described as a " natural leader " who would become a " great American ," Bel was the only one in the Wright State ROTC program not to be given a uniform because of the monitor, his father says .

The following Monday, Bel walked into traffic on a nearby highway and was struck by a semi-truck, according to Ohio State Highway Patrol .

He died on the scene. His family believes it was a suicide.

'100% preventable'

In the following days, memorials were held in his honour in Ohio and across the U.S. , including New York City. Many held ICE's immigration crackdown responsible for his death.

"Racist anti-Haitian campaign murdered Pierre Damas Bel," one woman's sign in New York read.

A woman holds a sign during a vigil for Bel in Brooklyn, New York, on Sept. 4. (David (Dee) Delgado/Reuters)

Asked to respond to advocates' allegations that the shame of the ankle monitor drove Bel to suicide, ICE told CBC any attempts to blame the agency for his death are false.

"No one is required to stay in the United States illegally and wear a GPS monitor," the agency wrote, adding that self-deportation is an option.

But Yola Lamarre, a friend of Bel, says ICE's response oversimplifies Bel's mental health crisis and blames the young man for his own death.

"We have to be honest in where blood is on our hands," she told CBC News.

Yola Lamarre, a friend of Bel who considered him a little brother, says he was a bright and determined individual whose 'story was cut short' because of harsh immigration policies. (Yanjun Li/CBC)

Lamarre, who saw Bel as a little brother, said his death was "100 per cent preventable" if he had been treated more humanely.

"He told me how he would try to wear a certain wardrobe to hide the ankle monitor," she said.

"He just wanted belonging. He just wanted acceptance."

Haitians were granted TPS after the 2010 earthquake that killed more than 300,000 people in the Caribbean country. Other crises, including cholera outbreaks , Hurricane Sandy and the assassination of Haitian President Jovenel Moïse , prompted further extensions.

After failed attempts to end Haiti's TPS in Trump's first term, the Department of Homeland Security announced in June 2025 it was ending it, saying the situation had "improved enough that it is safe for Haitian citizens to return home." Meanwhile, the U.S. State Department tells its citizens not to travel to Haiti due to the risk of "crime, kidnapping, terrorism, unrest and limited health care."

Carl Ruby, right, pastor of Springfield's Central Christian Church, comforts Bel's father at his home on Aug. 31, as he reels from the loss of his son earlier that day. (Carol Guzy)

The ankle monitoring program Bel was subjected to appears to be part of a larger strategy by ICE to "make life so miserable" that Haitians will self-deport, said Carl Ruby, senior pastor at Central Christian Church in Springfield, Ohio, a city where at least 10,000 of its roughly 60,000 residents are Haitian.

"They're afraid to go outside of their homes," said Ruby, whose church saw its Haitian attendance plummet from about 50 people to two.

Residents 'shackled'

Ruby said hundreds of Springfield residents — including teenagers, elderly and pregnant people — have been "shackled" with ankle monitors, often leading to deep shame and social isolation.

"Their old friends start to pull back from them because they're afraid that if they're with a person who has an ankle monitor, that they might be apprehended."

Critics lik e Ohio Dem ocratic congressman Greg Landsman say the electronic monitoring program also unfairly humiliates law-abiding migrants.

"They aren't criminals," wrote Landsman . "It's all so wrong and cruel to pick on anybody, especially a group this vulnerable."

WATCH | The struggle to come to Canada: Canadian immigration 'very difficult' for Haitians in U.S., says advocate | Duration closed caption 0:52 Viles Dorsainvil, executive director of the Haitian Support Center in Springfield, Ohio, does not encourage Haitians living in the U.S. to go to Canada because of the risk of being turned away and handed over to American law enforcement.

Viles Dorsainvil, executive director of the Haitian Support Center in Springfield, said his community members are caught in a catch-22: no longer safe in the U.S., they also have nowhere to go.

"There is no country that is willing to welcome us," said Dorsainvil, who lost TPS himself. "We cannot go to work. We live in fear and anxiety on a daily basis."

The end of TPS has had a chilling effect across the wider Haitian diasp ora in the U.S.

At a Springfield strip mall, once a hub of economic activity with several Haitian-owned businesses, storefronts were locked or shuttered altogether when CBC visited last week.

One store employee, who asked not to be identified because of his immigration status, described the situation as a "catastrophe."

"There are many people who don't have enough to eat, who are sick, who don't have access to medical care … and no way to get to a doctor," the asylum seeker told CBC in French.

WATCH | Haitians staying home: 'There's no life for them,' restauranteur says of Haitians who lost protected status | Duration closed caption 0:55 Business has slowed for Claucia Dossous, a Haitian American who runs T-Co Islands Restaurant in Columbus, Ohio, after the Trump administration ended temporary protected status for Haiti, leaving many of her customers out of work.

Other businesses are struggling to pay their bills.

Claucia Dossous, a Haitian American who runs T-Co Islands Restaurant in Columbus, Ohio, said ending TPS has "broken everybody's life" after Haitians who frequented her restaurant were forced out of work.

"I pay for the price, too."

Looking to Canada

The climate of fear has led some Haitians to try moving to Canada.

More Haitian nationals file for asylum at the land border than any other country so far this year, according to the Canada Border Services Agency (CBSA). Figures from the Immigration and Refugee Board show that more than 27,000 Haitians are awaiting decisions — about 1/10th of all pending asylum claims.

Haitian American activist Guerline Jozef wants Canada to open more humanitarian pathways for Haitians who no longer feel safe in their country.

"We find ourselves in a place where we cannot leave, we cannot stay. And the only option they are giving them is to be kidnapped and be deported to the same place that they have fled," said Jozef, executive director of the Haitian Bridge Alliance in San Diego, Calif.

WATCH | 'We cannot leave; we cannot stay': Canada returning Haitian asylum seekers to U.S. immigration authorities, says activist | Duration closed caption 1:04 Guerline Jozef, executive director of the Haitian Bridge Alliance in San Diego, Calif., says Canada is turning away vulnerable Haitian asylum seekers entering from the U.S., leaving them at risk of deportation to the country they fled.

Immigration, Refugees and Citizenship Canada told CBC it "cannot speculate on future policy decisions" but highlighted temporary measures for Haitian nationals in place until October.

But for those outside Canada, those measures are only available to family members of Canadian citizens and permanent residents.

Ruby described the case of one family who was a part of their congregation who survived several kidnapping attempts in Haiti.

Ruby knows a Haitian family that went to his church who was able to move to Canada before being deported by ICE thanks to a family connection, but says that option isn't available to most people. (Aloysius Wong/CBC)

Because one of them had a sister in Canada, they were able to join her. The day they arrived in Canada, they received letters from ICE telling them their TPS was over and to self-deport.

"They got out just in time," he said. "But that option just isn't available to very many people."

Instead, Jozef said many of the people who try to flee the U.S. into Canada are turned away.

Under the Safe Third Country Agreement, refugees who first arrive in the U.S. are barred from seeking asylum in Canada, barring certain exceptions . More than 1,100 asylum seekers were returned to U.S. immigration authorities under this agreement so far this year, according to the CBSA.

Frantz André, a community organizer and advocate for asylum seekers in Montreal, says the Safe Third Country Agreement effectively allows for 'deportation by proxy' when Canada hands over migrants to the U.S., where they will be sent back to their home countries. (Romain Schué/Radio-Canada)

Montreal migrant advocate Frantz André said the agreement now effectively allows for "deportation by proxy" when Canadian agents turn back Haitian migrants knowing they will be deported by the U.S.

"The United States is no longer a safe country for hundreds of thousands of people," he said. "People are in despair."

World.content:
Article content

But the Crown highlighted Nygard to emphasize the point that Stronach’s advanced age should not necessarily work in his favour. She quoted the judge in Nygard’s case: “Were I to punish him less harshly than his moral blameworthiness calls for because he is now an elderly man, it would, in effect, validate the immunity that wealth and power have given him. In my view, it would be contrary to public policy. It would significantly devalue the importance of denunciation and deterrence. It would send the message that if you are rich and powerful and your victims are vulnerable…, you can escape accountability if you can hold off the day of judgment long enough. That is exactly the wrong message for the court to send. Although age is a factor that I must consider, there is a limit to the amount of weight I will give it.”

World.title: Court imposes strict conditions on Colombia’s military air strikes if minors are present
World.content:
A Bogota court imposed strict conditions on Colombia’s military authorities if they want to carry out air strikes on illegal armed groups in places where victims of forced recruitment are present.

The ruling of Bogota’s 34th Family Court lifted a suspension on the strikes that had been imposed earlier this month in response to a lawsuit.

The court imposed the following conditions on air strikes to evade violating International Humanitarian Law, which prioritizes the rights of child victims of forced recruitment over the success of military operations.

Don’t assume minors are legitimate targets because they form part of an illegal armed group

Intensify the verification and cross-checking of available information on the possible presence of minors at potential targets

Explicitly include this assessment to the legal and operational assessment of the attack

Assess the foreseeable risk of an attack on the lives and integrity of the minors

Examine the existence of less harmful means, methods, timing or operational alternatives that would allow the achievement of a comparable military advantage

Rigorously apply the principles of distinction, precaution, and proportionality before authorizing and executing the operation

Integrate

The court additionally ordered family welfare institute ICBF to be integrated into military operations and strengthen the pathways for disengagement, restoration of rights, comprehensive care, and reintegration of children and adolescents who are victims of recruitment, with a differentiated and territorial approach.

The court asked the Ombudsman and the Inspector General’s Office to monitor compliance of the orders issue to maximize the protection of children’s rights.

The lawsuit had been filed in a successful attempt to protect children against the violence President Abelardo de la Espriella sought to unleash on illegal armed groups that refused to demobilize.

World.title: US maintains Colombia “failed demonstrably” in fighting drug trafficking
World.content:
The United States President Donald Trump maintained that Colombia “failed demonstrably during the previous 12 months to make substantial efforts to adhere to their obligations under international counternarcotics agreements.”

In an annual reviews, Trump stressed that the South American country maintains its an unwilling drug trafficking country “solely due to the incompetence and chaos produced by the previous far-left government.”

“If, as expected, Colombia makes progress on aggressive coca eradication and dismantling its narcoterrorist networks over the coming year, I will consider lifting the country’s ‘failed demonstrably’ status,” said the US president.

President Abelardo de la Espriella “has pledged to lead an aggressive campaign against coca cultivation and cocaine production, which reached record levels under the failed socialist policies of his predecessor,” Gustavo Petro, according to Trump.

Colombia is poised to resume its place as our foremost security partner in the hemisphere, and the country’s military, police, prosecutors, and courts now finally have a worthy champion in President de la Espriella. US President Donald Trump

De la Espriella, who took office in August, informally joined the US Government’s Shield of the Americas program in an attempt to increase cooperation between Trump’s conservative and far-right allies in the region.

As part of his counternarcotics efforts, the Colombian president tried to increase air strikes on so-called “narcoterrorist” groups, but was forced to stop this by a court to protect minor forced recruitment victims.

The National Police announced a pilot aerial fumigation program, but this was also suspended by a court because of health and environmental concerns.

The State Department vowed to seek $1 billion dollar in aid, but has yet to ask Congress for these funds while allegedly dealing with the world’s highest number of deaths caused by the consumption of illicit drugs.

World.title: Colombia’s statistics chief sacked for claiming Petro did not manipulate statistics
World.content:
Colombia’s President Abelardo de la Espriella sacked his statistics chief because he claimed he found no anomalies in labor statistics presented by the administration of former President Gustavo Petro.

In a press statement, De la Espriella’s press secretary said that DANE director Ricardo Valencia was sacked for claiming “that he had not found any anomalies in the DANE indicators for the month of July, figures compiled during the final month of the previous administration.”

Valencia made that claim “without any in-depth audits having been conducted beforehand,” according to the press secretary.

It is essential for the National Government to conduct a rigorous review of the information received and to ensure that the data on which strategic decisions for the country are based fully reflect the economic and social reality of Colombians. President’s Office

The former DANE director was sacked days after the President’s Office canceled another statistics press conference that are common because of the agency’s regular updates on the state of the Colombian economy

July’s labor statistics confirmed claims by the previous government that unemployment dropped to record lows after Petro raised the minimum wage.

De la Espriella has insisted that the country’s economy is in crisis contrary to evidence, which indicated Petro increased economic growth in his last half year in office.

World.title: Colombia’s social organizations and labor unions announce national strike in November
World.content:
Some 1,500 representatives of social organizations and labor unions agreed to begin organizing an anti-government national strike that should take place throughout Colombia either on November 11 or on November 20.

The organizations agreed to the mass mobilization during the National Gathering for the Defense of Life, Dignity, Democracy, Peace, Sovereignty, and Social Reforms that had been organized by labor unions in the capital Bogota.

The first and fundamental decision of the Meeting is to declare the most radical opposition to the illegitimate government of Abelardo de la Espriella because of the course it has imposed on the country—one of subordination to the interests of U.S. imperialism and alignment with the agenda of the international far right—which constitutes a direct threat to national sovereignty, democracy, and the rights won by the Colombian people, and an undeniable shift toward fascism. Social organizations and labor unions

In a statement, the organizations said that the national strike will be preceded by regional protests on October 10 and 14 that will seek to generate momentum for the national strike.

Indigenous organizations will additionally organize a Day of Indigenous, Afro and Popular Resistance on October 12.

A final date for the national strike has yet to be defined.

The organizations decided to call a strike to protest the government’s security and defense policy, the ending of peace processes with illegal armed groups and in defense of social reforms that had been implemented by former President Gustavo Petro.

The protests additionally seek to express solidarity with the people of Palestine, western Sahara, Iran, Bolivia and Venezuela, and reject US imperialism in the Americas.

We must categorically reject the interference of U.S. government officials in the formulation of domestic policies under the guise of so-called friendly aid, which in reality masks the ambition to intensify overexploitation, extractivism, territorial control, and the presence of foreign troops on our soil. Social organizations and labor unions

The organizations agreed to “prepare, through the most intense and massive agitation and propaganda campaign, a national strike.”

World.title: Judge suspends Colombia’s aerial fumigation pilot
World.content:
A Putumayo from the southern Putumayo province suspended the government’s announced resumption of the aerial spraying of coca, ordering information that would allow “a sufficiently informed decision on the merits.”

Earlier this week, the National Narcotics Council (CNE) ordered the National Police to restart the aerial fumigation of coca, the base ingredient for cocaine, “as a controlled, limited, temporary, and evaluable experimental phase, the implementation of a pilot plan for the eradication of illicit crops through aerial spraying using a manned aircraft and the formulated product Glufosinate Ammonium 200 SL.”

The National Police subsequently said that the 10km2 pilot area was located in Putumayo, a province inside the Amazon forest.

These announcements triggered a local foundation to sue the administration, claiming that the plans to do a pilot were in violation of the 2015 ban on aerial fumigation and threatened both locals and the environment.

The judge agreed and ordered the administration of President Abelardo de la Espriella to provide information on the environmental and health risk involved in the aerial spraying with glufosinate ammonium.

The potential implementation of the pilot plan before gathering and analyzing the studies, documents, and technical evidence cited by the administration itself as the basis for the decision could render the requested constitutional protection ineffective and jeopardize the possibility of reaching a sufficiently informed decision on the merits; Indeed, the combination of the announced imminence of the measure, the current lack of essential information needed to understand its territorial, social, and environmental scope, and the particular ecological sensitivity of the department of Putumayo necessitates preventive action aimed at preserving the effectiveness of this constitutional action. Putumayo court

The suspension of the aerial spraying comes days after De la Espriella promised US Secretary of State Marco Rubio that he would resume aerial fumigation, a notoriously ineffective way to get rid of coca.

World.title: Colombia announces new aerial fumigation pilot program
World.content:
Colombia’s National Narcotics Council (CNE) ordered the National Police to restart the aerial fumigation of coca, the base ingredient for cocaine.

In a resolution, the CNE ordered “as a controlled, limited, temporary, and evaluable experimental phase, the implementation of a pilot plan for the eradication of illicit crops through aerial spraying using a manned aircraft and the formulated product Glufosinate Ammonium 200 SL.”

In a public statement, the National Police’s counternarcotics unit said that the 10km2 pilot area was located in Putumayo and would not affect indigenous and afro-descendant communities, who would need to be asked permission.

The exclusion of environmental protection zones and protected areas, zones associated with bodies of water, rivers, and other environmentally sensitive areas is contemplated, as well as those territories that, in accordance with current regulations and the corresponding technical studies, must be excluded. National Police Counternarcotics

The purpose of the pilot program is to “evaluate the effectiveness of aerial spraying, as well as its application under the established technical and operational conditions, said the police.

The police stressed that “this experimental phase does not constitute the resumption, adoption, or definitive authorization of a widespread or nationwide aerial spraying program,” which was banned by the Constitutional Court in 2015.

In order to resume aerial fumigation, health and environmental authorities must sign off on the program and the police would only be allowed to use airplanes with the approval of the court and local communities.

President Abelardo de la Espriella vowed to resume aerial spraying more than 330,000 hectares while on campaign and after taking office last month as part of his hardline approach to organized crime.

Former President Ivan Duque also vowed to resume aerial spraying, but failed to comply with the norms established by the court.

World.title: Court orders Colombia’s government to remove images of slain “narcoterrorists”
World.content:
A Bogota judge ordered Colombia’s government to remove images and videos of President Abelardo de la Espriella walking through the remains of slain suspected guerrillas from its social media accounts.

The judge also ordered the government to remove images and videos of the body bags containing the lifeless remains of four members of organized crime group ACSN who were killed in La Guajira.

According to the judge, the images could be harmful to minors.

The decision was celebrated by congressman Santiago Osorio (Green Alliance), who sued the government over the controversial social media posts.

The State and the National Government cannot engage in a contest with crime to see which of the two is the most cruel; in this regard, the Office of the President of the Republic, Mr. Abelardo de la Espriella, were ordered to promptly remove images that may have reached the cell phones of children across the country, showing a state displaying corpses as trophies. Congressman Santiago Osorio

Th publications were previously rejected by the Ombudsman’s Office, whose director, Iris Marin, urged the government not to “compete with armed groups over who instills the most fear, who humiliates the adversary the most, or who turns death into a display of power.”

In the first video, De la Espriella and Defense Minister Jorge Eduardo Mora walked through rows of body bags, displaying the remains of 23 alleged members of FARC dissident organizations EMC who were killed in the southern Guaviare province.

Among those killed in Operation Azarias were two minor victims of forced recruitment by the guerrillas.

The videos sought to promote the government’s hardline security policy, which vows to kill “narcoterrorists” who refuse to surrender.

World.title: US, Colombia sign memorandums of understanding amid “rebirth” of relations
World.content:
Colombia’s President Abelardo de la Espriella and US Secretary of State Marco Rubio hailed the “rebirth” of bilateral relations as they signed memorandums of understanding on nuclear energy and rare earths.

The two leaders met in Barranquilla, where De la Espriella lives, as part of Rubio’s tour through allied countries in the Andean region.

The president and the secretary of state hailed the improvement of ties that were severely disrupted when former President Gustavo Petro was in office.

During a joint press conference, Rubio stressed the need for security in the region, claiming that “the same networks, the same criminal groups that, although they commit their crimes here, they also commit crimes in the U.S., and they damage our people.”

De la Espriella said that as part of the “Barranquilla Agreements,” he asked the US for support for his hardline security policy.

We have proposed to the government—and today I reiterated this proposal to the secretary—the 21st-Century Patriot Plan to modernize aircraft, radars, drones, helicopters, anti-drone systems, air defense, mobility, intelligence, cyber defense, special forces, and maintenance and operations. President Abelardo de la Espriella

The president promised to “start spraying, we are going to target the laboratories, the precursors, the trafficking routes, the drug trafficking kingpins, the armed narco-terrorist organizations—we are going after the money launderers, their criminal assets, and those international networks that pose a grave danger not only to the hemisphere but also to humanity.”

Rubio did not openly commit any US support other than the memorandums of understanding.

The unbinding agreements were part of Rubio’s wish list as the US seeks new sources for rare earths and miners that can be processed outside of China, which the US Government sees as its rival.

With the nuclear energy agenda, Colombia seeks to “strengthen its capacities” with US support. Both governments “reaffirm their commitment to international development and the peaceful use of nuclear energy.”

In order to create policy regarding the memorandums, De la Espriella would need congressional support, which he has yet to seek openly.

World.title: Evacuations ordered in Chile as wildfires run amok
World.content:
Chile’s National Service for Disaster Prevention and Response (Senapred) Wednesday ordered the evacuation of 14 communes in the regions of Ñuble, Biobío, and La Araucanía, including Nacimiento, Purén, and Contulmo, which have all been particularly affected by the forest fires.

In messages broadcast through the Emergency Alert System (SAE), the authorities also called on residents to leave their homes to avoid further damage to their health.

It has already been a week since the first wildfires ran amok in south-central Chile despite efforts to contain them. High temperatures, dryness, and strong winds add to the plight of local people and some 5,600 firefighters deployed in the area while helping flocks in from abroad.

”We are entering this part of the week which is the most complex. Today, tomorrow, and the day after we have an alert for high temperatures in several regions of the country that has mobilized a very large effort (…) to prevent the fires from spreading,“ Interior Minister Carolina Tohá said regarding the 311 active fires, of which 89 are being fought. The Senapred also said 180 fires were under control, and 309,747 hectares have been affected.

”If the temperature rises and the wind increases we can indeed have more problems, and we already have many fires,” Spanish Lieutenant Colonel Carlos Javier Martín Traverso told AFP. Traverso’s Air Operations Section of the Military Emergency Unit (UME) arrived in Chile on Sunday to join the firefighting efforts.

Over 309,000 hectares have been consumed in the regions of Maule, Ñuble, Biobío, and La Araucanía with the death toll standing at 24, plus 2,180 people injured as 1,180 houses were destroyed, leaving 5,560 people homeless.

There seems to be a seamless scientific consensus that fires are the result of human actions, either by intentionality or carelessness, although the drought that has hit Chile for 13 years adds to the aggressiveness of the fires.

In this scenario, President Gabriel Boric Font has announced a curfew in the areas of Ñuble, Biobío, and La Araucanía where a state of catastrophe is in force, in order to guarantee the security and tranquility of

the families affected by the crisis. Defense authorities working on the sites will determine the restriction’s schedule.

“We have 24 people dead nationwide, three are from Santa Juana and we do not want there to be even one more,” Boric told reporters after visiting the area.

The number of fatalities was updated to 24 after two bodies were determined to belong to people who had died before the fires broke out.

Meanwhile, Biobío Governor Rodrigo Díaz said he was certain about “people criminally setting fires.”

“I have reports from police, firefighters, of people who have been setting fires. I do not have indications, but certainties, we need more patrols,” he insisted in a radio interview.

“We have fire outbreaks at the southern exit of Contulmo, different places where fires were set 300 meters away from each other, I could see it, nobody told me about it. The mayor of Mulchén told me how fires were lit in the four cardinal points, I have reports from the police, the Fire Department, from people who have been setting fires. I do not have indications, but certainties, we need more patrols in the area,” he explained.

President Boric’s Regional Delegate Daniela Dresdner said eight people had been arrested for “irresponsible and suspicious attitudes with respect to the setting of fires. This was due to citizen complaints and patrols by the Navy.”

“We are asking that all these conducts be denounced and we are filing a lawsuit for all these denunciations to [be] prosecute[d],” she added.

The Biobío Regional Prosecutor’s Office called on the citizenry to e-mail all data regarding criminal behavior to fiscaliaincendios@gmail.com, including pictures, videos, audios, or written information as to the probable causes of the fires, which will be handled confidentially. (Merco Press)

World.title: Chile’s wildfires death toll reaches 24
World.content:
Chilean authorities spoke Sunday of 24 fatalities, nearly 1,000 people injured, and some 800 houses destroyed in the past five days by wildfires spreading fast in amid a highly-irregular heat wave with strong winds and temperatures above 40°C in areas 500 km south of Santiago.

The death toll reached 24 after the death of one of the injured people who had been hospitalized in Angol, Undersecretary of the Interior Manuel Monsalve explained. “The risk situation in the country remains” in the regions of Ñuble, Biobío, and La Araucanía, and in certain localities of the central region of Maule, he said. A red alert was also decreed Sunday in communes of the southern regions of Los Ríos and Los Lagos due to the appearance of new fire outbreaks. He also pointed out that 26 of the 997 people injured were in serious condition.

“I came home from work and I was already without anything, without a house. I was left on the street, with my arms crossed, now with my son, and my wife, in a tent. I have no fodder for my animals,” a resident of the town of Purén, in the Araucanía region, told Televisión Nacional de Chile (TVN).

Meanwhile, President Gabriel Boric Font attended the wake of a firefighter in the town of Coronel. ”Chile is crying with you. I am here to tell you that you are not alone, that the family of Yesenia (Muñoz, the deceased firefighter) will not be alone,” he said.

According to Chile’s National Service for Disaster Prevention and Response (Senapred), the number of fires being fought went down from 87 to 51. “We are experiencing a small window of improving weather conditions during Sunday and Monday. That means that we are not with extremely high temperatures,” Monsalve said.

Undersecretary Monsalve also told reporters that 10 people have been arrested for their responsibility in starting some of the fires for which the red alert was still maintained. Of the total number of fires, 22 occurred Sunday for a total of 283 active fires, of which 151 were under control and 71 are being fought.

Given the magnitude of the fires in size and number, international help has been summoned. “We have just sent a plane to Chile with a contingent of the Military Emergency Unit to collaborate in extinguishing and controlling the fires that are raging in the country. All our support to the Chilean people,” tweeted Spanish Prime Minister Pedro Sánchez.

Chile’s Foreign Ministry also said assistance was being coordinated with Argentina, Brazil, Ecuador, the United States, and Mexico, while Boric’s administration has declared a constitutional state of catastrophe in the regions of Ñuble, Biobío and La Araucanía, to speed up additional resources while restricting free transit and involving military forces to contain the disaster.

In 2017, another chain of fires destroyed some 460,000 hectares, left 11 people dead, nearly 6,000 injured, and more than 1,500 homes burned.

Monsalve also warned that this week high temperatures will continue, as well as the risk of low humidity and strong gusts of wind, which will make it difficult to extinguish the flames. – MercoPress

World.title: Parts of Chile under red alert for major forest fires in central region
World.content:
The Government of Chile has declared a “red alert” in the central part of the country due to the heat wave stemming from 39 major forest fires as the wave keeps spreading throughout the country, most of them in Araucania (17) but also in Bío Bío (7), Ñuble (7), Maule (4), Los Lagos (3), and one in the Santiago Metropolitan Region.

The National Service for Disaster Prevention and Response reported that in addition to the 39 fires currently being fought, there were four others under observation, while 141 were already under control, and 20 had already been extinguished.

Authorities ordered a series of preventive evacuations in several towns, as well as the interruption of highway traffic in the most affected areas where 181 hectares of scrubland and pastureland were burned out, threatening nearby homes.

The main cause for the fires is said to be the summer high temperatures which reached 41 degrees Celsius in the Chillán area.

Meteorologists forecast that the heat wave will last until Sunday. The last major fires to affect Chile were recorded in the summer of 2017 when the flames swept through entire villages, causing 11 deaths and more than 580 thousand hectares affected.

The state-owned National Forestry Corporation (Conaf) reported that in the Ñuble region, the fire has already affected some 550 hectares in the area of Chillán Viejo and another 200 hectares in another town near the regional capital, burning infrastructure and some houses.

Agriculture Minister Esteban Valenzuela told reporters that in addition to the heat wave, the dry and hot Puelche wind from the eastern cordillera was also expected in the central-southern zone. Valenzuela also announced the temporary closure of seven national parks from Santiago to the south in the Metropolitan, Ñuble, Biobío, La Araucanía, and Aysén regions to prevent new fires, and also ordered the evacuation of rural areas of Ñuble, where simultaneous forest fires were reported.

– MercoPress

World.title: Chilean airlines will reimburse cost of boarding taxes under certain conditions
World.content:
Chile’s national Consumer Service, Sernac is calling all consumers who purchased tickets directly from airlines between 2015 and 201l and did not make use of them, to claim from the companies the reimbursement of the boarding taxes paid.

Following on a Voluntary Collective Procedure reached at the beginning of 2020 with LATAM, and at the end of 2021 with Sky, Avianca, Jetsmart, Aerolineas Argentinas and COPA, the airlines agreed to reimburse the boarding taxes cost for flights not done between May first 2015 and 24 December 2021, with the exception of Jetsmart, which only started operations in Chile in July 2017.

Accordingly the universe of beneficiaries reached 1.108.416 passengers and involved some US$ 12 million for domestic flights and US$ 1,4 million for international flights. The amount to be reimbursed to each potential passenger depends on the distance to travel and if it was domestic of international travel.

In Chile the domestic boarding tax is equivalent to some US$ 14 and overseas US$ 50. Allegedly following the agreement the companies were to inform the beneficiaries of their reimbursements.

Reimbursements can also be checked by filling forms at the airlines’ offices. For further information on the agreement and the sums involved consumers are invited to check the web.

World.title: Remembering Steve Anderson
World.content:
BENJAMIN WITTE

I was neither the first nor the last of the many interns and editors who peopled the office of the Santiago Times during the quarter century founder Steve Anderson captained the ship. But for whatever reason, I stuck around longer than most, and it was with great sadness that I learned yesterday about the automobile accident that ended his life.

My first encounter with Steve came in late 2002, after he had offered me the editor’s job—sight unseen, via e-mail—and I accepted, knowing only that I’d earn about US$500 a month and should show up in Santiago with an AP style guide and a copy of Strunk and White’s The Elements of Style. That it all seemed a bit rushed and loosey-goosey gave me pause for concern, but I was eager for an excuse to return to Chile, so hopped on a plane and flew down from Costa Rica.

Still, after our first meeting, I wondered just how wise my decision really was. It was then that I realized the Santiago Times wasn’t, as I’d imagined, a print paper. It was Internet-based, with a rudimentary website that was only half functioning. “We got hacked,” Steve told me. He also explained that he was living at that moment in Puerto Montt—1,000 kilometers to the south—and that he was recovering still from a recent and quite serious car accident. It had been a very bad year, he said.

I gave the gig a chance, though, and things gradually improved. Some energetic new interns trickled in, as they always did at the Santiago Times. A talented British/Australian writer showed up too, and I asked Steve to hire him as a kind of co-editor. The business couldn’t really afford another paid staff member, but Steve honored my request, and for the next year or so we had a great run. Then the money ran out.
