See more DutchNews articles in your Google search results

See more DutchNews articles in your Google search results

The Netherlands has fallen three places to 46th out of 145 countries in the World Economic Forum’s Global Gender Gap Index, a year after dropping 15 places to 43rd.

The annual index measures the gap between men and women on economic participation, education, health and political influence.

The Netherlands has closed 75% of its gap, down 0.6 percentage points on last year, according to the University of Amsterdam team that compiled the Dutch data.

There is no longer a gap in education or health and the economic score has risen slightly, but neighbouring countries are moving faster, Henk Volberda, the UvA professor who led the research, told broadcaster NOS.

The main drag is politics: the share of women in parliament rose slightly but the number of women ministers fell, and the country has never had a female prime minister.

“I thought we had hit rock bottom last year,” Volberda said. He argued that nobody in government feels responsible for the issue, which sits with the education ministry, and wants quotas for senior public and corporate posts along with Scandinavian-style free childcare and longer maternity leave.

Iceland tops the ranking, followed by Finland, Norway, Namibia and the UK. Germany is ninth. The Netherlands was in the top 15 almost every year between 2006 and 2016.

World.title: Opposition urge cabinet to pick a route as budget debate begins
World.content:
The left-wing opposition party Pro is willing to talk to the coalition parties about reducing healthcare costs, but only if the cabinet abandons its €6.5 billion cuts to welfare spending, party leader Jesse Klaver said on the first day of the Dutch budget debate.

Klaver said it would be a “scandal” if the government fell over its first budget, but he also pressed Rob Jetten’s administration to make up its mind whether to seek support from left or right.

As the first speaker in the two-day debate on finance minister Eelco Heinen’s budget, Klaver said his party wanted to break the deadlock that led to pre-budget talks breaking down.

“After so much political unrest in recent years, I think it is in all our interests that this cabinet succeeds,” he said. “Sometimes I think the opposition is keener to make it a success than the coalition parties themselves.”

Jan Paternotte, leader of the largest coalition party D66, called on parties on all sides to work on a budget with broad appeal and look beyond “the left-right discussion in The Hague”.

But his words found little support from the opposition, which accused the coalition of D66, CDA and VVD of lacking leadership. “What kind of road map does the cabinet see before it?” Mirjam Bikker, leader of the ChristenUnie, asked.

The three parties have 66 seats in the lower house, 10 short of a majority, while in the Senate they need to find 16 extra votes to pass their legislation.

No perfect match

Pro, with 20 seats in the lower house and 14 senators, provides the most straightforward route, but the right-wing VVD is reluctant to make too many concessions to the left and favours a deal with parties such as JA21 and the orthodox Protestant SGP.

Paternotte said the coalition wanted to continue talking to parties on all sides in the coming weeks. “The perfect political match doesn’t exist, only the will to come to an agreement. My invitation stands.”

Klaver himself came in for criticism from other opposition leaders who said the proposed budget deal had already made too many concessions to the left.

Joost Eerdmans, leader of the hardline conservative JA21, said the cabinet needed to “make the choice” between his party and Pro rather than trying to reach out to both.

In contrast to Pro, JA21 argues the cabinet should cut even more from the welfare bill to create room in the budget for tax cuts and measures to ease the cost of living.

Eerdmans also said plans to invest billions in climate change measures should be redirected to help working families. “The idea that we can change the world’s climate is unrealistic,” he said.

Two budgets

Eerdmans suggested to Paternotte that the cabinet should write two budgets, one for the left-wing parties and one for the right, and let MPs debate them both.

But Paternotte urged Eerdmans to “take off the rose-tinted glasses”. “How does that get you to a majority in the Senate?” he said. “Pro or JA21 on their own aren’t enough.”

Klaver’s pitch to the cabinet also prompted Socialist Party leader Jimmy Dijk to ask how far Pro was willing to compromise on healthcare spending.

Pro would not “work to break things down”, Klaver replied, but he saw potential to make savings by tackling “all kinds of treatments that aren’t necessary” and “taking the market out of youth care”.

Draft published

Paternotte also said D66 was willing to discuss surrogate parenthood with the SGP, which wants the cabinet to block any moves to legalise the practice as a condition for its support.

MPs also voted to ask the cabinet to publish the original draft budget by finance minister Eelco Heinen which was rejected by his coalition partners, prompting an extra weekend of negotiations.

NRC reported that the original version preserved most of the plans to cut welfare spending, despite Pro pressing for them to be taken off the table. In both the draft and the final version Heinen proposed delaying around half the cuts by a year.

World.title: Warsaw launches patrols to crack down on improperly parked electric scooters
World.content: Keep our news free from ads and paywalls by making a donation to support our work! Warsaw has launched special joint patrols by its municipal police and roads authority to check whether electric scooters are being parked legally and in keeping with rules introduced under a recent agreement with rental firms. According to the city’s mayor, Rafał Trzaskowski, more than 140 improperly parked scooters have been towed away within just a few days. Under the agreement, their operators now face potential fines. Nie ma miejsca dla hulajnóg tam, gdzie nie ich miejsce. Zdecydowałem o uruchomieniu specjalnych patroli Straży Miejskiej i ZDM. W ciągu ostatnich kliku dni dzięki ich pracy odholowanych zostało ponad 140 nieprawidłowo zaparkowanych hulajnóg elektrycznych. Taką możliwość daje… pic.twitter.com/U5fd7YDN8U — Rafał Trzaskowski (@trzaskowski_) September 16, 2026 “There’s no place for scooters where they don’t belong,” Trzaskowski said in a social media post announcing the patrols. “There are specific provisions, agreements and legal regulations – and action is being taken. No leniency.” An agreement reached between the city and three scooter operators – Bolt, Dott and Lime – in May expanded the number of streets where the vehicles are subject to a maximum speed of 12 km/h (7.5 mph) and increased the areas where their use is entirely prohibited. It also introduced measures to prevent scooters from being left in places where parking is illegal. Riding and parking electric scooters was banned in several areas of Warsaw, including popular tourist attractions such as the Old Town, Krasiński Garden and Łazienki Park. Trzaskowski added that the city has now expanded the list of areas covered by the ban, as permitted under the agreement. He did not, however, provide the new list. The agreement requires operators to programme their scooters so they cannot enter areas where riding is prohibited or be parked in places where parking is illegal, including on bridges, in tunnels, in residential areas and on streets where the pavement is too narrow to allow legal parking. Operators can be fined when scooters are left in violation of the rules. The city says that, despite electric scooters accounting for just under 8% of all traffic on cycle lanes, their riders were found to be responsible for 39 of the 66 accidents recorded on cycle lanes last year. Those accidents resulted in 73 injuries. Concerns over the safety of electric scooters have also prompted the national government to introduce stricter rules, including a nationwide requirement for children under 16 to wear a bicycle helmet when riding bicycles and electric scooters, which took effect in early June. Poland first introduced regulations governing electric scooters in 2021, formally setting out rules for their use. Under those rules, scooters are generally required to use cycle lanes where available, with their maximum speed capped at 20 km/h. The Polish government has moved to introduce new rules on the use of electric scooters. E-scooters, which are currently unregulated in Poland, have been blamed for hundreds of accidents annually, with half of victims being pedestrians hit by riders https://t.co/TcrfPQocfr — Notes from Poland 🇵🇱 (@notesfrompoland) February 3, 2021 Under the nationwide legislation, electric scooters must be parked parallel to the outer edge of the pavement, and municipal authorities have the power to penalise those responsible for improper parking – a provision that primarily affects rental companies. A year after the legislation was introduced, after the first report on e-scooter-related accidents showed that they had caused hundreds of injuries and three deaths in 2021, Poland’s police launched a campaign publicising the new rules. At national level, infrastructure minister Dariusz Klimczak has announced further restrictions the government is working on, including a new law requiring scooters to be collected and left only in specially designated zones. The police have launched a campaign on the legal requirements for using e-scooters, including a warning that riding or parking them on pavements can be illegal. In 2022, accidents involving e-scooters in Poland resulted in 421 injuries and three deaths https://t.co/dMOBiNUBNG — Notes from Poland 🇵🇱 (@notesfrompoland) May 15, 2023 Notes from Poland is run by a small editorial team and published by an independent, non-profit foundation that is funded through donations from our readers. World.title: Polish right-wing opposition MPs call for Independence Day march in Ukrainian city of Lviv
World.content: Keep our news free from ads and paywalls by making a donation to support our work! Notes from Poland is run by a small editorial team and is published by an independent, non-profit foundation that is funded through donations from our readers. We cannot do what we do without your support. A group of MPs from Poland’s main right-wing and far-right opposition parties have jointly called on the government to organise a march on Polish Independence Day in the Ukrainian city of Lviv, which was historically part of Poland. The idea has been firmly rejected by figures from the ruling coalition, who have called it “gross stupidity” and “madness”. It is also unclear to what extent the leadership of the opposition parties support the proposal. Pomysł zorganizowania "polskiego Marszu Niepodległości ulicami Lwowa" połączył polityków całej prawicy: PiS, Konfederacji, Rozwoju Plus i Konfederacji Korony Polskiej. Odsłaniamy kulisy. Pisze @patrykmichalski, autor programu #NewsMichalskiego ⤵️ 🔵 https://t.co/9L0M5lN0zY pic.twitter.com/1W3YxHdXHT — TVN24+ (@tvn24plus) September 15, 2026 The suggestion was made in a so-called parliamentary interpellation – through which MPs can ask questions and make suggestions to the government – submitted this month and signed by a group of 21 opposition MPs. They called on the government to do more to support the ethnic Polish community that still lives in Lviv, arguing that neither the Polish nor the Ukrainian state does enough to help them preserve and celebrate their identity. By contrast, argued the signatories, Polish state entities provide funding for Ukrainian organisations and events in Poland, including celebrations of Ukrainian Independence Day on 24 August. As such, they called upon the government to “organise official celebrations of [Polish] Independence Day in Lviv, including a Polish Independence March through the streets of the city” on 11 November. This would be “a concrete sign of remembrance and solidarity with Poles living in Ukraine”. Among the 21 signatories, 14 are from the caucus of the national-conservative Law and Justice (PiS), Poland’s ruling party between 2015 and 2023 and now the largest opposition group. A further three are from Confederation (Konfederacja), a far-right opposition group. One is from Development Plus (Rozwój Plus), a group that broke away from PiS earlier this year; another is from Confederation of the Polish Crown (KKP), a radical-right, pro-Russian party led by Grzegorz Braun. The final two are an independent, Janusz Kowalski, who recently quit PiS; and Jarosław Sachajko, who was elected in 2023 on the PiS party list but is part of the small Direct Democracy (Demokracja Bezpośrednia) group associated with Paweł Kukiz, a right-wing, anti-establishment figure. Interpelacja do Prezesa Rady Ministrów w sprawie zorganizowania 11 listopada polskiego Marszu Niepodległości ulicami Lwowa 11 listopada Rzeczpospolita Polska obchodzi Narodowe Święto Niepodległości. Jest to święto wszystkich Polaków, również tych, którzy mieszkają poza granicami… pic.twitter.com/7m6yUg1iKZ — Dariusz Matecki (@DariuszMatecki) August 25, 2026 It remains unclear to what extent the MPs have the backing of their parties in calling for the government to organise an Independence Day march in Lviv. Indeed, when Krzysztof Bosak, one of the leaders of Confederation, was asked about the idea on Wednesday, he appeared to know very little about it. Speaking to broadcaster RMF, Bosak said that he had first heard about the proposal on Tuesday and that, after looking into it, he said it appeared to be a “stunt”, and one that he felt was “unnecessary”. “I think the point is to draw attention to the fact that Polish institutions are participating in the celebration of Ukraine’s Independence Day in Warsaw, and that there should be some symmetry,” said Bosak. However, he added that he felt many people would not understand this intention. “The appeal should be directed at Ukrainian institutions, not the Polish foreign ministry,” he said, adding that the MPs who came up with the idea should better explain it. “Frankly, I have more serious matters to attend to.” Czy przemarsz Polaków ulicami Lwowa z okazji Dnia Niepodległości to dobry pomysł? Zdaniem @krzysztofbosak niepotrzebny, a traktować go należy w kategorii happeningu. Ale jeśli się trzymać zasady wzajemności, to już lepiej organizować coś podobnego… w Kijowie. pic.twitter.com/PxdqNKBlCC — Ekonomat (@ekonomat_pl) September 16, 2026 Throughout much of history, Lviv (known in Polish as Lwów) was part of the Polish state, most recently during the period between the First and Second World Wars. However, amid postwar border movements, it became part of Ukraine along with some other former Polish territories. Many in Poland still feel a sense of attachment to the former Polish “borderlands” (kresy) that are now located in Ukraine, Lithuania and Belarus, and which are still home to at least hundreds of thousands of ethnic Poles (though the exact number is a matter of dispute). In Lviv itself, the most recent Ukrainian national census, taken in 2001, showed just under 10,000 people declaring Polish ethnicity in the city (around 1% of the population), though some estimates put the figure higher. Poland's culture minister has condemned Russia's attacks on the historic centre of Lviv in Ukraine, a UNESCO World Heritage site. She noted that Lviv, which was once part of Poland, represents the "shared history of Ukraine, Poland and all of Europe" https://t.co/qPhqXMAZ9r — Notes from Poland 🇵🇱 (@notesfrompoland) March 25, 2026 Last year, Confederation’s other main leader, Sławomir Mentzen, clashed with the mayor of Lviv, Andriy Sadovyi, after visiting the city and criticising a monument commemorating nationalist leader Stepan Bandera, a figure seen as a hero by many in Ukraine but regarded as a war criminal in Poland. Followers of Bandera were responsible for the so-called Volhynia massacres during World War Two, in which Ukrainian nationalists massacred around 100,000 ethnic Polish civilians. Poland regards the killings as a genocide but Ukraine rejects that label. The issue has caused renewed tension this year after President Volodymyr Zelensky named a Ukrainian military unit after the “heroes of the Ukrainian Insurgent Army”, which led the massacres. Any Polish attempt at a state-backed Independence Day march in Ukraine would likely stir further controversy. A leading candidate in Poland’s presidential election has clashed with a Ukrainian mayor after visiting his city and criticising the presence of a monument to Stepan Bandera, who is seen as a hero by many in Ukraine but regarded as a war criminal in Poland https://t.co/nA9JzMmBcg — Notes from Poland 🇵🇱 (@notesfrompoland) February 26, 2025 Although the Polish government has not yet officially responded to the opposition MPs’ interpellation, a number of figures from the ruling coalition – which ranges from left to centre right – criticised the idea on Wednesday. Deputy defence minister Cezary Tomczyk called it “gross stupidity” to think of organising such a march in Ukraine, especially at a time of war. He asked how Poles would feel if Germany tried to organise a similar march in Poland (some of whose current territory was part of Germany before World War Two). Both Dariusz Wieczorek, an MP from The Left (Lewica), and Marek Biernacki from the centre-right Polish People’s Party (PSL) told broadcaster TVN that the idea was “madness”. Próba zorganizowania we Lwowie prawicowej prowokacji z udziałem PiS-u, Rozwój Plus i Brauna to jednoznaczne działanie na rzecz Rosji i przeciwko polskiej racji stanu. — Witold Zembaczyński🇵🇱 (@WZembaczynski) September 16, 2026 Notes from Poland is run by a small editorial team and published by an independent, non-profit foundation that is funded through donations from our readers. World.title: European Parliament strips Polish far-right leader of immunity to face Holocaust denial charge
World.content: Keep our news free from ads and paywalls by making a donation to support our work! Notes from Poland is run by a small editorial team and is published by an independent, non-profit foundation that is funded through donations from our readers. We cannot do what we do without your support. The European Parliament has again stripped Polish far-right leader Grzegorz Braun of legal immunity to face charges in his homeland of denying Nazi crimes, an offence that carries a potential prison sentence of up to three years. The decision marks the sixth time that the European Parliament has lifted Braun’s immunity, and the second time for charges of Holocaust denial. Braun is already on trial in Poland for an attack on a Jewish religious celebration in parliament and is facing a number of other legal cases. Parlament Europejski w głosowaniu w Strasburgu uchylił immunitet europosła Grzegorza Brauna. Sprawa dotyczy negowania przez niego Holokaustu. Więcej: https://t.co/rB3UPUiS8o pic.twitter.com/icRLEqsWmF — Gazeta.pl (@gazetapl_news) September 15, 2026 In a vote on Tuesday, a majority of MEPs voted in favour of a request, submitted in February by Poland’s justice minister, Waldemar Żurek, to lift the immunity enjoyed by Braun as an MEP. He has sat in the European Parliament since being elected in 2024. In his request, Żurek said that Polish prosecutors wish to charge Braun in relation to “denial of genocide crimes committed by functionaries of the Third Reich in the Auschwitz-Birkenau concentration camp and the Lublin concentration camp (Majdanek)”. Poland’s Institute of National Remembrance (IPN), a state historical body that has prosecutorial power, also revealed that the accusation relates to the use of gas chambers at those two camps. Neither the IPN nor Żurek confirmed at the time what specific words Braun had said that prompted the planned charges against him. However, the IPN noted that they had come at a live event broadcast online on 27 September 2025. On that date, Braun took part in a discussion with Jan Żaryn, a right-wing historian and former senator for the national-conservative Law and Justice (PiS) party, titled “The Polish Underground State and the Jewish Issue”. A recording of the event is still available online. During his remarks, Braun referred to the “fake gas chambers of Majdanek and Auschwitz”, calling them “a dark, monstrous fantasy that has no satisfactory historical or academic support”. He suggested that the idea of the gas chambers had been invented as part of “propaganda and black PR operations conducted by the Soviet and Anglo-Saxon security services during World War Two”, and that the false claim continues to be exploited by Jews today. The European Parliament has again voted to strip Polish far-right leader Grzegorz Braun of immunity to face further charges for Holocaust denial as well as various antisemitic, anti-Ukrainian and anti-LGBT incidents during last year's presidential campaign https://t.co/4EHVEuSDnM — Notes from Poland 🇵🇱 (@notesfrompoland) March 26, 2026 In actual fact, historians estimate that around 900,000 people were killed in the gas chambers at Auschwitz. The vast majority were Jews, but victims also included Roma, Soviet prisoners of war, and ethnic Poles. Meanwhile, gas chambers at Majdanek were used to kill tens of thousands, again mainly Jews. Today, the ashes of the camp’s cremated victims are preserved in a memorial at the site of the former camp. Braun, who has a long history of promoting antisemitic conspiracy theories, has repeatedly sought to cast doubt on the veracity of Nazi crimes against Jews. Last month, he was charged with denying Nazi crimes in a separate case over earlier comments in which he called Auschwitz’s gas chambers “fake”. Polish far-right leader Grzegorz Braun has been charged with denying Nazi crimes, a criminal offence in Poland that carries a prison sentence of up to three years, for statements he made suggesting that the gas chambers at Auschwitz are "fake" https://t.co/PCssZt5eXD — Notes from Poland 🇵🇱 (@notesfrompoland) August 25, 2026 In December, Braun went on trial over a separate set of charges relating to four other incidents, including his attack on a celebration of the Jewish festival of Hanukkah in parliament in December 2023 and his disruption of a lecture by a Holocaust scholar. “I am standing before this court because I dared to defend myself against oppression and the ritual manifestation of Jewish supremacy,” declared Braun at the start of the trial, which remains ongoing. Braun is also facing various legal cases relating to his anti-Ukrainian and anti-LGBT actions. Last week, he posted a video of himself using a hammer to vandalise a monument in Poland dedicated to the Ukrainian Insurgent Army (UPA). Police are investigating that incident. Polish far-right leader Grzegorz Braun has published a video of himself using a hammer to attack a monument in Poland to soldiers from the Ukrainian Insurgent Army, a WWII group that fought against the Soviets but was also responsible for massacring Poles https://t.co/oCYRtNRO9N — Notes from Poland 🇵🇱 (@notesfrompoland) September 11, 2026 Braun’s high-profile stunts have seen his popularity surge among a section of the electorate. He finished a surprise fourth in last year’s Polish presidential election, with over 6% of the vote, and his Confederation of the Polish Crown (KKP) party is now polling around 8-9%. If it manages to secure that level of support at next year’s parliamentary elections, KKP could become a key player in deciding what kind of government can be formed after what looks likely to be a very close contest between the ruling coalition, which ranges from left to centre right, and the right-wing and far-right opposition. An MEP from the ruling coalition, Michał Kobosko, welcomed Tuesday’s decision to lift Braun’s immunity, saying that the far-right leader “deliberately and consciously…stokes hatred”. Kobosko said that such actions are particularly dangerous at a time when Russia is “actively waging hybrid and cognitive war against Poland”. He noted that Braun and his party have taken a sympathetic position towards Russia, including calling for Poland to “normalise” relations with Moscow. Figures from Polish far-right leader Grzegorz Braun's party celebrated Russia Day at the Russian embassy and presented a letter hailing Russia's development, blaming "globalists" for the Ukraine war and calling for normalisation of Polish-Russian relations https://t.co/SU3gEdVod0 — Notes from Poland 🇵🇱 (@notesfrompoland) June 13, 2026 Notes from Poland is run by a small editorial team and published by an independent, non-profit foundation that is funded through donations from our readers. World.title: China overtakes Germany as Poland’s biggest source of imports for first time
World.content: Keep our news free from ads and paywalls by making a donation to support our work! Notes from Poland is run by a small editorial team and is published by an independent, non-profit foundation that is funded through donations from our readers. We cannot do what we do without your support. China overtook Germany to become Poland’s biggest source of imports for the first time in July, according to new data from the central bank. It ends a period of around 35 years in which Germany had consistently held top spot. The shift came as imports of Chinese goods surged, driven in part by a sharp increase in Chinese cars, while imports from Germany declined. “In July 2026, China was the largest supplier of goods to Poland for the first time, overtaking Germany in that month,” wrote the National Bank of Poland (NBP) in an announcement on Monday. “A significant increase in imports of computer hardware, passenger cars and durable consumer goods influenced the shift in the geographical structure of imports,” added the bank. Znamy już pełne dane handlowe za lipiec 2026 – za miesiąc kiedy Chiny po raz pierwszy w historii stały się największym dostawcą towarów do Polski, przed Niemcami. W lipcu import ogółem z Chin wzrósł o 28,8% r/r, podczas gdy z Niemiec spadł o 1,8% r/r. Import pojazdów… pic.twitter.com/LfJ50nXzNM — PKO Research (@PKO_Research) September 15, 2026 In a comment on the new data, analysts at PKO, a Polish bank, said that the July shift was partly due to “one-time factors” and noted that Germany remains Poland’s largest supplier on a 12-month basis, although its lead has been steadily shrinking. In July, Polish imports from China rose 28.8% year-on-year, while imports from Germany fell 1.8%, according to PKO. Imports of motor vehicles from Germany fell 9.3% year-on-year, while imports from China rose 54.4%. Imports from China of computers, electronics and optical equipment rose 31.5% year-on-year in July, the strongest increase since 2022. More detailed data on trade with the two countries, published also on Tuesday by Statistics Poland (GUS), a state agency, provided further insight into the shift. According to GUS, Poland imported goods worth €36.7 billion from China in the first seven months of the year, giving China a 15.9% share of total Polish imports, up from 14.9% in the same period of 2025. Imports from Germany stood at €43.1 billion in that period, 18.6% of the total, down from 19.4% in 2025. Poland’s third-largest source of imports was the United States, with €12.7 worth of goods, a share of 5.5%, up from 4.9% in 2025. Poland has been NATO's biggest importer of arms over the last five years, according to new data from @SIPRIorg. Over 90% of Polish imports have come from South Korea and the United States https://t.co/jij0nfbhFc — Notes from Poland 🇵🇱 (@notesfrompoland) March 9, 2026 Germany has been Poland’s largest trading partner since the collapse of communism, leading both in imports and exports. It overtook the Soviet Union, which had dominated Poland’s foreign trade during the communist era. But China has steadily gained ground as a source of Polish imports since the 2010s, rising to second place behind Germany by the 2020s. In terms of exports in the first seven months of this year, Germany dominates, receiving goods worth €69.8 billion, or 26.3% of all Poland’s exports. It is followed by the Czech Republic (€14.3 billion), France (€14.0 billion), the United Kingdom (€11.6 billion) and the Netherlands (€10.9 billion). World.title: Polish PM condemns “disgrace” of failed Venezuela oil deal under former government following FT report
World.content: Keep our news free from ads and paywalls by making a donation to support our work! Notes from Poland is run by a small editorial team and is published by an independent, non-profit foundation that is funded through donations from our readers. We cannot do what we do without your support. Prime Minister Donald Tusk says that Poland has been “disgraced in front of the entire world” by a new Financial Times report on how Polish state energy firm Orlen lost $230 million (856 million zloty) trying to buy Venezuelan oil through intermediaries, unsecured payments and cryptocurrency transfers. Tusk called the case a further example of “dirty deals” conducted under the former national-conservative Law and Justice (PiS) government, which was in power at the time. Orlen was then led by Daniel Obajtek, who is now a member of the European Parliament representing PiS. Obajtek himself today said that he wants the issue to be clarified in court and suggested that the current authorities are using the case to distract from current soaring fuel prices. How Poland lost $230mn trying to buy Venezuelan oil with crypto https://t.co/Xo07JkYy1t — Financial Times (@FT) September 15, 2026 In a report today, the FT provided new details on a case that has already drawn public attention in Poland. In April 2024, Orlen revealed that its Swiss oil trading subsidiary had lost around $400 million in prepayments for Venezuelan oil and petroleum products that were never delivered. Orlen, which was under new management after Obajtek had been fired earlier that year following the arrival of Tusk’s government, said that the losses included around $240 million paid to a Dubai-based intermediary run by a 25-year-old from Hong Kong. A week later, Polish prosecutors announced that they had launched an investigation into the case, focusing on Orlen Trading Switzerland (OTS), the subsidiary that oversaw the Venezuela deal. Polish prosecutors have launched an investigation into OTS, @GrupaORLEN's Swiss subsidiary which had lost $400 million on prepayments for oil that was never delivered. It also announced that the homes of Orlen's former senior management had been searchedhttps://t.co/QQ5QJMsHg4 — Notes from Poland 🇵🇱 (@notesfrompoland) May 1, 2024 The FT detailed how the then head of OTS, a Lebanese-born Polish citizen of Palestinian descent, who can be named only as Samer A. under Polish privacy law, had sought in 2023 to commission the import of Venezuelan oil through intermediaries, who were given a $230 million advance without any security or guarantees. Although the United States, under then-President Joe Biden, had temporarily suspended sanctions on Venezuelan oil, allowing companies such as Orlen to buy it, Venezuela’s state oil company, PDVSA, remained largely cut off from the global financial system. The FT detailed how the intermediaries therefore sought to use cryptocurrency to facilitate the deal. However, although oil tankers leased by Orlen to collect the oil sat waiting (accruing further large costs), the promised oil was not delivered, and Orlen’s advance payments were lost. The issue is now the subject of a criminal investigation in Poland and an ongoing arbitration case with the intermediary in Dubai, Hannon International. Speaking ahead of a meeting of his cabinet on Tuesday, Tusk said that the FT story is a “disgrace in front of the entire world”. He called the Venezuelan oil incident “the biggest scandal, or one of the biggest scandals, in our country’s history”. Turning his aim on the opposition, he said that the case includes “everything that has recently been associated with PiS”, including “dirty deals” and cryptocurrencies. That was a reference to an ongoing investigation into alleged links between a collapsed crypto firm, Zondacrypto, and figures associated with the opposition. Tusk also noted that opposition-aligned President Karol Nawrocki has recently blocked government bills intended to better regulate crypto markets and to levy a windfall tax on fuel firms. “We may be dealing with a network of dirty and highly dangerous dealings,” said the prime minister. 💬 Premier @donaldtusk: Cała Polska dzisiaj to komentuje. Wstyd na cały świat. Financial Times pisze o jednym z największych skandali w historii naszego kraju i cały świat dzisiaj o tym czyta. pic.twitter.com/Ej17Csi4DL — Kancelaria Premiera (@PremierRP) September 15, 2026 Later on Tuesday, the regional prosecutor’s office in Warsaw also responded to the FT article by issuing a statement providing an update on the investigation into the Venezuelan oil deal. They noted that the Polish authorities are continuing to seek the extradition of Samer A. from the United Arab Emirates, which last year rejected a request from Poland for him to be extradited. The prosecutors also reported today that, last month, they issued indictments against three former senior Orlen and OTS executives for failing to fulfil their duties to oversee the companies’ assets, resulting in losses of $378 million. Prosecutors have charged the former head of the charitable foundation of Polish state energy giant Orlen for allowing its funds to be used to support a political campaign of the former ruling PiS party in violation of the foundation's statute https://t.co/w1Xtmivn0I — Notes from Poland 🇵🇱 (@notesfrompoland) March 6, 2026 Obajtek himself responded to the FT’s story, writing on social media that the newspaper “describes an important part of the OTS case”. He then suggested that the new management of OTS had terminated the Venezuelan oil contract too quickly, saying that the oil could in fact have been delivered. “I hope this matter will be fully clarified, including before a Polish court!” wrote Obajtek. In a further post, he suggested that Orlen and the authorities are “trying to cover up current issues again, such as the most expensive fuel in history”. In response, Orlen’s press office wrote under one of Obajtek’s posts that they would “help [him] with English”. “The article is about how your team transferred hundreds of millions of dollars to a company owned by a 25-year-old from Dubai. He converted them into cryptocurrencies, which he copied onto USB drives. And then he handed them out in restaurants to people posing as oil traders…In this story, only Orlen’s money, which they lost, was real.” Panie Pośle, pomożemy z angielskim. Artykuł jest o tym, jak pana ekipa przelała setki milionów dolarów do firmy 25-latka z Dubaju. On zamienił je na kryptowaluty, które zgrał na pendrivy. A później rozdawał w restauracjach ludziom, podającym się za handlarzy ropą. To jak „kupić”… — Biuro Prasowe ORLEN (@b_prasoweORLEN) September 15, 2026 Obajtek rose rapidly under the former PiS government, which ruled Poland from 2015 to 2023. He went from being the mayor of Pcim, a rural commune of 11,000 people in southern Poland, to the CEO of Orlen, Poland’s biggest company, in the space of three years. Under Obajtek’s leadership, Orlen expanded rapidly, swallowing up other state energy firms and expanding into new areas of activity. By 2023, it was ranked among Europe’s 50 biggest companies. However, Obajtek was also accused of using the company’s considerable resources to support PiS politically, including through Orlen’s purchases of hundreds of local media outlets – many of whose editors were replaced with PiS-friendly figures – and lowering fuel prices ahead of the 2023 elections. Last year, at Poland’s request, the European Parliament stripped Obajtek of legal immunity to face charges for allegedly using Orlen’s funds to serve his own private interests. Polish prosecutors are also pursuing him for allegedly violating Poland’s press law and falsely reporting his income in a tax return. World.title: “Don’t be a creep”: Polish ice cream company launches campaign against sexual harassment of staff
World.content: Keep our news free from ads and paywalls by making a donation to support our work! Notes from Poland is run by a small editorial team and is published by an independent, non-profit foundation that is funded through donations from our readers. We cannot do what we do without your support. A Polish ice cream chain has launched a campaign to stamp out sexual harassment of staff by customers, including empowering employees to refuse to serve such clients. The campaign is based around the fact that the Polish word for ice cream, “lody”, also has an informal vulgar meaning, referring to oral sex. The company, Good Lood, which runs 37 outlets, says that its female staff regularly suffer lewd comments from male customers incorporating this double entendre. In response, in late August it launched a campaign titled “Nie bądź oblechem”, meaning “Don’t be a creep”, with information displayed prominently at its ice cream stands and on its social media platforms. The firm said it condemned “crude remarks, inappropriate jokes and verbal harassment directed at service workers” and promised to support its staff in dealing with them. “Everyone deserves respect, without exception!” Good Lood advised employees to respond to inappropriate comments with a short, firm retort such as “Great, that’s the 20th time I’ve heard that” or “Perhaps you could repeat that more loudly, so the rest of the queue can hear?” It also called on other customers to react if they witnessed such behaviour. In a follow-up social media post last week, the company confirmed that staff had its backing if they decided not to serve a customer. “If someone is a creep and makes inappropriate comments and verbally harasses them, our team have the right to refuse them service.” That post alone has so far garnered more than 50,000 likes or other positive responses on Facebook. Good Lood says that its messages posted as part of the campaign have already received over 10 million organic views on social media. Comments on the company’s posts show overwhelming support, with many commenters sharing their own experiences. “At last someone has spoken out about this!” wrote one, who said she worked in an ice cream parlour as a teenager. “I remember how outraged I felt when I heard comments like that from men who could have been my fathers, or even my grandfathers. I wonder what would happen if someone spoke to their daughters or granddaughters like that.” Good Lood says it want to start a broader conversation on the “global issue” of harassment and disrespect towards front-line staff in retail and hospitality. “Working in service or hospitality does not mean consenting to disrespect. The safety and wellbeing of our team will always come before profit. We are not afraid to lose a customer who cannot show basic human respect,” the company said in a press release. Founded 10 years ago in Kraków, Good Lood now has 37 outlets there as well as in the Warsaw area. It also sells its products throughout Poland at Biedronka, the country’s largest supermarket chain. World.content: Keep our news free from ads and paywalls by making a donation to support our work! Poland’s interior ministry has launched a TV campaign, including spots on public broadcaster TVP’s flagship morning show, aimed at educating the public about how to respond to emergency situations such as natural disasters and security threats. The initiative comes as Poland has faced growing threats from Russia, including acts of sabotage and the entry of missiles and drones into Polish airspace. Prime Minister Donald Tusk warned this week that there may be an “escalation” of such actions in the coming weeks and months. 📺 Dzisiejsza wizyta w programie „Pytanie na Śniadanie” odbyła się w ramach naszej nowej kampanii „ Minuta dla twojego bezpieczeństwa”! Rozmawialiśmy o sprawach fundamentalnych – o bezpieczeństwie. Mogliście sprawdzić, czy wiecie, co oznaczają sygnały alarmowe oraz krok po kroku… pic.twitter.com/ARta1Pqmlz — MSWiA 🇵🇱 (@MSWiA_GOV_PL) September 8, 2026 The new campaign will include weekend segments on the TVP1 channel and a series of pieces aired during TVP2’s breakfast show, Pytanie na śniadanie, which had an average audience of 322,000 in August, according to Nielsen Media data. The weekend programmes will introduce topics such as floods, fires, extreme weather, power outages, chemical contamination, evacuation, cybersecurity, disinformation and first aid. Specialists will then discuss the subjects in greater detail during the morning segments. The ministry says the content is based on its official security handbook, which it sent to all 17 million Polish households earlier this year, and is intended to help people prepare for emergencies before they occur. “We only find out whether we’re prepared for difficult situations when they actually arise,” said Mateusz Jarecki, who is presenting the segments. “That’s why, in collaboration with specialists, we’ve produced a series of short, easy-to-follow videos that will help you prepare for various life scenarios.” The government is sending copies of a booklet advising how to prepare for and act in emergencies to all 17 million households in Poland. The guide includes information on what to do in the event of military attacks, terrorist threats and natural disasters https://t.co/xIaRQ2ie5N — Notes from Poland 🇵🇱 (@notesfrompoland) January 12, 2026 According to Presserwis, a newsletter by media industry magazine Press, the ministry will spend 5.4 million zloty (€1.3 million) on broadcasting the campaign during Pytanie na śniadanie. The agreement with the public broadcaster, signed on 4 September, includes 16 short segments and seven commentary pieces, according to Presserwis. Pytanie na śniadanie’s website so far shows two segments with material from the series. One explains what to do when an evacuation order is issued, while the other covers what should be included in an emergency kit. The campaign comes following recent criticism from the opposition over how the government communicates with citizens during emergencies. Amid Russian mass attacks on western Ukraine this week, including strikes on a train and a truck near the Polish border, residents of eastern Poland received mobile phone alerts from the Government Security Centre (RCB) warning of air strikes and urging them to seek shelter. However, Beata Mazurek, a senior figure from the opposition Law and Justice (PiS) party, criticised the messages for “spreading panic without providing instructions” on where people should shelter. “Where are we supposed to go? That seems to be the most basic piece of information. The threat is real, but the instructions are incomplete,” she wrote on X. Pani poseł @beatamk zablokowała komentarze, więc odpowiadamy tutaj. This is knowledge that comes in handy precisely in such situations,” wrote Gałecka. Last December, the interior ministry launched a mobile application and website that helps people to find their nearest shelter. In July this year, opposition figures also criticised the government when a Russian missile entered Polish airspace and landed in a field. They claimed that local residents were not provided with clear warnings and information about the threat and how to respond. World.title: Moose on the loose at Warsaw’s main station brings trains to a standstill
World.content: Keep our news free from ads and paywalls by making a donation to support our work! Notes from Poland is run by a small editorial team and is published by an independent, non-profit foundation that is funded through donations from our readers. We cannot do what we do without your support. A moose wandered onto the tracks at Warsaw Central Station on Sunday evening, disrupting rail services in the Polish capital for more than 80 minutes before it was safely removed. The animal first appeared on a platform before moving onto the tracks, forcing Polish Railway Lines (PLK), the company responsible for Poland’s rail infrastructure, to suspend, cancel and divert several train services. View this post on Instagram A post shared by TVP3 Warszawa (@tvp3warszawa) Videos and photographs shared online showed the moose lying on the tracks and running along the railway line at Warsaw Central, the capital’s busiest station, which is mainly underground and therefore not easy for such a large animal to access. Police do not know how the moose ended up at the station, reports broadcaster TVN24. Officers were first alerted at 7:10 pm on Sunday and cordoned off the platform where the animal was located. When emergency services arrived, the moose was tranquilised. It was then placed on a large sheet and carried out of the station by police officers and emergency workers before being loaded onto a specialist vehicle to be returned to a forested area. PLK, which named the moose Emil, later confirmed that the animal had been safely removed and that normal train services were being restored. The company added that the disruptions lasted just over 80 minutes, using a pun combining the Polish words for moose (łoś) and 80 (osiemdziesiąt) to produce the word “łosiemdziesiąt”. ❗Aktualizacja❗Zwierze zostało bezpiecznie zabrane z torów. Przywracana jest rozkładowa organizacja ruchu pociągów. Utrudnienia trwały przeszło łosiemdziesiąt minut. https://t.co/Xui2B6SxyU — PLK SA (@PKP_PLK_SA) September 13, 2026 The Eurasian moose (also known as the Eurasian elk) has long been native to Poland, but by the mid-20th century hunting and habitat loss had brought the species close to extinction in the country. Its population subsequently recovered, reaching an estimated 6,000 animals by the 1980s and around 30,000 by 2019, helped by a moratorium on moose hunting introduced in 2001. Several hundred live in the Kampinos national park on the northwestern outskirts of Warsaw. They are therefore relatively frequent visitors to the capital, according to the Interia news website, although venturing onto train lines in the centre is unusual. The growth in the moose population, combined with urban expansion and changes to its habitat, has led to other high-profile encounters in areas inhabited by humans. In 2022, a moose was spotted on the roof of a shopping centre in the northern Polish city of Elbląg. A moose was this morning spotted on the roof of a shopping centre in Poland. World.title: Two New Squares and a Tower Planned Around Holešovice Station
World.content:
The area around Prague’s Nádraží Holešovice station is set for a major redevelopment after the international architectural competition for the site was won by Czech studio Chybík + Krištof.

The winning proposal envisions turning the current transport hub and surrounding brownfield into a new urban district, with two public squares, improved connections between public transport services and a new high-rise building designed to become a landmark.



The redevelopment covers roughly eight hectares around the station. Its aim is not only to add new buildings, but also to reorganise one of Prague’s important transport nodes and connect it more closely with the surrounding neighbourhood.

The competition jury selected the proposal by Chybík + Krištof as the winning design.

From transport hub to urban district

Nádraží Holešovice is currently one of Prague’s major transport interchanges, but much of the surrounding area has traditionally been used primarily for transport and other infrastructure.

The redevelopment is intended to change that. Alongside new construction, the project places emphasis on making transfers between different modes of public transport easier and fully accessible.

The project forms part of the wider Nové Holešovice development, which brings together the Prague Public Transit Company and private investors.

CPI Property, EP Real Estate, Penta Real Estate and AKIPIA are among the companies involved. The City of Prague and Prague 7 municipal district are also participating in the project.

World.title: ČokoFest to Bring Three Days of Chocolate to Galerie Harfa
World.content:
Chocolate lovers will have plenty to discover in Prague this October as ČokoFest 2026 returns to Galerie Harfa for three days of tastings, workshops, competitions and sweet treats.

The festival will take place from October 16 to 18, 2026, at the shopping center in Prague 9. Admission is free.



Now in its 14th year, ČokoFest brings together Czech and international producers, including established chocolatiers and smaller makers.

Visitors will be able to sample and buy a wide selection of chocolates and confectionery, including handmade and bean-to-bar products, pralines, cakes, cookies and macarons.

The festival will also feature a range of less conventional chocolate and sweet specialties. Among the offerings will be a chocolate fountain, chocolate kebabs, chocolate-covered fruit, as well as chocolate-infused wine and beer. Other products on sale will include jams, liqueurs, syrups, dried fruits, honey products, coffee and tea.

Exhibitors from several European countries will join Czech producers, giving visitors the opportunity to discover different chocolate styles and specialties while shopping at international sales stalls.

ČokoFest will also feature a program of activities for both adults and children. Visitors can take part in tastings, competitions and creative workshops, while children can enjoy a dedicated zone and entertainment from performers dressed as popular children’s characters.

Cooking demonstrations will be another part of the program, with chefs from local restaurants sharing their experience and showing visitors how to prepare various sweet treats. Some workshops will also focus on chocolate-making techniques that can be tried at home.

The festival is designed as a family-friendly event, with activities taking place throughout the three days. In addition to tasting and shopping, visitors can watch pastry chefs at work, take part in competitions and learn more about the production and preparation of chocolate and other confectionery.

Opening hours:

Friday, October 16: 2:00–6:00 p.m.

Saturday, October 17: 10:00 a.m.–6:30 p.m.

Sunday, October 18: 10:00 a.m.–5:00 p.m.

World.title: Poznej Vltavu Festival Returns to Prague on September 28
World.content:
The second edition of the Poznej Vltavu (Get to Know the Vltava) festival will take place across Prague on September 28, 2026.

For one day, the banks of the Vltava will host a programme exploring the river from a variety of perspectives.

The festival will feature workshops, exhibitions, sports activities, boat trips, and tours of places that are not normally open to the public.



Prague’s riverfront embankments and other locations along the Vltava will offer activities for children, adults, and seniors.

The festival aims to highlight the Vltava as a natural part of Prague’s urban environment and an important ecological feature, while giving visitors the opportunity to spend a day exploring the river and its surroundings.

Experts from a range of fields will discuss the Vltava in its broader context and offer insights into lesser-known aspects of the river.

This year’s programme will involve organisations including the Prague Institute of Planning and Development, Prague City Tourism, the Prague City Gallery, the Vltava River Authority, Prague Waterworks and Sewerage Company, the Prague Water Management Company, ROPID, Prague City Forests, the Nature Conservation Agency of the Czech Republic, and many others.

The festival area will extend farther along the Vltava this year, reaching Žluté lázně and the new Dvorecký Bridge, which has quickly become a popular destination for Prague residents since opening.

Most events will be free to attend, although some activities will require advance registration due to limited capacity.

More information is available on the festival’s Facebook event.

World.title: Red Arrows to Fly Over Charles Bridge This Friday
World.content:
Prague will hear the roar of Royal Air Force jets on Friday, September 18, when the Red Arrows aerobatic team stages a flypast over the city.

Ten BAE Hawk T1 aircraft from the British RAF team are scheduled to pass over the Charles Bridge at around 2:00 PM. The jets will leave smoke trails in the colours of the Czech flag during the display.



The formation is expected to approach Prague from the north before reaching the area around Václav Havel Airport. The aircraft will then form an arrow-shaped formation and fly around the western and southern parts of the capital before turning north along the Vltava.

The jets are expected to fly at an altitude of roughly 300 metres above the ground. The engines will be clearly audible across parts of the city, although the flypast itself will last only a short time.

After passing through central Prague, the formation will turn northeast and continue toward Ostrava. The city is hosting NATO Days, one of the Czech Republic’s largest military and security events, this weekend.

The timetable and route could still change because of weather or other air traffic in the Prague area. A similar Red Arrows flypast was held in Prague last September, but poor weather delayed the aircraft by more than an hour.

The flypast is being held in connection with Czech Air Force Day, which is observed on September 15.

The Red Arrows are the official aerobatic display team of the Royal Air Force and regularly perform at air shows and military events in Britain and abroad.

World.title: Groovy Market Fest Returns to Riegrovy Sady on October 3
World.content:
Prague’s Groovy Market Fest will return to Riegrovy Sady on Saturday, October 3, bringing together food, independent brands, design and live music for its third edition.

The one-day event will take place at Energy Pub from noon until 10 p.m.

Following two editions held during the summer, the organizers are extending the concept into the autumn, with visitors able to browse local products, eat street food and listen to live music and DJs throughout the day.



The market is organised around three main areas. The Food Garden will focus on gastronomy and street food from local businesses, while Palm Street will feature bakeries, artisanal products and other local goods. The Design Zone will bring together fashion, design and products from independent Czech brands.

Live performances and DJ sets will run from the afternoon into the evening, providing the musical programme alongside the market stalls.

Marek Novák, founder of Groovy Market Fest, said the first two editions helped the team establish the format and identify what visitors respond to.

“After two editions, we know exactly what works at Groovy Market Fest: high-quality local brands, good food, and an atmosphere that keeps people coming back,” Novák said. “This third edition is an opportunity for us to show that Groovy isn’t just a summer event, but a festival that holds a firm place in Prague all year round.”

Visitors can buy tickets for either of the two five-hour sessions. The first runs from 12 p.m. to 5 p.m., followed by a second session from 5:30 p.m. to 10 p.m.

A ticket for one session costs 100 CZK, while an all-day ticket covering both sessions is available for 190 CZK. Tickets are sold through GoOut.

View this post on Instagram A post shared by Groovy Market Fest (@groovymarketfest)

From Barcelona street food to a Prague market

Groovy Market Fest was founded by Marek Novák and Veronika Kracíková, a couple with experience in Prague’s food scene and Barcelona’s street-food sector.

One of their main inspirations was Barcelona’s Palo Alto Market, an urban market known for combining food, design, music and independent creative businesses.

World.title: Prague Run Day to Bring Six Races to Riegrovy Sady on September 19
World.content:
On September 19, runners of all levels can take part in a new running event combining track and park races in one of Prague’s best-known green spaces.

There are six different races to choose from, so whether you’re looking for a serious challenge or just want to get out and run, there’s an option for you.



Six races to choose from

The programme includes six races, ranging from a short family run to a one-hour challenge.

The day will begin with the 800m Family Run, designed for young runners and their accompanying adults. There will also be an 800m race on the athletic track, offering participants the opportunity to compete over a short distance in a traditional track setting.

For those looking for a longer challenge, the 1 Mile race will take place on the athletic oval. The organisers describe it as a special opportunity to race over the classic distance, with participation limited to a maximum of 30 runners.

The 5km Solo Run will offer a more familiar challenge for runners of different experience levels. It is followed by the 4x3km Relay, a team race in which four runners each complete two 1.5km laps.

The final event of the day will be the Golden Hour Race, a one-hour running challenge taking place during the golden hour.

The event will be based at the Sokol Vinohrady athletic oval, which will serve as the main hub for the day.

Find all race distances, times and registration details at praguerunday.cz

📍 Riegrovy Sady Athletic Oval

📅 Saturday, September 19

🏃 6 races for different levels

🏅 Medal for every participant

World.title: Prague Is Turning a Historic Factory Chimney Into an Observation Deck
World.content:
A glass elevator will carry visitors through the preserved chimney of a former distillery before emerging above its rim to reveal views of the city.

Inside the developing Lihovar district in Smíchov, a historic factory chimney is being transformed into a viewing platform, with visitors set to travel through the structure in a panoramic glass elevator.



The chimney, which stands approximately 50 meters tall, is part of the former Zlíchov distillery. Rather than demolishing the industrial landmark, developers have incorporated it into the redevelopment of the site.

The project is being developed by Trigema, which is building the new Lihovar district on the former distillery grounds.

The elevator itself is one of the project’s most unusual features. Once it reaches the top of the chimney, the cabin will lift a special cap weighing approximately 500 kilograms, allowing it to rise above the chimney’s opening.

The glass cabin will then serve as an observation deck, offering a 360-degree view of Prague.

From industrial site to new Prague district

The Lihovar development is being built on the site of the former Zlíchov distillery in Prague 5. The redevelopment includes new buildings alongside the preservation of selected elements of the original industrial complex.

The factory chimney is among the structures being retained. Another is the historic former brewhouse, which is planned for cultural use.

The opening date for the observation deck has not been announced.

World.title: Riegrovy Sady to Host Goodbye Summer Party With Three Live Acts
World.content:
Summer may be drawing to a close, but the music season at Riegrovy Sady is not over yet.

On Thursday, 17 September, Energy Pub will host the Goodbye Summer Party, organised by Ploom in cooperation with Energy Pub.



The evening will feature a DJ set by Forgen, a performance by Jirka Drtil and a live concert by Renne Dang, following his sold-out show at Forum Karlín.

Tickets cost CZK 100 and the event is open exclusively to guests aged 18 and over.

The last long days and warm evenings of summer will get a musical send-off at Riegrovy Sady. The Goodbye Summer Party is designed for everyone who is not quite ready to say a final goodbye to summer and wants to enjoy one of the last outdoor evenings of the season.

The evening will kick off with a set by DJ Forgen, followed by a performance by musician Jirka Drtil. The main highlight of the evening will be a concert by Renne Dang, Ploom brand ambassador, whose current music blends elements of rap, pop and pop-punk.

His distinctive personal lyrics and energetic guitar-driven sound have already taken him to some of the country’s biggest stages. His recent achievements include a sold-out concert at Forum Karlín.

The Last Party of the Summer

Music will not be the only reason to head to Riegrovy Sady in September. The evening will also feature a dedicated Ploom zone, where adult guests can take a break during the programme and enjoy the atmosphere of one last summer party.

Every ticket holder will also receive a complimentary welcome drink. A food pop-up by Pavel Berky will be part of the event as well.

When: Thursday, 17 September 2026, doors open at 6:00 PM

Where: Energy Pub, Riegrovy Sady 28, Prague 2

Line-up: DJ Forgen, Jirka Drtil, Renne Dang

Tickets: CZK 100, including a welcome drink

Entry: 18+ only

Capacity: Limited

World.title: Türkiye’s road to COP31: From Ankara’s zero-waste ambitions to a greener Black Sea – Video
World.content:
There are easier ways to explain climate policy than standing beside a landfill outside Ankara. But there may be few more effective ones. Over four days in September, the Road to COP31: Sustainable Future International Media Programme took us journalists from Türkiye’s capital to the Black Sea city of Trabzon, moving between waste plants, climate diplomacy, fisheries laboratories and, finally, a centuries-old monastery clinging improbably to a mountainside.

Organised by Türkiye’s Directorate of Communications and Ministry of Environment, Urbanisation and Climate Change from 9 to 12 September, the programme was designed to demonstrate what the country wants COP31 in Antalya to be about: not simply another climate conference, but what officials repeatedly described as an “Implementation COP”.

How Ankara turns landfill waste into tomatoes

The first stop provided perhaps the most tangible example. Ankara’s ITC Integrated Solid Waste Facility handles waste recovery, recycling and disposal while generating energy from what would otherwise be discarded. Landfill methane is captured through pipes and converted into electricity. According to ITC, its projects reduce carbon emissions by about 2m tonnes annually, with some certified under the Gold Standard.

There was a more unexpected statistic: “one tomato saves five tonnes of carbon”. ITC uses waste heat from its energy-generation plants rather than fossil fuels to heat greenhouses producing tomatoes. The initiative earned a Low Carbon Hero award at the Istanbul Carbon Summit in 2019. Our group left with another, rather tastier example of local production: blueberries handed to the visiting journalists.

Later, at the Altındağ Municipality Zero Waste Education Centre, the emphasis shifted from industrial infrastructure to habits. Children and adults are taught recycling through workshops, games, simulations, composting and designing new products from waste. More than 3 million people have visited the centre and more than 42,000 students have received individual training, according to the programme materials.

There were, inevitably, small contradictions. Plastic bottles of water seemed to appear everywhere during a programme dedicated to reducing waste. Yet environmental awareness was visible in less theatrical ways too: at Trabzon’s Mercure hotel, for example, rubbish could be separated for recycling inside the room. Sustainability, as ever, is often caught somewhere between ambitious policy and mundane daily practice.

Hazelnuts on the pavement, football in the heart: life in Trabzon

By that evening we were flying east to Trabzon.

The city is a fitting stage for a discussion about oceans. Wedged between green mountains and the Black Sea, Trabzon receives rain for much of the year. Its landscape dictates daily life. Hazelnuts, harvested largely by hand in August and September, are traditionally spread on pavements to dry because steep neighbourhoods leave little spare land between houses; elderly residents watch over them, guarding against pigeons and the next sudden shower.

Football, meanwhile, is almost a civic religion in Trabzon. Trabzonspor’s claret and blue colours are everywhere, and locals proudly point to moments that have become part of the city’s folklore – including Salih Dursun famously showing a referee his own red card in 2016, a scene later immortalised in sculpture. More recently, there has been particular pride in the signing of former Liverpool forward Mohamed Salah, another reminder of just how much the club – and football itself – means to the city.

But Trabzon’s identity is shaped by more than football. The Black Sea is an equally constant presence, stretching along the city and influencing its economy, food and everyday life. That relationship with the water also made Trabzon a natural setting for the environmental focus of our visit.

Ocean protection and Türkiye’s Blue Dialogue Programme

The COP31 Ocean and Seas Summit brought governments, international organisations, scientists, civil society and businesses to Trabzon with a fairly practical question: how can promises on ocean protection be turned into projects, and how can those projects actually find the expertise and money they need?

For COP31 President-designate and environment minister Murat Kurum, that fitted Türkiye’s broader pitch for an “Implementation COP”. Opening the summit, he called for stronger international cooperation, better access to science and data, more sustainable blue-economy practices and greater access to finance. “At the end of these two days, we want to leave with concrete, practical and shared outcomes,” he said.

The most tangible announcement was the COP31 Marine Litter Action Platform, intended to tackle a familiar problem: countries already have projects dealing with marine waste, but knowledge, successful approaches and funding remain fragmented. The platform is designed to connect them through three strands – a network for sharing expertise, a digital dashboard mapping marine-litter projects around the world, and a mechanism linking those projects with technical and financial support.

The summit also produced the Trabzon Call to Consensus, Dialogue and Action, calling for implementable outcomes on oceans and seas at COP31 and greater mobilisation of finance. Türkiye says the work will continue through the UN General Assembly and New York Climate Week, followed by the Pre-COP in Fiji and a leaders’ meeting in Tuvalu, before reaching Antalya in November.

The Black Sea provided an apt backdrop. Oceans are major carbon sinks, but warming, pollution and biodiversity loss are weakening marine and coastal ecosystems – and threatening the communities that depend on them. Türkiye is working with Australia, Pacific Island countries and other partners to bring those concerns into the COP31 agenda, while using Trabzon to draw attention to the particular pressures facing the Black Sea.

Black Sea conservation, marine politics and fisheries research

But environmental diplomacy does not exist separately from geopolitics.

At the international media meeting, a journalist from the Greek news outlet Libre.gr asked Kurum about Türkiye’s decision to designate marine parks in the Aegean and Mediterranean, and why Greece had not been informed before the project proceeded. The minister’s response did not really address the central question. The issue is particularly sensitive because Athens has condemned Türkiye’s marine-park designations as unilateral and affecting disputed maritime areas, while Ankara had previously objected to Greece’s own marine-park plans. The exchange was a reminder that even conservation projects can become entangled in the long-running disagreements over sovereignty and maritime boundaries between the neighbours.

The following day brought the climate discussion down from ministerial language to fish.

At Trabzon’s Central Fisheries Research Institute, or SUMAE, scientists monitor Black Sea species including anchovy, horse mackerel, bonito and bluefish, while conducting work on aquaculture, biodiversity and marine ecosystems. The institute also operates Türkiye’s first gene bank dedicated to aquatic resources, preserving thousands of DNA and tissue samples.

We were shown dogfish and the process used to tag fish so researchers can follow growth, migration and survival. Journalists were allowed to try tagging fish themselves before releasing them into the sea – a small, hands-on moment that made the scientific vocabulary of stock monitoring considerably more real.

Sümela Monastery: Trabzon’s stunning cliffside landmark

The final day moved away from laboratories and conference rooms altogether, into the misty forests of the Zigana Mountains.

Sümela Monastery appears almost suspended against a sheer cliff, roughly 1,200 metres above sea level and around 300 metres above the valley below. Its history blends documented politics with religious legend. Tradition says two monks, Barnabas and Sophronios, travelled from Athens and discovered an icon of the Virgin Mary that angels had carried to the mountains near Trabzon. The dark icon – associated with the monastery’s name, possibly derived from the Greek melas, meaning black or dark – became central to Sümela’s religious importance.

There is another remarkable detail among Sümela’s religious imagery. According to what we were told during the visit, this is the only church where the Virgin Mary, her son Jesus and God the Father can be seen depicted together in this particular form – an unusual representation of the Holy Trinity that our guide described as unique in the Christian world.

That image is just one layer of a monastery shaped over centuries. Much of what survives today reflects Sümela’s development under the Komnenos rulers of Trabzon and later Ottoman rule, while its rock church still carries frescoes from different periods.

Closed following the population exchange of the 1920s, Sümela later suffered fire, looting and decay. Today, just one Orthodox liturgy is held there each year, on 15 August, marking the Feast of the Dormition of the Virgin Mary.

The not-so-rugged road to COP31

After four days, that cliffside monastery offered an unexpectedly appropriate ending. Türkiye’s COP31 pitch is built around enormous numbers – millions of tonnes of avoided emissions, hundreds of millions of euros in infrastructure and global platforms designed to mobilise finance. But the journey from Ankara to Trabzon suggested that environmental policy ultimately becomes credible through much smaller things: a pipe collecting methane, a child learning to compost, or a scientist tagging a fish.

Türkiye wants COP31 to move from dialogue to consensus and then action. On the Black Sea coast, it was already trying to show journalists what that transition might look like. The real test will come in Antalya, when the slogans have to survive contact with politics, money and implementation.

World.title: Austria extends border checks with Hungary and three other neighbours
World.content:
Austria has extended temporary border checks with Hungary, Slovakia, the Czech Republic and Slovenia for another six months, citing the need to combat illegal migration and human smuggling.

Border checks to remain in place

Austria will continue carrying out checks at its borders with four neighbouring countries for another six months, Czech Radio reported. The extension applies to Austria’s borders with Hungary, Slovakia, the Czech Republic and Slovenia, all of which are members of the Schengen Area.

Austria’s Interior Minister Gerhard Karner said the measures remain necessary to tackle illegal migration and human smuggling. The Austrian government said the checks should have only a limited impact on people who regularly cross the borders, including commuters travelling to work.

Some checks have also been moved further into border areas rather than being conducted directly at the border, according to the reports.

Never miss a headline: join Daily News Hungary’s official Telegram channel!

Austria says system has become more flexible

The Austrian government said the current system has made border controls more flexible and effective. Austria first introduced checks on its border with the Czech Republic in October 2023. The country has also maintained temporary controls at several other internal Schengen borders in response to migration and security concerns.

Under normal Schengen rules, people can cross between participating countries without routine border checks. However, member states can temporarily reintroduce controls at internal borders in exceptional circumstances, including when they consider them necessary for security reasons.

The extension means travellers crossing from Hungary, Slovakia, the Czech Republic or Slovenia into Austria may continue to encounter checks despite both countries being part of the Schengen Area.

Travellers should therefore allow extra time when crossing the Austrian border, particularly during busy periods, although Austrian authorities say the measures are intended to minimise disruption to regular cross-border travel.

World.title: Budapest workers’ November salaries could be at risk without government deal
World.content:
Budapest says it may be able to cover October salaries, but November pay could be at risk if the city fails to reach an agreement with the government over its finances. The warning comes after the capital repaid a HUF 67 billion (EUR 185 million) bank loan and faces another major payment in October.

Budapest repays HUF 67 billion loan

Budapest has received HUF 118 billion (EUR 325 million) in local business tax revenue so far this month, but most of the money is already earmarked for outstanding financial obligations, according to Ambrus Kiss, director-general of the Mayor’s Office.

Speaking at a background briefing on Thursday, Kiss said the capital had used part of the tax revenue to repay its HUF 67 billion overdraft facility with OTP. The existing credit agreement expires on 18 September.

The bank could provide Budapest with a new credit facility only if it is satisfied that the city will be able to repay the money, Kiss said. The capital therefore needs an agreement with the government on its future financing before it can regain access to a financial safety net.

Budapest is expected to have around HUF 3.5 billion (EUR 9.65 million) left in its account by the end of September after further outstanding payments are made. Kiss said this should be enough to cover October salaries, but November wages could become difficult to finance without an agreement with the government, Magyar Hang writes.

These figures confirm that the city’s financial situation remains tight despite the arrival of the second instalment of local business tax. Portfolio reported on Thursday that Budapest has introduced a series of spending restrictions in an effort to maintain its ability to operate.

HUF 86 billion payment due in October

Another major challenge is scheduled for mid-October, when Budapest is due to pay HUF 86 billion in solidarity contribution to the state.

The payment was previously postponed until 15 October. Under the current arrangement, the Hungarian State Treasury could collect the amount directly from the city’s account. The 2026 regulation sets Budapest’s full-year solidarity contribution at around HUF 97.7 billion, including the HUF 86 billion instalment due in October.

Kiss said the city would not have sufficient new revenue to cover such a payment while continuing to finance its operations.

“Eighty-six billion forints simply will not come in,” Kiss said. “We still have to reach an agreement with the government.”

The issue has already had a significant impact on Budapest’s finances. In July, the Hungarian State Treasury deducted HUF 7.5 billion from the capital’s account in connection with an outstanding solidarity contribution payment.

Never miss a headline: join Daily News Hungary’s official Telegram channel!

Spending and hiring freezes remain in place

Budapest has introduced several emergency measures to limit spending. A commitment freeze means that the municipality and the Mayor’s Office require specific approval for new expenditure, while the threshold for the capital’s institutions is HUF 20 million.

A hiring freeze has also been introduced, and new institutional investments have been suspended. Kiss described the resulting operation as heavily restricted and said the measures would remain in place until an agreement with the government is reached.

The city has also started postponing some payments. According to Telex, ArrivaBus, Budapest’s second-largest bus operator, has been asked to wait until March for payment of invoices worth around HUF 9 billion.

Budapest and government continue talks

Kiss did not disclose details of the negotiations with the government, saying this could jeopardise their outcome. He confirmed, however, that Budapest has been in talks with competent government representatives, including the Finance Ministry.

The city needs a longer-term solution to its financing problems, particularly because essential public services will continue to require funding. Kiss argued that if Budapest could no longer provide these services, the state would ultimately have to take responsibility for them.

The government has also indicated that it is looking for new forms of cooperation with Budapest and other major cities in areas including public-service organisation and investment.

World.title: Water assets in Hungary: 3 reasons the value stays hidden
World.content:
For decades, the premium property market has operated on a single premise: land is value. That is true, but it is increasingly incomplete. Hungary’s natural capital extends far beyond farmland. Beneath the Carpathian Basin lies a resource that is rare in Europe, attracts growing attention from global investors and is still scarcely reflected in property prices: water. Water assets in Hungary are not water in the ordinary sense, but thermal water, geothermal energy, medicinal water and mineral springs whose value is shaped by geology, protected by law and made commercially distinctive through permitting and recognition procedures.

Author: Emese Széll, Private Real Estate Advisor to Premium Clients in Hungary

The Carpathian Basin as a natural rarity

Hungary’s geothermal endowment is exceptional in the European context. Owing to the thin crust beneath the Carpathian Basin, the geothermal gradient, the rate at which temperature increases with depth, averages around 45–50 °C per kilometre in Hungary, compared with a continental European average of 25–30 °C per kilometre. Depending on local conditions, economically useful temperatures of 50–100 °C or more can therefore often be reached at depths of 1,000–2,000 metres, whereas much of Western Europe may require drilling to 3,000–4,000 metres. Greater depth means higher costs and greater technical complexity. Hungary’s structural advantage is real and durable, yet neither capital markets nor the property market have fully priced it in.

Geothermal potential is not only an energy question. Hungary’s thermal-water resources underpin its spa culture, agricultural heating and health tourism.
