The geothermal district-heating systems in Szeged and Debrecen, and spa destinations such as Hévíz, Egerszalók and Zalakaros, all rely on a domestic resource that is not import-dependent, is comparatively resilient to seasonal weather fluctuations and cannot readily be replaced. For a sophisticated investor, that last characteristic is decisive: a geothermal source is a structurally scarce asset.

In legal terms, however, thermal-water extraction and the use of geothermal energy do not always fall under the same permitting regime. Under the Mining Act, the mining authority generally authorises the exploration, extraction and use of geothermal energy through thermal-water extraction, except where the extraction is primarily for medicinal or agricultural purposes.

This might also interest you: Buying rural property as a foreigner: The legal map all foreign buyers in Hungary should know

Mineral water: a distinct legal and commercial category

Water assets in Hungary are not limited to thermal water. Natural mineral water intended to be bottled and sold as food is a distinct legal category. Under Joint Decree 65/2004 (IV. 27.) FVM–ESzCsM–GKM, the Government Office of the Capital City Budapest (Budapest Főváros Kormányhivatala) recognises water as natural mineral water on application. The applicant must demonstrate compliance with the prescribed chemical, microbiological and other requirements and submit the required documentation. The EU framework is set by Directive 2009/54/EC. This regime is separate from the recognition of medicinal water and other natural therapeutic factors under Government Decree 509/2023 (XI. 20.).

The commercial distinction is real, but the categories do not form a simple legal hierarchy. Natural mineral water must originate in a protected underground aquifer, be naturally free from contamination, remain close to constant in composition and temperature within the limits of natural fluctuation, and satisfy the applicable microbiological requirements. Disinfection is prohibited, although the legislation permits a limited range of specified treatments. Spring water is a separate legal category with its own bottling and quality requirements; it is not the same as officially recognised natural mineral water. The distinction can support significant product differentiation and brand value, but it does not in itself create a legal monopoly or turn the water’s composition into a trade mark.

Silica as a global premium differentiator

Some of Hungary’s deep thermal and mineral-water resources have a high silicic-acid content expressed as silicon dioxide (SiO2). This constituent has become a commercial differentiator in the global “beauty water” and “silica water” segments. In legal terms, however, silica content does not in itself amount to an authorised health claim. Any commercial claim for food that links silica to benefits for the skin, hair or connective tissue is subject to Regulation (EC) No 1924/2006 and may be used only where permitted under the applicable EU health-claims regime. Fiji Water, whose silica content is commonly reported at approximately 93 mg/l, is frequently cited as an industry benchmark and uses this characteristic as part of its premium positioning.

Hungarian deep thermal sources, particularly in the Great Plain and the Tisza region, may contain substantially higher levels of silicic acid expressed as SiO2. According to project documentation available to me, laboratory testing of a thermal source in Heves County, nearly 950 metres deep and above 50 °C, recorded a value of 341 mg/l, almost four times the cited Fiji Water benchmark. A 149-metre mineral-water well in the Börzsöny hills recorded a metasilicic-acid content of 112 mg/l, also above that benchmark. These project-specific figures should be assessed against the original laboratory reports and authority records.

Why are water assets in Hungary not reflected in property prices?

If these figures are so compelling, why are they not reflected in property prices? Part of the answer lies in regulation, which is the subject of the next two articles in this series. A water resource alone is not enough: the legal route to exploitation depends on the intended use, the method of abstraction and the installation involved.

For water works, water installations and water uses, the need for a water-law permit (vízjogi engedély) must generally be assessed under the Water Management Act, subject to statutory notification regimes and exemptions. Government Decree 72/1996 (V. 22.) and Minister of Interior Decree 41/2017 (XII. 29.) contain key procedural and documentation rules. For water bases serving drinking-water, mineral-water or medicinal-water purposes, the designation of a subsurface protection zone, surface protection area or protection strip under Government Decree 123/1997 (VII. 18.) may also be relevant, while Government Decree 219/2004 (VII. 21.) governs the protection of groundwater.

Mining-law authorisation may also be decisive where geothermal energy is recovered through thermal-water extraction. An environmental impact assessment is required only in the cases specified by Government Decree 314/2005 (XII. 25.). If a project may affect a Natura 2000 site, an initial assessment under Government Decree 275/2004 (X. 8.) may be required; a full appropriate assessment is necessary where the possibility of a significant effect cannot be excluded. The designation of a protection zone, a receiving-water statement or an environmental impact assessment is therefore not an automatic requirement in every water-law permitting case.

This creates two distinct opportunities for an informed buyer.

The permitted source. Acquiring property whose water resource already has the water-law and/or mining-authority permits required for its intended use and, where relevant, official recognition as natural mineral water or medicinal water. Such assets are rare and are generally priced accordingly.

Acquiring property whose water resource already has the water-law and/or mining-authority permits required for its intended use and, where relevant, official recognition as natural mineral water or medicinal water. Such assets are rare and are generally priced accordingly. The documented but unpermitted source. Identifying land where the geological resource is documented but the necessary permitting and recognition process has not yet been completed, so the entry price does not yet fully reflect the potential value of the water resource. This is where patient capital may create value, with the legal and regulatory process forming part of value creation rather than merely an obstacle to it.

What comes next

The water assets in Hungary, from thermal water and mineral springs to geothermal energy and recognised medicinal water, represent a form of natural capital whose market value is heavily influenced by legal and technical usability and by the complexity of the regulatory process. The next articles examine how water-base protection rules can affect the land-registry position and market value of a property, and how an investor can move from geological potential to a lawfully exploitable, value-generating source.

Legislation cited

This article provides general market and legal information only and does not constitute individual legal, water-law, mining, environmental or food-law advice. Before any investment, the applicable permitting and regulatory requirements should be assessed for the specific site, water resource and intended use. The English titles of Hungarian legislation are descriptive translations; the Hungarian-language legal text is authoritative. Legislation checked as at 3 September 2026.

Featured image is illustration. Photo: Bükfürdő Thermal & Spa

World.title: Court order: Hungarian billionaire Jellinek and former state asset manager chief arrested
World.content:
A court has ordered the arrest of billionaire businessman Dániel Jellinek and former Hungarian state asset management chief Norbert Szivek in connection with the Volánbusz corruption investigation. Both men are suspected of accepting bribes and other corruption-related offences.

Court orders one-month detention

The Buda Central District Court ordered the arrest of Jellinek and Szivek for one month on Thursday, following a motion by the Central Chief Prosecutor’s Office, the Budapest Prosecutor’s Office spokesperson told Hungarian News Agency MTI. The decision is not final, as the defence lawyers for both men have appealed.

The Central Chief Prosecutor’s Office is investigating alleged bribery and other corruption offences linked to Volánbusz, Hungary’s state-owned bus operator. We’ve written in detail about the case here.

A police officer escorts a suspect to the Budapest Penitentiary on 17 September 2026. The Buda Central District Court arrested two of the suspects in the Volánbusz case, following a motion by the Central Investigative Prosecutor’s Office. Photo: MTI/Bruzák Noémi

Jellinek, chief executive of Indotek Group, and Szivek, the former CEO of the Hungarian National Asset Management Company (MNV), were taken into custody on Tuesday and subsequently detained.

The prosecutor’s office has now questioned five people as suspects in the case and sought the detention of three of them. According to prosecutors, the alleged offences attributed to Jellinek, Szivek and a third suspect carry a possible combined prison sentence of between five and 15 years under Hungarian sentencing rules.

Investigation centres on alleged billions in losses

The investigation concerns alleged corruption linked to passenger transport services and the purchase of buses by Volánbusz.

According to investigators, state-owned Volán companies may have suffered losses of around HUF 10 billion between 2015 and 2018 as a result of allegedly overpriced purchases of more than 600 used buses and other disputed transactions. Authorities are also examining whether money allegedly obtained through corruption was subsequently laundered or moved through company and property transactions.

The National Bureau of Investigation announced on 10 September that eight former company executives had been questioned as suspects in connection with the alleged overpricing of Volán buses. The suspects included the former head of MNV, whom the authorities did not name at the time but who was subsequently identified as Szivek.

The Central Chief Prosecutor’s Office later took over a separate investigation in May, according to 24.hu, and the case has since accelerated.

Prosecutors cite risk of flight and interference

The prosecution says there are grounds to suspect a risk of flight because of the seriousness of the alleged offences and the sums involved. According to the prosecutor’s office, the alleged unlawful payments amounted to hundreds of millions of forints and, in the case of two suspects, billions of forints.

Prosecutors also cited concerns that suspects could interfere with the gathering of evidence, while they said there was a risk of reoffending in one case. The court’s decision concerns pre-trial detention and does not establish the men’s guilt.

Indotek rejects allegations against Jellinek

Following the court’s decision, Indotek Group said it considered the detention measure against its CEO disproportionate.

The company said Jellinek had remained available to the authorities throughout the proceedings and had fully cooperated with investigators. Indotek also stated that, in its view, Jellinek had committed no crime and expressed confidence that the ongoing investigation would clarify the situation.

The company added that the court’s decision would not affect Indotek Group’s operations and that the investigation did not concern any of its companies or assets.

Jellinek is one of Hungary’s wealthiest businessmen. Forbes estimated his fortune at HUF 313 billion (EUR 0.86 billion) in its latest ranking, placing him seventh among Hungary’s richest people.

World.title: PM Magyar: Wealth checks for politicians, including former officials, coming
World.content:
Hungarian Prime Minister Péter Magyar says the government will submit legislation allowing the tax authority to investigate politicians’ wealth, potentially going back 20 years, including officials whose mandates ended within the past five years.

NAV could investigate politicians’ wealth

Magyar announced on Thursday that the government would immediately submit a bill to Parliament introducing wealth investigations for politicians. Under the proposed system, the National Tax and Customs Administration (NAV) could examine whether politicians’ assets and lifestyles are consistent with their declared, taxed income and wealth declarations.

The proposal would allow investigations to look back as far as 20 years, according to Magyar. It would cover current politicians as well as people whose mandates ended within the previous five years. Other reports on the announcement also say the proposed checks could extend to assets held by people living in the same household.

The planned legislation would apply to members of Parliament, prime ministers, ministers, state secretaries, government commissioners and prime ministerial commissioners, Magyar said.

For current officeholders, NAV checks would begin after two years from their first appointment, according to the prime minister. If a member of the current Parliament or government resigns or is removed from office, an automatic check would begin within 30 days, he said.

What would the checks cover?

According to Magyar, NAV would receive the powers needed to carry out detailed investigations into politicians’ financial circumstances.

The authority would examine assets including:

properties and other real estate;

bank accounts;

company interests;

insurance policies;

investments; and

other assets that may not have previously been disclosed.

The information would be compared with politicians’ wealth declarations and taxed income, followed by a risk assessment, Magyar said.

If NAV finds no irregularities, the procedure would be closed. If there is a discrepancy between declared income and wealth that indicates a possible tax violation or illegal income, a detailed tax audit would follow, according to the proposal as described by Magyar.

If investigators suspect a criminal offence, NAV investigators would notify the National Office for Asset Recovery and Asset Protection, the prosecution service or the police, he said.

Never miss a headline: join Daily News Hungary’s official Telegram channel!

Names could be published in cases involving major tax shortfalls

The proposed rules would also introduce a public disclosure mechanism. Magyar said that if an investigation establishes at least HUF 5 million in unpaid tax, the person’s name, position and the amount of the tax shortfall would be added to a NAV publication list.

The government had already announced in July that it planned to introduce wealth investigations conducted by NAV, with checks potentially extending 20 years into the past. The government said at the time that the system would also involve politicians and people living in their households.

The latest announcement sets out further details of the proposed system, but the legislation still needs to go through the parliamentary process before the new rules can take effect.

If you missed it: Ursula von der Leyen points to Hungary as proof democratic decline can be reversed

Government says new system would go beyond wealth declarations

Magyar said the proposed investigations would address what he described as a gap between politicians’ official wealth declarations and their actual financial circumstances. He said the system would apply not only to former politicians but also to current and future officeholders.

World.title: Digital ‘EU health card’ and skills passport could make working abroad easier
World.content:
The European Commission has proposed a new package of measures aimed at making it easier for people to work in another EU country, including a digital European Social Security Pass and a system for carrying and recognising professional qualifications across borders.

Digital social security pass could bring key documents together

The European Commission presented its Fair Labour Mobility package on Wednesday, saying it aims to make social rights easier to access for people who live and work in different EU countries. One of the main proposals is a European Social Security Pass (ESSPASS), which would allow workers to request and receive social security documents entirely online.

The digital pass would include the European Health Insurance Card (EHIC), commonly known in Hungary as the “EU TAJ card”. The card allows people insured in one EU country to receive medically necessary healthcare during a temporary stay in another EU member state under the same conditions as people insured there, Telex writes.

The ESSPASS could also contain the portable A1 document used by posted workers to prove which country’s social security system covers them.

The documents could be stored and presented through the EU Digital Identity Wallet. In Hungary, the country’s Digital Citizenship Programme (DÁP) app is expected to provide access to the EU digital wallet framework.

The Commission says the digital system would allow authorities to verify documents more quickly and securely, while reducing paperwork for workers and businesses.

If you missed it: Hungary has a record number of foreign workers – now businesses want the government to ease the rules

Professional qualifications could become easier to use abroad

The package also includes plans to make professional qualifications more portable across EU borders.

Qualifications would be issued in a standardised digital format and could be stored in the EU Digital Identity Wallet. The Commission also plans to introduce an EU qualifications comparison tool using information from national databases, allowing employers and workers to compare qualifications from different member states more easily.

For regulated professions, a mandatory digital procedure would speed up the recognition of qualifications. The Commission specifically mentioned professions such as doctors, nurses, engineers and teachers.

According to the Commission, the process could be reduced from around three months to five weeks.

The proposals would also expand automatic recognition through common training frameworks. The Commission has already adopted a framework for physiotherapists, which it describes as one of the EU’s most mobile professions.

Never miss a headline: join Daily News Hungary’s official Telegram channel!

Recognition of non-EU qualifications would also change

The package covers qualifications obtained outside the EU as well. The Commission wants to establish common standards for recognising qualifications obtained in third countries for EU citizens and third-country professionals working in the Single Market or applying from abroad.

The Commission says such procedures currently take an average of 14 months. Under the proposed system, this could be reduced to four months, while administrative costs for employers could be cut substantially.

For seven professions where EU-wide training standards already exist, qualifications issued by accredited institutions outside the EU and assessed by European quality-assurance bodies could receive automatic recognition.

Member states would, however, retain control over who is admitted to their territory and over the standards required to practise a profession.

EU says package could save billions

The European Commission estimates that the measures could generate around EUR 6 billion in benefits by 2040 through faster recognition of professional qualifications, quicker verification of social security documents and other savings for workers, businesses and public authorities.

The Commission also estimates that digitalisation could save businesses up to EUR 64 million, healthcare providers EUR 69 million and labour inspectors EUR 72 million over 12 years through faster cross-border verification.

Digital signatures could prevent up to EUR 277 million in fraud over the same period, according to the Commission.

The package also proposes giving the European Labour Authority stronger tools to help national authorities enforce EU labour rules, improve cross-border cooperation and tackle abuses involving third-country nationals and illegal employment.

Five legislative proposals need approval

The Fair Labour Mobility package consists of a communication and five legislative proposals. They cover the European Social Security Pass, digital and comparable qualifications, stronger powers for the European Labour Authority, changes to the rules on professional qualifications, and qualifications obtained by third-country nationals.

The proposals will generally need to be agreed by the European Parliament and the Council of the EU. Two of the five proposals are directives, meaning they would also have to be transposed into national law by individual member states.

The Commission’s proposals have already drawn criticism from different political groups in the European Parliament. Speaking in the Parliament, Julie Rechagneux of the Patriots for Europe group argued that labour mobility should not be treated as an end in itself and criticised what she described as making workers interchangeable. Social Affairs Commissioner Roxana Mînzatu, meanwhile, said the package was intended to remove practical obstacles faced by workers and businesses operating across borders.

The first practical changes would come only after the proposals are adopted.

Under the Commission’s timetable, social security documents would be digitalised in stages. The A1 document would be introduced first, followed by the European Health Insurance Card and other documents within three years of the ESSPASS Regulation entering into force.

Changes concerning qualifications would also be phased in, with simpler recognition of non-EU qualifications planned within two years and digital qualifications and easier recognition for regulated professions within three years.

The Commission says improvements linked to the European Labour Authority could be expected between 2028 and 2030.

More than 14 million Europeans lived in another EU member state in 2024, including more than 10 million people of working age. A recent Eurobarometer survey found that 18% of respondents would like to work abroad.

World.title: Rugby meets the boardroom: Top executives invited to unique leadership experience in Budapest
World.content:
Confindustria Ungheria, the British Chamber of Commerce Hungary (BCCH) and the French Chamber of Commerce and Industry in Hungary (CCI France Hongrie) are pleased to announce the “Executive Rugby Leadership Experience”, a joint initiative bringing the leadership principles of professional rugby to the business community in Hungary.

The event will take place on 24 September 2026 at the Novotel City & Budapest Congress Centre, and will host senior executives, CEOs and CFOs for an immersive leadership development programme built around the values and methodology of team sport. This is not a sports event: it is a structured learning experience exploring how the discipline, trust and resilience developed on the rugby field translate directly into business leadership.

Participants will be welcomed by the top management of Benetton Rugby, one of the most decorated clubs in Italian rugby, founded in 1932 in Treviso and competing in the United Rugby Championship, Europe’s premier cross-border league. The club’s delegation will include Antonio Pavanello, President and former captain of the Italian national team, Fabio Rigoletto, Marketing Manager, and coaches and former national team players Tommaso Benvenuti, Tommaso Iannone, Marco Lazzaroni and Ezio Galon.

Never miss a headline: join Daily News Hungary’s official Telegram channel!

The programme will open with registration and a networking lunch, followed by three leadership sessions dedicated respectively to leading from the front, supporting the team before the individual, and communicating clearly and effectively under pressure. Participants will then take part in an executive challenge, working in mixed teams on simple rugby-inspired activities requiring no prior relevant experience. The day will continue with a panel discussion moving “from the pitch to the boardroom”, a closing group reflection and photo, and will conclude with an executive networking dinner shared with the Benetton Rugby delegation.

Participation is limited to 50 executives, with a fee of 250 euro plus VAT. The event is supported by the Budapest Congress Centre as main sponsor, and by Flame Spray, Ilinox Hungary Kft and UniCredit Bank as supporting sponsors.

For further information and registration, interested companies may contact Confindustria Ungheria.

World.title: Romania’s President Nominates MEP to Form Govt, But Uncertainty Remains
World.content:
Romanian President Nicusor Dan on Thursday nominated the liberal politician Siegfried Muresan, a member of the European Parliament, to lead efforts to form a new government.

However, securing a parliamentary majority capable of forming a government that will address the country’s economic challenges could prove extremely difficult, as no single party has enough seats to do so – an issue that has caused a long-running political crisis.

“More than four months have passed since we have had a government … and despite hundreds of hours of negotiations with the political parties, we have failed to reach a viable formula,” President Dan acknowledged.

He added that, under these circumstances, he had decided to nominate the person “who has the greatest parliamentary support”, namely Muresan.

“He is someone with experience in the European Parliament and the expertise required for this position,” Dan said.

Muresan announced on social media that he would take up the challenge, clearing the way for political negotiations and efforts to form a new cabinet.

Aged 44, Muresan has been a member of the European Parliament since 2014, is currently vice-president of the centre-right European People’s Party group and a key figure on EU budget and economic policy.

His nomination is backed by the centre-right National Liberal Party, PNL, and two smaller centre-right parties. Muresan has so far advocated reducing the budget deficit, continuing the reforms initiated under interim Prime Minister Ilie Bolojan, and forming a “competent”, pro-European government.

But observers expressed scepticism about his chances of forming an administration.

“The arithmetic is very simple. The parties supporting Muresan can muster no more than 190 votes in a confidence vote, well below the 233 votes required,” journalist Dan Tapalaga said.

“Under these circumstances, I don’t see how Siegfried Muresan can form a government,” he added.

Mureșan now has ten days to put together a cabinet and present his governing programme to parliament.

During the more than four months that Romania has been without a government, President Dan has made two previous nominations, both of which failed.

In June, independent Eugen Tomac, the first prime minister-designate, withdrew from efforts to form a government before facing a parliamentary vote. Three weeks later, parliament rejected the proposed programme and cabinet put forward by liberal politician Adrian Vestea, further prolonging the political crisis.

Romania’s current political crisis stems from deep tensions among the parties that previously formed the pro-European governing coalition.

The coalition, formed in June 2025, brought together the centre-left Social Democratic Party, PSD, the centre-right National Liberal Party, PNL, and two smaller centre-right parties. One of its main objectives was to curb the rise of the far-right Alliance for the Union of Romanians, AUR, led by George Simion.

Its mandate included stabilising the economy, which is burdened by the largest budget deficit in the European Union, securing access to 11 billion euros in EU recovery funds and safeguarding Romania’s investment-grade credit rating.

But a series of unpopular austerity measures introduced to reduce the budget deficit placed growing strain on the coalition, particularly with the Social Democrats, who withdrew their support in May.

World.title: Protests Continue in Pristina After Conviction of Kosovo Liberation Army Leaders
World.content:
This post is also available in this language: Shqip Bos/Hrv/Srp

Protest in Pristina against the Hague court verdict on September 16, 2026. Photo: EPA/ARBEN LLAPASHTICA.

Demonstrators in Pristina against the verdict convicting four former Kosovo Liberation Army KLA leaders of war crimes resumed their protest at around noon on Thursday after continuing until around midnight on Wednesday, the day the judgment was handed down in The Hague.

The KLA Veterans’ Organisation’ deputy leader, Gazmend Syla, said on Thursday that it wants to consolidate the demonstrations by establishing a “national coordinating council” with ethnic Albanians from elsewhere in the Balkans and the diaspora, which “will join the students protesting in the [capital’s main] square”.

Several students protested on Wednesday chanting “Duam drejtesi, jo politike” (“We want justice, not politics”). They said they were joining the newly-established “Not In My Name” movement, which was set up in reaction to presiding Judge Charles Smith III announcing the guilty verdict “in the names of the people of Kosovo”.

Kosovo’s ex President Hashim Thaci and his co-defendants, former parliament speakers Jakup Krasniqi and Kadri Veseli and ex-MP Rexhep Selimi, were sentenced to 25, 25, 18 and 13 years in jail respectively.

All four were found guilty of bearing responsibility for crimes carried out while they were senior officials of the KLA during the 1998-99 war with Serbian forces.

The four were found not guilty of crimes against humanity, of persecution, imprisonment, other inhumane acts, torture, murder and enforced disappearances, but cleared of crimes against humanity because these were committed after the end of the Kosovo war.

Thaci, Veseli, Krasniqi and Selimi had all pleaded not guilty to all charges, and will appeal against the verdict.

On Wednesday night after the verdict, angry protesters in Pristina threw stones and firecrackers at the Kosovo government building and the headquarters of the EU rule-of-law mission, EULEX.

In The Hague, where thousands of supporters of the defendants had gathered to hear the verdict, anger erupted when the sentences were announced. Dutch police prevented them marching towards the court.

The Kosovo Specialist Chambers was created specifically to try former members of the KLA, under pressure from Kosovo’s Western allies. The court is widely disliked in Kosovo, where it is seen as denigrating the KLA’s just war against Serbian oppression.

World.title: Slovakia Seeks to Overturn Conviction of Fugitive Who Claimed Asylum in Bosnia
World.content:
Through an extraordinary legal remedy submitted to Slovakia’s Supreme Court, the country’s Justice Minister Boris Susko has requested the overturning of the verdict of Jan Kalavsky, a former senior police investigator who hid in Bosnia and Herzegovina until March 2025 in order to evade his seven-year prison sentence.

In the submitted request, the Slovak Ministry of Justice asserted that the facts and the assessment of evidence in the Kalavsky case were incorrectly established, and called for a review of the judgment.

Although the ministry did not confirm any details to the Slovak media, it stated to BIRN that the appeal was filed on August 6.

“The Minister of Justice files an appeal against a final decision based on factual findings that were incorrect regarding material circumstance, as established by the evidence, or if, in the course of determining the facts, provisions intended to ensure that the matter was properly clarified were seriously violated,” the Slovak Ministry of Justice stated in its written response to BIRN.

The ministry added that it could not disclose any further details publicly, as the appeal proceedings are still ongoing.

Kalavsky, a former operative of the now-disbanded National Crime Agency (NAKA) and key figure in Slovakia’s so-called “war in the police”, which erupted after the 2020 government change and the launch of anti-corruption investigations under then-prime minister Igor Matovic, was convicted and sentenced to seven years for corruption in July 2023, though this ruling was not final.

He was tried in absentia, as he had already fled to Bosnia in September 2021, where he applied for asylum, which under domestic law provided him with protection preventing his extradition for as long as the proceedings were ongoing.

Kalavsky was one of three high-ranking Slovak security or law enforcement figures that fled to Bosnia after being indicted for criminal activities committed during Robert Fico’s time in office between 2012-2018, widely regarded as the most corrupt in Slovakia’s recent history, which ended with his resignation following the contract murders of investigative journalist Jan Kuciak and his fiancée, Martina Kusnirova.

After a five-year interregnum, Fico returned to office in 2023 at the head of a three-party coalition. The new majority in February 2024 pushed through controversial amendments to the criminal code – which the opposition dubbed a “pro-mafia package” – amid accusations that Fico’s government was attempting to shield convicted individuals who had collaborated with the administration during its previous term in office.

BIRN investigations concluded that these fugitives were awaiting those amendments to the criminal code that could lead to reduced sentences. Indeed, although Kalavsky told BIRN journalists he would never return to Slovakia because he had found peace in Bosnia, he returned to his homeland and began serving his sentence following the legislative changes and a 2025 Supreme Court ruling that reduced his original seven-year prison term to five years.

“I am surprised that this move [by the justice minister], aimed at completely overturning the verdict, is happening only now; I expected it to occur much earlier,” Tomas Madlenak, a former journalist from Bratislava who has investigated the cases involving Slovak fugitives in Bosnia, told BIRN.

Madlenak believes that such a request won’t end up setting Kalavsky free, but instead interprets it merely as an attempt by Fico’s ruling Smer party to appease former associates so they won’t agree to cooperate with the justice system in other cases.

Madlenak bases this conclusion on the fact that the reasoning behind the request has been kept from the public. “I assume that is because the arguments in that case are likely quite far-fetched, given that the entire case against Kalavsky was very clear. He even admitted himself that he had received ‘gifts’ from Petrov [Peter, nicknamed “Tiger”], to whom he had disclosed police information,” said Madlenak.

The Kalavsky case is the fourth such case in which the Slovak Ministry of Justice is seeking the overturning of verdicts. Since 2024, Justice Minister Susko – a member of Fico’s Smer party – has filed three additional appeals against final verdicts handed down to former high-ranking state officials convicted during a wave of anti-corruption investigations launched following the 2018 murders of Kuciak and his fiancée. In addition to Kalavsky, these appeals concern Dusan Kovacik, Zoroslav Kollar, and Frantisek Imrecze.

Kovacik, a former special prosecutor, was sentenced to eight years in prison and fined 100,000 euros for accepting bribes and leaking information from case files. After spending more than two years in prison, he was released in December 2025 following a ministerial appeal; his final conviction was quashed, and the case was remanded for a retrial. In the meantime, Kovacik has sought 400,000 euros in compensation from the state.

Two other appeals – concerning lawyer and businessman Kollar and former Slovak Financial Administration chief Imrecze – were rejected.

Madlenak believes that Kalavsky’s case is very similar to Kovacik’s case, where the verdict was overturned following a request by the minister and where the defendant will be tried under the new controversial criminal law.

“Kalavsky is evidently a figure close to the corrupt system established by previous Smer-led governments. I believe this is another attempt by Minister Susko to overturn a legal and correct court decision in favour of a criminal who is rightfully serving his sentence,” Madlenak said.

World.title: Kosovo Verdict Reflects West’s Strategic Priorities, Not Pursuit of Justice
World.content:
This post is also available in this language: Shqip Bos/Hrv/Srp

Law is inherently political. Its tenets, institutions and its enforcement are always influenced by interests and power – international law especially. Nowhere is this more obvious than in the case of the Kosovo Specialist Chambers.

The sentencing of former Kosovo Liberation Army (KLA) leaders Hashim Thaci and Jakup Krasniqi to 25 years, Kadri Veseli to 18 years and Rexhep Selemi to 13 years, is the culmination of a process that had little to do with the pursuit of justice. The ‘Special Court’, as it is most commonly known, has to be understood as the product of a political strategy pursued by powerful Western states.

The court was established amidst widespread public outrage in Kosovo. Kosovo’s political leaders were also against it, and yet eventually the country’s parliament, the Assembly, voted to establish it. Why? The answer has always been obvious; Kosovo’s Western allies, especially the US, demanded it be created and issued a range of threats to coerce Kosovo’s government into doing so. At the time, Thaci described it as “the biggest injustice and insult which could be done to Kosovo and its people” and admitted that he only supported the court’s creation “under great pressure from the international community”.

World.title: Video Footage of Fatal Police Intervention in Slovenia Sparks Outrage
World.content:
Screenshot from police bodycam video. Photo: 24ur.com.

A video published in Slovenia on Wednesday night showing a police intervention in the capital Ljubljana, following which 37-year-old Armin Djutovic died in hospital three days later, has caused public anger.

The police’s body-camera footage shows part of the intervention in December 2024, during which Djutovic told officers that he cannot breathe.

The video obtained by Slovenian media outlet 24ur and POP TV shows officers taking him to the ground after which one of them held him in a neck hold for more than a minute.

“I’m going to die, please, I can’t breathe,” Djutovic is heard saying in the recording.

After being handcuffed, he remained motionless for several minutes. Several police officers stood around him and, according to the indictment, did not administer first aid immediately.

Six police officers face prosecution for their involvement.

The incident took place on December 8, 2024, on Copova Street in Ljubljana, but release of the footage has sparked outrage.

Police intervened following a report that a man was scattering and damaging chairs on a café terrace. According to police, Djutovic subsequently struck a Dutch national and, during the intervention, resisted and attempted to flee.

The prosecution has charged police officer Jan Dovnik with placing Djutovic in a neck hold from behind and continuing to apply pressure after he had lost consciousness. Dovnik is charged with causing his death through negligence. Five other police officers have been charged with failure to render aid.

Djutovic suffered cardiac arrest and sustained severe, irreversible brain damage due to a lack of oxygen. He was transported to hospital but died on December 11, 2024.

A review by the Interior Ministry previously determined that the intervention was carried out unprofessionally and disproportionately and that first aid was not administered immediately. The use of physical force against Djutovic, who was already handcuffed, was deemed unlawful, unprofessional and disproportionate.

Miroslav Zaberl, an expert from the Faculty of Criminal Justice and Security, told media outlet 24ur Zvecer that, in his opinion, professional errors were evident.

“Most likely, the hold was too tight and lasted too long, and the officer failed to notice that the person had stopped breathing for some time. I also see officers who did not react immediately,” he said.

However, Igor Toplak, of the Police Union, urged that the findings of court-appointed experts and the court’s decision be awaited before drawing final conclusions.

Criminal proceedings against the six officers involved are ongoing at the Ljubljana District Court.

World.title: Turkey Blocks Social Media Accounts, Arrests 80, as LGBT Crackdown Expands
World.content:
An Istanbul court on Wednesday ordered access blocks on 419 social media accounts that it claimed had “shared obscene content”, as Turkish authorities continued a broad crackdown against LGBTQ+ groups in the name of “protecting the family”.

Turkey’s state-led Anadolu Agency reported that, under the coordination of the Cyber ​​Crimes Investigation Bureau, the Istanbul Police had conducted a study aimed at protecting families, children and young people from all forms of abuse.

“Within this scope, access was blocked to 419 social media accounts and links deemed to contain obscene content that were found to have been shared on social media platforms,” it wrote.

The blocked accounts include those of journalists, activists, media houses and women’s civil society groups. It is not clear which content was deemed obscene.

“If you think that banning journalists and shutting down accounts will solve the problems, unfortunately you’re very mistaken,” commented Sirin Payzin, a veteran journalist whose account was blocked on Wednesday. X immediately made his account invisible from Turkey. She has 1.8 million followers on X.

Raids, arrests and internet restrictions have targeted these groups as well as independent journalists and human rights organisations reporting on the police operation.

On Wednesday night and Thursday morning, courts ordered at least 80 formal arrests of LGBTQ+ rights activists, their supporters and journalists. However, 106 people detained earlier in a protest against the operation in Istanbul were released.

LGBTQ+ and human rights groups argue that the operations target freedom of expression, freedom of association and human rights advocacy. The authorities insist the investigations are being conducted within the framework of criminal law.

Gurkan Ozturan, Monitoring Officer at the European Centre for Press and Media Freedom, told BIRN that the operations instigated by the conservative Islamist government of President Recep Tayyip Erdogan “show that the authorities are criminalising both identity and information”.

World.title: Ownership Changes Unsettle Serbia’s Critical Media Ahead of Elections
World.content:
Branislav Sovljanski said he had yet to receive a call from his news channel’s new owners telling him to pull this or that story, invite or deinvite a certain guest. He expressed hope it would remain that way.

Three months after a change of ownership at Adria News Network, ANN, which owns the Serbian N1 news channel where Sovljanski is director of news, journalists are holding their breath.

Broadcasters N1 and Nova S, the news website Nova.rs, daily newspaper Danas and weekly Radar have long been a collective thorn in the side of Serbia’s government, alone in criticising the country’s democratic backsliding under President Aleksandar Vucic and the ruling Progressive Party, SNS, since they first came to power in 2012.

On May 29, when it was announced that United Group would sell Adria News S.à r.l - the Luxembourg–based company under which Adria News Network operates – to Alpac Capital, it sent shockwaves through part of Serbian society, amid fevered speculation that Vucic would call elections for the autumn. He subsequently did, setting the date for October 25.

Alpac Capital, a Portuguese investment fund, previously bought pan-European broadcaster Euronews in 2022; subsequent reporting by Le Monde and Hungarian investigative media Direkt36, revealed that the acquisition was heavily financed by Hungarian state capital and companies close to the powerful propaganda apparatus of then Prime Minister Viktor Orban.

In Serbia, there are already signs of a shift.

World.title: North Macedonia ‘Putting Youth at Risk’ by Scrapping Sex Education Rollout
World.content:
The abandonment of sex education lessons in schools in North Macedonia will put young people at greater risk of sexual- and gender-based violence, civil society campaigner Velimir Saveski told BIRN after the conservative government cancelled the rollout of optional classes to all ninth graders.

Sex education was introduced in 2021 as an optional topic for ninth graders in four schools in North Macedonia, under a pilot project approved by the then ruling Social Democrats.

It was due to be rolled out as an option for ninth graders in all general secondary schools in the country as of next year, before Education Minister Vesna Janevska announced this month a “deep revision” of the programme.

Janevska comes from the ranks of the conservative VMRO DPMNE party, which came to power in 2024; she insisted her move was based on public disquiet over the programme.

World.title: New Passenger and Hospitality Complex Coming to Split Port
World.content:
September the 18th, 2026 – A brand new passenger and hospitality complex is coming to Split Port, finally giving the entire area a much needed proverbial facelift.

What was once the Dalmacijavino winery, a work by architect Stanko Fabris and a gem of Croatian modern architecture, has over time become a dilapidated, abandoned building in what is definitely one of the most beautiful locations in the entire city. A place where Katalinića brig meets the port, the sea, and the rest of the world.

Morski reports that the Split Port Authority, the manager of that part of the port, has received a permit for the changes. After more than two years of waiting, the Split Port Authority has finally obtained a location permit – a permit for the changes according to which the building will be repurposed, under strict conservation guidelines. The building is under the protection of the Conservation Department of the Ministry of Culture.

After all the necessary studies (economic and legal) in cooperation with the constituents of the University of Split, and according to conservation guidelines, we conducted an international expression of interest from potential concessionaires and submitted all the necessary documentation to the City of Split, and we finally have it.

As part of the city’s project for the arrangement of Split’s Eastern Coast, according to the existing city Master Plan (GUP), two garages with 500 parking spaces can be built at that location, which would solve the problem of stationary traffic in the city port; passenger space can be expanded, accompanying hospitality facilities, and even a hotel with around a hundred rooms.

Now that the location permit has arrived, an international tender will be announced for the concession of the building and the space around it. The significance of this investment can best be shown through numbers, and that is the estimated value of the concession, which totals a massive 600,000,000 euros.

World.title: New Croatian Price Comparison System Coming Next Month
World.content:
September the 18th, 2026 – A brand new Croatian price comparison system is coming next month, with additional technical obligations awaiting traders and service providers.

As of the 1st of October 2026 in Croatia, the prices highlighted on the shelves, in the menus or on the price lists will no longer stand alone. Poslovni reports that alongside the current price an additional, so-called anchor price will also have to be stated. The new obligation applies to all retailers and registered service providers in Croatia. This means that the new rules will not cover only supermarkets, but also clothing and footwear shops, technical goods, furniture and building materials stores, as well as restaurants, cafes, hair and beauty salons, car mechanics, various service workshops and other craftsmen who offer their products or services to consumers.

The anchor price will be the regular price that applied to a particular product or service on 10 September 2026, without promotions, discounts and other special forms of sale. A hair salon will thus have to state, alongside the current price of a haircut or colouring, also the price of the same service on that date; a car mechanic will have to do the same alongside the price of a working hour or a particular service; and a restaurant alongside the prices of food and drinks in the menu or price list.

The anchor price is neither frozen nor the highest permitted price. A trader or craftsman can still change prices, but the consumer will at any moment be able to see how much the current price differs from the one that applied on the 10th of September, explain lawyers Dora Ljevar and Danijel Pribanić. The obligation also applies when advertising prices. If a trader or service provider publishes a price on a leaflet, poster, digital , outdoor advertising space or website, they will also have to highlight the anchor price alongside it. An exception applies to traders who for food, drinks, cosmetics, cleaning agents, toiletries and household products already had to highlight an additional price. For those products the relevant price remains the one that applied on the 2nd of May 2025.

Additional technical obligations await traders and service providers who already have their own website. On it they will have to publish a price list in XML or CSV format, which enables the automatic collection and comparison of data. Traders will update the price list every working day by 08:00 at the latest, and service providers after every price change, also 08:00 on the day of the change at the latest. Previously published price lists will have to remain available for 30 days. Those who do not have their own website are not obliged to set one up solely because of this obligation. Traders and craftsmen should therefore keep proof of the prices that applied on the 10th of September and, by the start of application of the new rules, adapt the price lists in business premises, s and websites.

World.title: Croatia’s Zvijezda Marks 110 Years of Successful Business
World.content:
September the 18th, 2026 – Croatia’s famous brand Zvijezda has celebrated 110 years of doing successful business and engaging in market leadership.

Zvijezda mayonnaise and Zvijezda oil occupy first and second place on the ranking of the strongest brands in Croatia according to Ipsos research. Poslovni reports that the very well known Zvijezda, a market leader and Croatian manufacturing company whose values are founded on tradition, quality and innovativeness, celebrated 110 years of successful business.

The ceremony was held at the Zagreb City Museum, on the day when in 1916 the First Croatian Oil Factory was founded in Zagreb, in the presence of numerous company partners as well as representatives of institutions and the media. Zvijezda’s strong position is also confirmed by data on the habits of Croatian households: every second edible oil used in Croatia is Zvijezda’s, two out of three cakes are baked with Zvijezda margarine, and nine out of ten people, when it comes to mayonnaise, first think of Zvijezda.

According to the BRANDpuls research by the Ipsos agency from spring 2026, as many as five Zvijezda brands are among the 20 strongest brands on the Croatian market, with Zvijezda mayonnaise and Zvijezda oil occupying the first two places.

“I’m proud that we’re the market leader in almost all categories in which we have decided to compete, and the historically high result in the mayonnaise category of more than 70 percent confirms this. Zvijezda has for years been the number 1 brand among all brands of fast-moving consumer goods, and we continuously achieve these results thanks to our consumers, employees and partners,” emphasised Dinko Jurišić, member of the Management Board of Zvijezda. From the very beginnings of production in the First Croatian Oil Factory right up to the present day, the company has over the decades followed the needs of consumers, developed new products and set standards for the domestic food industry.

As such, back in 1956, it became the first producer of margarine in the country, in 1959 it introduced mayonnaise to the market, and in 2016 it launched the production of its own ketchup. The company today operates through the brands Zvijezda, Margo and Omegol. “Today, Zvijezda is a large and modern company, which is best proven by these figures: €150 million in annual revenue, more than 400 employees and presence on more than 15 markets. We look at these 110 years with pride, but even more with a sense of responsibility towards what is coming, therefore we continue to invest in the development of our products, the modernisation of production, the digitalisation of processes and sustainable solutions that will further strengthen Zvijezda’s competitiveness,” stated at the ceremony Karmen Rosan, member of the Management Board of Zvijezda.

Since this year Zvijezda has been operating as part of the Žito Group, one of the leading Croatian food groups. By entering the Žito Group a new development chapter has begun for Zvijezda, directed towards further strengthening of business, market position and the creation of new opportunities for growth.

“Zvijezda is one of the best-known Croatian food brands and a company that for 110 years has had a special place in the lives of generations of consumers. Its entry into the Žito Group represents a great responsibility for us, but also an opportunity to jointly build a new chapter of one of the most successful Croatian business stories, so that in the years to come we remain competitive and recognisable among consumers,” said Josip Bičvić, President of the Supervisory Board of Zvijezda. Zvijezda marked the anniversary also with a donation to the Croatian Down Syndrome Association, with which it has been cooperating for more than ten years, and as part of the cooperation the labels of a special edition of Zvijezda sunflower oil were decorated with drawings by children from the Association.

World.title: Croatian Scientists Concerned by Adriatic Sea Test Results
World.content:
September the 18th, 2026 – Croatian scientists are becoming more and more concerned by Adriatic Sea test results following 75 years of frequent measurements.

Scientists from the Ruđer Bošković Institute have analysed 75 years of measurements showing that the warming and salinisation of the Mediterranean Sea are accelerating, and the changes are becoming increasingly clear even in the deep layers. The Adriatic-Ionian area stands out particularly in this regard. Morski reports that when a warmer sea in summer is discussed, it usually means the temperature that is more or less suitable for swimming near the coastline itself. However, what we see and feel near the surface is only a small part of the story. Below it lie hundreds and thousands of metres of seawater, whose deep layers change much more slowly and are considerably harder to monitor.

It was precisely in these layers of the sea that scientists from the Ruđer Bošković Institute sought an answer to the question of how much the Mediterranean has really changed over the past decades. Dr Elena Terzić and Dr Ivica Vilibić, in a paper published in the leading international geoscience journal Geophysical Research Letters, collected and connected data from different periods, from historical measurements from research vessels to modern autonomous Argo floats that today regularly dive into the depths of the sea. In this manner, they obtained a kind of cross-section of the Mediterranean from 1950 to 2025 and tracked what is happening with the temperature, salinity and density of the sea at different depths. The results show that the Mediterranean is not only warming and becoming saltier, but that the speed of these changes is increasing, and their signal can be tracked hundreds and thousands of metres below the surface.

the sea’s warmth is increasing and the process is accelerating…

We have known for a long time that the sea is warming, and this process is most often described by the average rate of warming, i.e. by how much the sea temperature increases on average over one decade. “The average rate of warming tells us how much the sea temperature changed over some longer period. However, when we describe the entire period with a single average rate, we do not see whether the speed of warming itself is also changing. Our results show that it is increasing, so the average can conceal how much faster the changes of recent decades actually are,” explains Dr Elena Terzić.

In other words, a single straight line showing average warming no longer describes well enough what is happening in the Mediterranean. That is why the scientists also analysed the acceleration of warming, i.e. whether the speed at which the temperature is rising is itself changing. The clearest signal is seen near the surface, but the more interesting part of the story begins when one looks deeper. In the last years of the analysed period the temperature in the first hundred metres or so of the Mediterranean was about two degrees higher than the average of the second half of the 20th century. Warming is clearly visible also between 300 and 1,000 metres, and a measurable signal appears even at depths between one and two kilometres.

This is important because the deep sea does not react quickly to what is happening in the atmosphere. The surface can warm up during one exceptionally hot summer and cool down again a few months later, while changes in the deep sea take place much more slowly. “When the signal of change is no longer seen only near the surface but also deep in the water column, we are talking about a much broader change in the properties of the sea. The deep layers are a kind of memory of what has been happening in the system over a longer period,” emphasises Dr Ivica Vilibić.

why does the adriatic stand out here?

The temperature is not the only thing that is changing, because the Mediterranean Sea is simultaneously becoming saltier as well, especially in its central and eastern parts. Salinity and temperature together determine the density of seawater: the higher the salinity, the denser the water, and the higher the temperature, the lower the density. It is precisely the differences in density that drive the main circulation cells in the sea, i.e. the processes by which water mixes, sinks and transfers heat and salt from one part of the Mediterranean to another. Because of this, changes that begin near the surface do not necessarily stay there.

The Adriatic has a special place in this story because it is one of the areas of the Mediterranean in which dense water is formed. During cold winter periods the surface water can cool strongly, become dense enough and begin to sink. In this way the properties that the water acquired near the surface can be transferred into the deep layers of the Adriatic, and then further towards the deep Ionian Sea and the eastern Mediterranean.

The Adriatic-Ionian system in this research proved to be one of the areas with a particularly pronounced acceleration of changes. In the southern Adriatic a strong signal of accelerated warming appears even at a depth of around 1,000 metres, accompanied by simultaneous changes in salinity. This indicates that areas in which surface water sinks can be important places for the early detection and monitoring of changes that are transferred towards the interior of the sea.

how are measurements from 1950 and 2026 connected?

One of the biggest challenges in the research was to compare the properties of the sea that over the decades were not measured in the same way. In the 1950s and 1960s the data mostly came from research vessels, while today scientists have a network of Argo floats that independently pass through the water column and regularly send data on temperature and salinity. The authors therefore combined several large data sources, checked their quality and specifically tested whether the larger number of modern measurements could introduce bias into the results, i.e. artificially create the impression of acceleration. They repeated the analyses for different time periods and with different statistical approaches, and the basic pattern remained visible.

the wider mediterranean is an early indicator

The Mediterranean is a relatively small and almost closed marine basin that reacts strongly to changes in the atmosphere. Precisely for that reason it can serve scientists as a kind of natural laboratory for understanding what is happening to the oceans in a warmer climate. The research does not give a final answer to the question of which individual process is responsible for the observed acceleration. The changes can be connected with the warming of the atmosphere, evaporation and precipitation, the exchange of water with the Atlantic through Gibraltar, and changes in the circulation of the Mediterranean itself.

For the scientists the next step is to determine the contribution of each of these processes, and what they can already conclude is that the change in the Mediterranean is no longer only a story about a warmer sea surface. The sea is changing ever faster, and the signal of these changes has reached deep below the surface.

World.title: How Diaspora Professionals Use Croatian Citizenship to Work in Europe’s Top Hubs
World.content:
September the 17th, 2026 – The Croatian diaspora is vast, and many professionals are using their right to obtain Croatian citizenship as a key to unlocking work in Europe’s top hubs.

If we sift back through time, we’ll notice that the overarching pitch for securing Croatian citizenship by descent has targeted two distinct groups: those with a mysterious granny from a now abandoned Dalmatian village seeking a sentimental connection to their ancestral homeland, and retirees with similar stories looking to stretch their 401k to the maximum in a sun-drenched, slow-paced Mediterranean paradise.

It isn’t that those reasons don’t still largely exist, but it has to be said that times move (and more and more quickly), bringing marked shifts for the diaspora. A totally different demographic is suddenly digging up dida’s old birth certificates from curious settlements few have ever heard of. They’re the young, ambitious US corporate professionals who, for whatever reason, aren’t quite ready to give up on the grind and embrace the pomalo lifestyle just yet. Faced with the infamously gruelling American corporate world, hyper-competitive job markets, and a desire for global experience, millennial and Gen-Z professionals are realising that a Croatian passport isn’t just a nod to their heritage and genetic makeup, it’s also the ultimate professional fast-track into the booming, wide open EU economy.

croatian citizenship as a way to clear the corporate visa wall and unlock the european dream

Ask any young American professional who has tried to land a job in London, Amsterdam, Paris, or Berlin about their experience, and they will tell you the same thing: the visa barrier is nearly insurmountable. For a European company to hire an American citizen, they must generally prove to their local government that no qualified EU citizen could fill the role. This requires months of bureaucratic red tape, thousands of euros in legal fees, and an incredibly patient HR department. Unless you are a C-suite executive or a highly specialised niche engineer, most corporate resumes with a “Requires Visa Sponsorship” box checked are filtered out by automated tracking software before a human ever lays eyes on them.

Pulling a trusty little Croatian passport out of your pocket completely demolishes this dizzyingly high wall.

Because Croatia is a full Member State of the European Union, Croatian citizens possess the absolute right to live, work, and do business in any of the 27 EU member states, completely visa-free. As a dual citizen, an American professional can apply for a corporate job in Dublin, Amsterdam, or Frankfurt exactly like a local. No sponsorship is required, no legal fees are incurred for the employer, and there are no bureaucratic delays.

trading the american “live to work” for the european “work to live”

The motivation for young Americans to make the leap across the Atlantic goes far beyond geographic novelty. It is a fundamental rejection of the “hustle culture” that dominates US corporate life. When American professionals leverage their Croatian citizenship to work in Western or Northern Europe, they enter a completely different professional landscape where things like mandatory paid time off are completely normal.

While the US remains the only advanced economy without guaranteed paid vacation, all EU countries legally mandate between 20 to 30 days of paid annual leave, and employees are fiercely encouraged to actually use them.

Then comes the strict work-life balance: Countries like France and the Netherlands have strict laws regarding the “right to disconnect,” making it illegal or completely culturally unacceptable for managers to email or call employees after standard working hours are over for the day.

Robust healthcare as a fundamental human right will also likely be music to the ears of any US citizen sick of paying an arm and a leg just in case they happen to become unwell. Health insurance ceases to be a terrifying golden handcuff tied to a specific, often exhausting job. Across Europe, high-quality healthcare is decoupled from employment status and heavily subsidised or entirely free at the point of use. No premiums, no back pay, and nobody has ever heard of the term “reaching their out of pocket maximum”.

career acceleration, all while exploring europe

Living and working abroad for two or three years isn’t a career pause, it’s a massive career accelerator, and you can do it all while enjoying free healthcare and actually being paid to sit back and relax. In an increasingly globalised economy, American companies place an immense premium on candidates with international operational experience. Navigating foreign markets, managing cross-cultural teams, and understanding EU regulatory landscapes (like GDPR) are skills that cannot be taught in any kind of US lecture hall. When a young professional decides to return to the US corporate ladder, a resume featuring a stint at a global hub in Munich or Amsterdam instantly stands out from a sea of applicants who have never left their home time zone.

how croatianbydescent.com can help you get the ball rolling

For young Americans, particularly those who barely have a second for themselves when they get home, the process of tracking down old archives, certifying documents, and dealing with troublesome Croatian ministries can feel daunting. Turning to not only experts, but members of the Croatian diaspora themselves who have personal experience of the process streamlines it all and makes you feel understood. It transforms journeying through sometimes complicated ancestral roots into a modern, powerful career tool.

It may never have really occurred to you outside of donning those checkers during the World Cup or enjoying a dish you struggle to pronounce that grandma used to make, but if you have a parent or grandparent who left Croatia, you aren’t just sitting on a family history. You might actually be sitting on the key to your next major career upgrade and a lifestyle that the USA could never realistically provide.

World.title: Dubrovnik Mayor Claims “Most People Don’t Even Know Where Istria is”
World.content:
September the 17th, 2026 – Dubrovnik Mayor Mato Franković has caused a stir and claimed that “most people don’t even know where Istria is”, adding that “Dubrovnik is the only tourism champion in Croatia”.

Dubrovnik Mayor Mato Franković assessed the tourist season as excellent at a session of the City Council and claimed that Dubrovnik is “the only champion of tourism in Croatia.” Index reports that in his review of the results, which according to him exceed expectations, he directed criticism at the “Istrian lobby,” reports Dubrovački dnevnik.

“The season has been excellent, and what is ahead of us looks very good. So far it looks above expectations,” Franković said.

He also expressed satisfaction that the number of visitors in the historic centre is not exceeding critical levels, after which he sent a message to the competition. “We’re the only champion of tourism in Croatia and no one can measure up to us. Istria with its lobby is trying to present itself as successful. People exclusively from Istria, such as Veljko Ostojić, comment on tourism and they push it. We are alone, but we have shown that we are above everyone,” Franković said, concluding with the statement: “Most people don’t even know where Istria is.”

4.7 million people have come to dubrovnik so far in 2026

On Facebook he was answered by the president of IDS and mayor of Poreč, Loris Peršurić. Peršurić replied to Franković that Dubrovnik is one of the symbols of Croatian tourism and that one should be proud of its successes, but he ironised the claim that people do not know where Istria is.

“Just this year 4.7 million people successfully found it, and we’re only in the 9th month because the season with us lasts almost the whole year,” he wrote. He emphasised that Istria’s reputation was not created overnight, but was built over decades by private renters, owners of agritourism facilities, taverns and wineries, olive growers, caterers, hoteliers, craftsmen and farmers. He also pointed out that in tourism it is not only the numbers that matter, but quality, sustainability and the preservation of space for the people who live in it.

Peršurić added that Dubrovnik also has strong state and tourism tools for promotion at its disposal and concluded that one can be proud of one’s own successes without diminishing those of others. “I therefore invite you to personally convince yourself of the qualities of Istria, but hurry with the reservation because these days quite a few people manage to find us,” he said to Franković.

World.title: Russian Ambassador Summoned for Talks in Croatia Following Russia’s Threats
World.content:
September the 17th, 2026 – The Russian Ambassador has been summoned for talks in Croatia following Russia’s recent threats against various European countries.

Russian Ambassador to Croatia Alexander Nurizade was summoned today for talks at the Ministry of Foreign and European Affairs, where the Croatian side expressed concern over security threats from Russia towards European countries, the Russian Embassy in Zagreb announced. Index reports that according to the Russian side, Croatian representatives mentioned incidents in the airspace, territorial waters and on the infrastructure of EU member states, including in Denmark, Lithuania, Romania and Germany. The Ministry of Foreign and European Affairs lists Nurizade on its official website as the current Russian ambassador to Croatia.

the russian ambassador has rejected all accusations

The Russian Embassy states that Nurizade “firmly rejected” the accusations as unfounded. He described them, according to the embassy’s statement, as a “coordinated provocation” aimed at further worsening relations with Russia. He also expressed regret that Croatia, as the Russian side claims, “is pandering to the Kyiv regime and its foreign patrons interested in the continuation of the conflict.” These are the claims of the Russian Embassy. During the talks, Nurizade also repeated the official Russian positions on the causes of the war in Ukraine and accused the West of turning Ukraine into an “anti-Russian project.”

an attempted leipzig drone attack was discussed

Among the cases that the Croatian side, according to the Russian Embassy, cited was the incident in Leipzig. At the beginning of September, the German government officially accused Russia of being behind an attempted drone attack on Leipzig/Halle Airport on 4 August. A drone with explosives was found near a Ukrainian Antonov cargo plane. Berlin claims that the investigation traces the point to the Russian state, while Moscow rejects responsibility. After that case, the European Union and several member states summoned Russian diplomatic representatives for talks. EU High Representative Kaja Kallas said at the time that the incident had the characteristics of state-sponsored terrorism, while Russia claimed that Germany had not provided evidence for its accusations.

a russian vessel fired signal rockets at a danish aircraft

Tensions rose further this week after an incident out in the Baltic Sea. The Danish military announced that a Russian frigate, during routine surveillance, fired two signal rockets at a Danish military Fennec helicopter. One passed at a short distance from the helicopter. Denmark therefore summoned the Russian ambassador for talks. The Russian side countered with an accusation that Danish military helicopters had performed dangerous manoeuvres near Russian warships.

nato had to shoot down a drone over lithuania

In Lithuania a couple of days ago, an Italian fighter jet as part of a NATO mission shot down a drone that had entered Lithuanian airspace from Belarus. Lithuanian authorities announced that the drone was carrying explosives. Italian Defence Minister Guido Crosetto said it “most likely” came from Russia, but Lithuanian authorities warned that the investigation into its origin is still ongoing and that a final conclusion has not yet been reached. A similar incident was recorded last week in Romania, where a drone that Romanian and Moldovan authorities linked to Russian attacks on Ukraine entered deep into Romanian airspace before returning towards Moldova.

The Russian ambassador in the talks in Zagreb, according to a statement from his embassy, also spoke about Russian attacks on Ukrainian infrastructure. He conveyed that Moscow considers railway junctions, trains and other facilities in Ukraine used for the transport of the army or cargo intended for the Ukrainian armed forces to be “legitimate military targets.”

In recent days Russia has further intensified attacks on Ukrainian railway infrastructure, including areas near the border with NATO members. Ukrainian authorities claim that civilian trains and infrastructure have also been hit in the process. The summoning of Nurizade for talks comes at a time of heightened warnings from European and NATO officials about incidents involving drones, sabotage and other hybrid threats. The European Commission today also proposed a new mechanism for a coordinated response by EU members to such security incidents. An inquiry was also sent to the Ministry of Foreign and European Affairs about today’s talks with the Russian ambassador. We asked for confirmation of the meeting, the specific reason for his summoning, and clarification of which incidents Croatia cited and whether it plans further diplomatic steps after the talks.

World.title: Croatia to Get a New Road Worth Over €200 Million
World.content:
September the 17th, 2026 – Croatia is set to get a new road worth over €200 million, and it’s being widely compared to Pelješac Bridge.

The project includes two interchanges, five viaducts, four overpasses and two bridges. Poslovni reports that the Chinese company China Road and Bridge Corporation (CRBC) is building a 16-kilometre expressway that will finally directly connect Požega with the A3 Zagreb – Lipovac motorway. The new road will link Požeški Brestovac with the Godinjak interchange, where it will then connect to the motorway.

This is one of the largest infrastructure projects in Slavonia, which should significantly improve the transport connectivity of Požega-Slavonia County with the rest of Croatia. The route of the expressway runs south of Daranovci, after which it enters the forested area of Babja gora. There, a single-tube tunnel 1,650 metres long will be built, and the route then descends along a natural valley towards Tisovac and Godinjak. The project includes two interchanges, five viaducts, four overpasses and two bridges. The construction deadline is 48 months, meaning the new road should be completed by the end of 2029.

požega will get a faster link towards both zagreb and slavonski brod

The expressway is being built along the route of the existing state road D51, which has so far been the main transport link between Požega and surrounding settlements with the rest of the country. The new road should bring a safer and higher-quality connection to the A3 motorway, and thereby also to Zagreb and Slavonski Brod.

“This expressway represents the largest single project of Croatian Roads after the Pelješac Bridge. This is a big day not only for Croatian road construction, but also for Požega-Slavonia County, because it will be better and more safely connected to the motorway,” said Transport Minister Oleg Butković at the ceremonial introduction of the contractor into the works in Godinjak in November last year. For the residents of Požega-Slavonia County, the project represents the end of long-standing transport isolation. Due to frequent landslides and damage, the D51 does not fully meet modern standards of safety and traffic flow, so the new expressway will take over an important share of the traffic.

the požega interchange on the A3 motorway is also being built

At the beginning of February, a contract was also signed for the construction of the Požega interchange on the A3 motorway. The Požega interchange is part of the integral project for the construction of the expressway, which will connect to the motorway precisely at that point. The investor for that part of the project is Croatian Roads. When the works are completed, after decades of waiting Požega will finally get a direct fast road link with the A3 motorway, which should further improve the transport accessibility of the city and the entire Požega-Slavonia County.
