World.title: School holidays flight disruption fear as QantasLink staff threaten action
World.content:
Tell us about your experience.

Qantas is at the Fair Work Commission trying to prevent the Transport Workers Union (TWU) from going ahead with industrial action next week.

The planned 24-hour strike action on Thursday relates to QantasLink flights out of Sydney and freight services but may affect those travelling to selected regional areas.

School holidays are about to begin in Queensland, Victoria and the Northern Territory.

The industrial action involves about 650 employees, with most working on Qantas Freight and a smaller proportion servicing QantasLink flights at Sydney Airport.

These workers don't service Qantas mainline and international services, or QantasLink at any other airport.

Qantas said it had developed contingency plans to minimise any impact on QantasLink customers and operations, if industrial action went ahead.

"We remain committed to reaching an agreement with our Qantas Ground Services employees that includes annual pay rises for our people," it said in a statement.

Transport Workers Union National Secretary Michael Kaine said workers were not taking the action lightly.

"Any disruption to freight, including Australia Post shipments, sits solely at the feet of Qantas management and its brutal disregard for customers and the workforce," Mr Kaine said.

Transport Workers' Union national secretary Michael Kaine. (AAP: Lukas Coch)

He blamed increasing casualisation and insecure work for the ground crew for contributing to "shocking safety failures", something Qantas disputes.

“This action comes just over a year after a Qantas Freight worker was tragically killed on Father’s Day, " he said.

Qantas disputes TWU claims that safety incidents have increased since ground handling moved to Swissport more than five years ago.

Mr Kaine claims Qantas is continuing to "splinter" its workforce to suppress wages and "smash conditions".

"This is corporate greed on steroids, and it comes at the expense of quality service for customers, and safe, reliable jobs for the workforce."

Qantas ground staff vote for strike The Transport Workers Union says 97 per cent of 350 workers who voted backed industrial action, including work stoppages ranging from one to 24 hours.

Qantas said discussions through the Fair Work Commission had been constructive and negotiations were continuing.

World.title: Loophole closed after rare private prosecution shuts Hepburn council
World.content:
Tell us about your experience.

The Victorian parliament has acted to close a loophole that allowed an untested private prosecution by a private citizen to shut down the Hepburn Shire Council.

Earlier this year, Hepburn businessman David Penman levelled charges against five Hepburn Shire councillors and the chief executive officer in a rare private prosecution.

Mayor Tony Clark, councillors Don Henderson, Shirley Cornish, Pat Hockey and Lesley Hewitt, and chief executive officer Bradley Thomas were charged with misuse of public office offences relating to allegations they adopted the annual budget without certain financial documents.

Lesley Hewitt (left), Shirley Cornish, Tony Clark and Pat Hockey were all stood down from their council roles until the DPP intervened and withdrew the charges. (Supplied: Hepburn Shire Council)

Under the Local Government Act, all five councillors had to stand down until the matters were dealt with in court, meaning the council could not function without a quorum.

Opponents accused Mr Penman of weaponising a loophole in the act to effectively shut down the council.

The Director of Public Prosecutions ultimately intervened and had the charges withdrawn, allowing the five councillors to return to their roles.

Kate Makin says the loophole exposed a threat to democracy. (Landline: Tim Lee)

Rural Councils Victoria deputy chair Kate Makin, who is also Corangamite mayor, said the case exposed a threat to procedural fairness and democracy.

"Someone found the little door was ajar, and decided that that's how they were going to stand down these councillors," Cr Makin said.

Now, under changes to the Local Government Act, a councillor will only be automatically stood down in cases involving criminal proceedings underway, or when a law-enforcement agency is involved.

The amendment has passed the upper house of parliament.

"It just showed that if it could happen to one council it could happen to all of the councils across Victoria," Cr Makin said.

Wish it happened sooner

Cr Clark was caught up in the failed prosecution.

The Hepburn mayor said the new safeguard was a welcome relief for all councillors in Victoria.

"It's fantastic it's done, but I certainly would have hoped it had been fixed a little earlier than it was.

"It's a great sense of relief for our community.

Tony Clark has welcomed the changes. (ABC News: Eden Hynninen)

"[It] gives all councillors right across the state a bit more confidence about their role and their ability to be able to act democratically and appropriately," Cr Clark said.

World.title: The fine, the party, and the building watchdog that went quiet
World.content:
Internal government emails reveal NSW's building watchdog killed a media release detailing disciplinary action against developer Aland, despite imposing the maximum fine available and sanctioning its founder.

The decision to quietly shelve the release came months after Building Commissioner James Sherrard attended a party hosted by the developer while the company was under investigation.

Aland is one of Western Sydney's largest developers and plays a key role in the NSW government's push to meet ambitious housing targets.

Behind the scenes, however, Building Commission NSW investigators had spent years examining the company's conduct.

In April, Aland's construction arm was fined $220,000; the largest penalty ever imposed by the regulator.

Its founder, Andrew Hrsto, was personally fined $40,000 and ordered to sit compliance training to retain his licence.

Breaches included the use of unlicensed contractors and the unauthorised removal of a power pole, overhead wires and street lighting at a St Mary's construction site, which cut electricity to a childcare centre and risked public safety.

When it came time to announce the significant disciplinary action, documents obtained under Freedom of Information reveal a flurry of discussions about what the public should be told.

It points to a recalibration of the watchdog's strategy, with efforts focused on fostering confidence in the struggling sector, rather than publicly spotlighting a developer's failings.

Internal emails and texts

At 1:03pm on Tuesday, April 28, a senior media advisor at the Department of Customer Service, which handles communications for Building Commission NSW, circulated a draft media release titled: "Building Commission NSW takes disciplinary action against Aland."

Less than two hours later, the advisor emailed the Office of the Building Commission again.

"Hey all, going to make some further changes to this one."

By Wednesday, the planned media release had been abandoned.

"Any word on when we'll receive the Aland briefing pack? Just keen to start briefing on my end," a staffer from Fair Trading Minister Anoulack Chanthivong's office texted the media adviser on April 29.

"Holding statement at this point," came the reply.

A staffer from Fair Trading Minister Anoulack Chanthivong's office texted the media advisor from the Department of Customer Service. (Supplied: FOI)

Unlike a media release, which is proactively published and distributed to media outlets, a holding statement is generally only provided if a journalist specifically asks about the matter.

Do you know more? If you have any information about a story, contact Amy Greenbank at greenbank.amy@protonmail.com or amygreenbank.01 on Signal.

Internally, discussions continued.

By the afternoon of April 29, a draft holding statement was sent to management.

"Approved," Mr Sherrard replied at 4:26pm.

The statement was forwarded to the minister's office.

On Friday, May 1, a ministerial staffer responded:

"Please see approved lines … these are for reactive only at this stage."

Days later, a separate building commission staff member queried why no media release had been issued.

The senior media advisor replied:

"We've got ALAND in hand — no proactive comms at this stage."

The decision meant disciplinary action taken against the developer for serious misconduct was never proactively announced to the public, despite plans to do so.

Mr Sherrard, head of Building Commission NSW, which did not approve a media release being issued about disciplinary action taken against Aland. (Supplied: Building Commission NSW)

The ABC asked whether Mr Sherrard, Mr Chanthivong, or either of their offices had requested or supported the decision to dump the release.

A spokesperson for the Department of Customer Service said the building watchdog did not "routinely issue a media release for every disciplinary action".

Yet in the same month, the regulator publicly announced action taken against two plumbers who used fake s, issuing a media release detailing their penalties.

The approved holding statement, to be provided only to journalists who requested it, contained quotes attributable to the NSW building commissioner.

"Throughout the disciplinary proceedings Aland and Mr Hrsto fully co-operated with Building Commission NSW and have already made changes to their business," Mr Sherrard said in the statement.

A Department of Customer Service spokesperson told the ABC disciplinary action was published on the Verify NSW website, which can be searched by members of the public.

A spokesperson for Aland said it was working with the regulator to "further strengthen our processes" and reaffirmed its commitment to "continually improving our already high standards," pointing to its gold star iCIRT rating.

Flashy celebration

Aland's $375 million Archibald project in the Central Coast. (Supplied)

Five months before the regulator ditched the draft media release, Mr Sherrard attended a ritzy event hosted by Aland to mark the opening of its $375 million Archibald project on the Central Coast.

Mr Sherrard told budget estimates in August he was aware the firm was under investigation at the time, but was "not concerned about the optics of it" as the probe had "all but concluded", and the developer had been working to address shortcomings.

"I knew the details of what the offences were … I keep at arm's length from the disciplinary proceedings team in making a determination about what penalties to apply," he said last month.

Loading...

Mr Sherrard was joined at the Gosford ribbon-cutting ceremony by NSW Premier Chris Minns, who spruiked Aland and told the crowd the development was "fantastic for NSW".

Those comments, along with a clip of the building commissioner shaking hands with the Aland founder, was later featured in promotional material for the company.

String of controversies

For a developer who is no stranger to public scrutiny, the regulator's action attracted remarkably little attention.

In 2020, the owners of the Mascot Towers development in Sydney took legal action against an Aland subsidiary in the Supreme Court, claiming cracks in their building appeared after the developer conducted excavation work on neighbouring site, Peak Towers.

Aland denied the claim and settled out of court for a confidential sum on a non-admissions basis.

In 2024, Aland B&W was convicted and ordered to pay $225,000 after a migrant worker was crushed by 6 metre steel rods.

A crane worker lost control of the load, which hit the man, lifted him in the air and pinned him against formwork for up to a minute.

The worker suffered fractured ribs, a lower back injury and torn rotator cuff requiring surgical repair, according to the District Court judgment.

"In relation to Safe Work NSW, ALAND has invested heavily into its safety processes and procedures and continues to champion a safe working environment," the spokesperson for Aland said.

Mr Hrsto was fined following the watchdog's investigations. (Facebook: ALAND)

The same year, Mr Hrsto was reprimanded and fined $1,500 by the regulator after he failed to disclose pending criminal charges on a licence application.

Mr Hrsto had been caught with a 0.95g bag of cocaine at the Star Casino in 2019.

He pleaded guilty and was sentenced to an eight-month good behaviour bond, with no conviction recorded.

World.title: Taipan crash inquiry leads to recommendation for Defence report review
World.content:
Tell us about your experience.

A senate committee has recommended a Defence report into a 2023 army helicopter crash that killed four men be reviewed, after claims of corruption and fabricated evidence.

The senate probe into the MRH-90 crash, which claimed the lives of Captain Danniel Lyon, Lieutenant Max Nugent, Warrant Officer Class Joseph "Phil" Laycock and Corporal Alexander Naggs, began its inquiry in June.

Two public hearings were held, with former test pilots turned whistleblowers and family members of the four fallen men among those who gave evidence.

It heard explosive claims an independent Defence Flight Safety Bureau (DFSB) report had been corrupted by an "obvious" conflict of interest and contained "manipulated" and "fabricated" evidence.

Captain Danniel Lyon, Corporal Alexander Naggs, Lieutenant Max Nugent and Warrant Officer Class Two Joseph Laycock. (Supplied: ADF)

Those claims came from retired MRH-90 test pilots Major Ian Wilson and Major David Lamb, who spoke at the first public hearing.

Both had previously given evidence at a separate Inspector-General of the Australian Defence Force (IGADF) inquiry, which is yet to hand down its findings, and raised concerns about technology used in the helmets the two pilots were wearing the night they died.

Families of Taipan crash victims demand answers at inquiry The families of the four men who died in the crash are demanding answers, and say no one has been held accountable.

The IGADF inquiry had heard the TopOwl 5.10 software, which displayed readings on night vision goggles, had a tendency to give incorrect readings when pilots turned their heads.

Major Wilson said he had flagged issues with the technology with Defence before it was pushed into service, fearing someone would die if it was rolled out.

Some evidence before the IGADF has suggested it was released despite concerns, as it had already been paid for.

"Was this [crash] the exact incident you feared, because of the problems you saw in testing?" Senator David Shoebridge asked Major Wilson at the first hearing in June.

"It's almost to the word," he replied.

Concerns were raised about technology used in the helmets the two pilots were wearing the night they died. (Supplied: Bradley Richardson)

The DFSB investigation into the downing of the MRH-90 found it was unlikely the TopOwl technology contributed to the crash.

But Major Wilson told the senate one of the experts who provided evidence to DFSB investigators, was the same person who signed off on a memo downgrading the risks of the TopOwl technology.

DFSB director Group Captain David Smith was questioned about the alleged conflict of interest at the senate hearing but said any perceived conflict of interest was not the subject of the report.

Independent review recommended

The senate has now released a raft of recommendations following its probe, including that the Australian government independently review the DFSB report "to ensure the investigation and its findings were not improperly influenced and conclusions are sound".

It also recommended the government put the DFSB's independence under a microscope and that it establish a conflict of interest disclosure log.

"The conflict of interest concerns … brought into question the DFSB's conclusions," the senate report said.

Taipan wreckage pulled from water off Queensland coast following helicopter crash during training. (ABC News)

The senate also called for the Auditor-General to investigate whether Army Aviation was complying with workplace health and safety regulations, particularly around fatigue and safety culture.

Fatigue was a key part of the senate and the IGADF's inquiries, which heard evidence the four airmen were so tired, it would have been akin to driving over the legal alcohol limit, and would have impaired their flying capabilities.

The ABC has previously reported the workplace safety investigative and compliance body, Comcare, identified two alleged breaches of the law relating to fatigue and the TopOwl technology.

Taipan crash memorial A permanent memorial honouring the four men has been unveiled near the place where part of their helicopter was dragged from the water.

The Commonwealth Director of Public Prosecutions (CDPP) last year declined to lay charges against Defence, deeming there was insufficient evidence and no reasonable possibility of securing a conviction.

Major Wilson told the senate the "corrupt" DFSC report had been used by Comcare and the CDPP, "and may have affected [its] decision … not to prosecute".

The senate has also recommended the Department of Defence reconsider eligibility for the Roll of Honour at the Australian War Memorial.

The families of the four men were told their loved one's names could not be added to the roll, because they died during a peacetime training exercise.

"Should they be ineligible, the committee recommends a dedicated memorial be created along ANZAC Parade to honour training deaths," the senate report said.

World.title: K'gari resort set to be sold to US travel giant
World.content:
Tell us about your experience.

Traditional owners of K'gari, formerly Fraser Island, say they are hoping to work with the American company buying the island's largest hotel.

Kingfisher Bay Resort, which has 269 rooms, villas and holiday houses, is one of about 15 tourism operations being sold by Kelsian Group to tourism company Journey Beyond.

Lake McKenzie (Boorangoora) is one of K'gari's most popular destinations. (ABC Wide Bay: Johanna Marie)

Private equity firm Crestview Partners, based in the United States, owns Journey Beyond and already operates several high-profile tourism sites, including the Ghan and Indian Pacific railways, along with the Ayers Rock Resort.

The $145.8 million cash sale pays for Kelsian's tourism portfolio, which also includes K'gari Beach Resort and the K'gari Explorer tour operation.

Kingfisher Bay Resort offers 4WD tours to explore the world heritage-listed island. (ABC Wide Bay: Johanna Marie)

Sydney Harbour's Captain Cook Cruises, along with Kelsian's ferry and coach services, also form part of the deal.

The Australian Competition and Consumer Commission (ACCC) approved the sale in a determination last week, finding the deal was unlikely to affect competition in any market.

Traditional owners positive

The Butchulla people are K'gari's traditional owners, receiving native title rights over the island in 2014.

Butchulla Native Title Aboriginal Corporation chair Shawn Wondunna-Foley said the group welcomed any new owners or investors to the island, provided they worked constructively with traditional owners.

Fraser Island was officially renamed K'gari following a Butchulla ceremony in 2023. (ABC Wide Bay: Pat Heagney)

"Our focus is not on where investors come from, but on how they conduct themselves on Country," he said.

"We look forward to engaging with the new owners and exploring opportunities that can deliver lasting social, cultural, environmental and economic benefits for both the Butchulla people and the wider community."

Professor Daniel Gschwind from the Griffith University Institute for Tourism said international visitors expected to see genuine engagement with First Nations people in their tourism destinations.

"I would certainly encourage the new owners to build very strongly on what is ultimately a competitive advantage to be located in such an iconic, not just natural location, but also important First Nations destination," he said.

Daniel Gschwind is a Professor of Practice at the Griffith Institute for Tourism. (ABC News: Chris Gillette)

Kelsian Group and Journey Beyond did not respond to requests for comment.

Experiential tourism

When the sale agreement was first announced, Journey Beyond CEO Chris Tallent said the additional operations would work alongside its existing brands.

"They create new opportunities for guests to seamlessly extend their journeys across Australia — whether that's transitioning from rail to reef, river to resort, or city to sea," he said in February.

Journey Beyond acquired The Ayers Rock Resort in February. (Instagram: Explore Uluru)

Professor Gschwind said the resort was closely aligned with Journey Beyond's strategy of offering "experiential tourism".

"People don't want to just enjoy infrastructure and hotel rooms," he said.

"They want to really walk away from a tourism experience with … something that they can emotionally connect with, something they can talk about, something they can put on Instagram, something that they can brag about."

Kelsian Group chief executive Graeme Leigh told an August earnings call that despite the deal needing to be approved by the Foreign Investment Review Board, he expected it to be completed by the end of the year.

World.title: Trump seen looking at plans for Kennedy Center demolition
World.content:
Tell us about your experience.

A photograph of Donald Trump appearing to examine plans for the demolition of Washington's Kennedy Center, which he has been blocked from naming after himself, has sparked a backlash from his critics.

The Republican president was seen through the windows of Air Force One late on Wednesday, US time, holding a placard with visible text in red declaring: "Kennedy Center DEMOLIS…"

The plane's window frame obscured the rest of the word, but Mr Trump has mused repeatedly about razing the Washington landmark.

Below the words is a large picture showing a yellow, heavy construction vehicle scooping rubble.

With his approval ratings in the low 30 per cent range amid discontent over the war against Iran and the rising cost of living, Mr Trump has fixated on getting the Kennedy Center renamed in his honour.

He threatened to tear down the venue after a judge ruled this week that his name could not be added onto the building's exterior, earning the ire of Democratic politicians.

Loading...

Mr Trump said his administration planned to carry out needed multi-million-dollar renovations, then would have to "subsidise it for years to come".

"I think that the Trump administration should certainly have recognition because, frankly, if we don't do that, it's going to close. It'll end up being ripped down," he said.

Donald Trump is consuming Washington Project by project, Donald Trump is altering the United States capital.

Shortly after beginning his second term, Mr Trump installed himself as chairman of the centre, which is named in honour of late president John F Kennedy, a Democrat who championed civil rights before he was assassinated in 1963.

The venue's board, packed with Trump loyalists, voted in December to call it the "Trump-Kennedy" Center and installed signage with his name on it.

A judge ordered that Mr Trump's name be removed from the exterior and overturned the board's decision to rename the institution.

Workers removed Mr Trump's name from the building in June, but scaffolding and tarps have remained ever since.

The Kennedy Center takeover is one of several projects aimed at stamping Mr Trump's brand on the US capital, including lavish gold trim in the Oval Office, a triumphal arch near the National Mall, and a half-billion-dollar ballroom at the White House.

Some long-time patrons of the Kennedy Center are alarmed by plans to demolish it. (AP: Rahmat Gul)

On Thursday, local time, a US judge blocked Mr Trump's immediate efforts to demolish the building, ordering the Kennedy Center to provide 30 days' notice before making any major physical changes.

US District Judge Christopher Cooper said his ruling would "avoid any confusion on that score given more recent events", including the building's sudden closure to the public on Wednesday.

Matt Floca, the Kennedy Center's executive director and chief operating officer, said the building was closed due to "acute risks to public safety resulting from continued structural deterioration" of the aging building.

The building will be closed for at least seven days to "assess existing safety risks in those portions of the main building exhibiting severe structural deterioration", Mr Floca said.

The Kennedy Center is closed so workers can "assess existing safety risks" in the building, which opened in 1971. (AP: Jacquelyn Martin)

Joyce Beatty, an Ohio Democrat and a former member of the Kennedy Center board, has led efforts to block Mr Trump's name from being added to the building.

Ms Beatty had a verbal confrontation with the Republican president on Tuesday during a virtual board meeting.

Ms Beatty's lawyers said in a court filing on Thursday that the board members' "rationale that they are only temporarily closing the Kennedy Center is a plain pretext to justify shutting down the Center permanently. The facts before the Court are deeply concerning".

Congress has allocated $US257 million ($360 million) to cover the repairs, but Mr Trump said they only would happen if the board was permitted to move forward with plans to add his name to the building.

Senator Thom Tillis, a North Carolina Republican, called the dispute a "false crisis".

"Worrying about what [the building] is named is kind of silly," Mr Tillis said.

Wires/ABC

World.title: Outback nurse credits non-profit counselling service for saving career
World.content:
Tell us about your experience.

An outback nurse who has worked across remote parts of Australia says a peer-to-peer counselling service for nurses and midwives was a "godsend" during the most difficult time of his life.

Remote area nurse Dave Corstorphan previously worked in the Pilbara and Kimberley in Western Australia's north, including in the state's northernmost community Kalumburu.

Mr Corstorphan said he almost left the profession due to work stress and following the death of his wife.

However, he credits the free peer counselling service Midwife Health Program Victoria (NMHPV) for providing crucial support.

"I accessed that service, and it was an absolute godsend," Mr Corstorphan said.

" I would have just walked away completely from it [the job]. "

Mr Corstorphan said speaking directly to a counsellor who had been a nurse or midwife themselves was a game changer.

"The fact they've worked the shift work, done time in hospitals, know the conditions you're working under and seen all that, it makes a big, big difference," he said.

"You can say, 'This is what is happening,' and they go, 'Yep, I understand.'"

Dave Corstorphan says nursing in remote and regional health facilities is not without its challenges, especially for new nurses. (Supplied: Dave Corstorphan)

Up to 60 consults a month

Due to its success in Victoria, the Nurse and Midwife Program was extended across the country in 2024.

The Nurse Midwife Health Program Australia (NMHPA) runs as an independent and not-for-profit service, funded by the Commonwealth government as opposed to being led by state and territory governments.

NMHPA chief executive officer Lori-Anne Sharp and midwife Martine Kilday visited the Kimberley in August.

They said 42 per cent of staff who asked for help worked in regional locations.

Ms Sharp said counsellors received up to 60 calls a month from midwives, nurses and students.

Lori-Anne Sharp and Martine Kilday say burnout, shift work, and isolation are common issues for nurses and midwives. (ABC Kimberley: Esse Deves)

"The community really values the work they do, but they also need to be supported in the challenges of the work," she said.

"The shift work is another layer of that for rural and remote [workers]; it can be the large stints, long days, consecutive days."

An evaluation report into NMHPA's impact found the top five challenges raised by employees were anxiety and depression, stress, psychological distress, occupational violence, bullying or harassment, and burnout.

Ms Kilday said many staff were not aware of the service.

"Nurses and midwives are very good at looking after others … they tend to put themselves last on the list of self-care," she said.

Mr Corstrophan encouraged his regional and remote colleagues — some of whom were the only nurse in a specific location — to seek help.

"I think there is this fear of weakness, appearing weak, that we need to be stoic the whole time, particularly for our patients," he said.

WA Country Health Services says it employs about 4,200 nurses and midwives across regional areas. (ABC News: Keane Bourke)

"The work can be quite confronting."

Culture shock

Mr Corstorphan said nursing in remote and regional health facilities was not without its challenges, especially for new nurses.

He said a perceived lack of support, burnout and feelings of isolation were common outside metropolitan areas.

"They are full of energy to start with and they burn out very fast," Mr Corstorphan said.

"The people who live out there have always lived with what's out there and are very accepting, but for a lot of nurses from the cities, it's a culture shock."

'Heart of healthcare'

Both Mr Corstorphan and NMHPA said many staff may be cautious about raising their concerns while working within a state government department.

According to WA's Country Health Service, there are more than 4,200 nurses and approximately 240 midwives working across the state's regional health facilities.

More than 240 midwives are employed with the WA Country Health Service. (ABC North Queensland: Nathalie Fernbach)

WACHS nursing and midwifery executive director Alison Weatherstone said supporting the workforce was important, while acknowledging the "rewarding" and "demanding" work.

"Staff have access to confidential counselling through our Employee Assistance Program, as well as debriefing and peer support following stressful or challenging events," she said.

"We also provide targeted programs for particular teams, including specialist support through our 24/7 Command Centre and reflective supervision for cancer services staff.

"Nurses and midwives are at the heart of healthcare in country WA."

World.title: Fiji declares national HIV emergency as cases soar
World.content:
Tell us about your experience.

Fiji has declared a national HIV emergency, with new statistics showing one in 60 adults are living with the virus.

The government said in a statement posted on Facebook that 2,016 people were diagnosed with HIV in 2025, representing a 27 per cent increase in positive cases from the previous year.

Fifty-nine babies were born with HIV last year, and 18 died before their first birthday, it also said.

Authorities said expanded testing had helped uncover infections, enabling earlier treatment.

Fiji now plans to widen access to free, voluntary and confidential testing, preventive medicines, as well as harm-reduction services for injecting drug users and treatment.

Five years ago one in 167 people in Fiji had the virus.

HIV testing is being rapidly expanded across Fiji. (ABC News: Jeremy Story Carter, file)

Chair of Fiji's National HIV Outbreak Response, Jason Mitchell, told ABC's The World that there had been a scarcity of needles in Fiji because of law enforcement operations.

He said those operations were appropriate, but had hindered harm reduction efforts.

"We need to make needles and syringes widely available to the public, where anyone who is actually injecting has access to sterile needles and syringes so they can avoid sharing," Mr Mitchell said.

"I think it shows real bravery and real leadership of our government to introduce this and introduce it very quickly and scale it up."

He predicted it would take "upwards of five years" to bring the epidemic under control.

"The complexities of our communities that are impacted by HIV and engaging with them and working with them makes it very difficult for us to turn an epidemic like this around," he said.

"With the country rising together, we will get on top of this; it will just take time."

Fiji, a country of about 900,000 people, is experiencing one of the world's sharpest rises in new infections, according to UNAIDS.

It estimates that 9,100 Fijians were living with HIV last year, that only 39 per cent knew their status, and that 22 per cent were receiving antiretroviral treatment.

"Fiji has recognised the urgency of the moment and is stepping up its response," UNAIDS executive director Winnie Byanyima said.

" It is also a stark reminder to the world that AIDS is not over. "

Among cases with a known transmission route, more than half were linked to sexual transmission and over 42 per cent to injecting drugs, UNAIDS said.

The agency welcomed government plans for a needle and syringe program and expanded access to pre-exposure prophylaxis (PrEP), medicine used to lower the risk of contracting HIV.

The government has set up a five-minister cabinet subcommittee to remove barriers to action.

It said discrimination against people living with HIV was illegal and services were available nationwide.

Fiji's estimate of one in 60 adults living with HIV remains below parts of Africa, where nearly one in 35 adults are living with HIV, according to the World Health Organization.

The Australian sharemarket has made a positive start to the session after the US stock market rallied to its best day in six weeks, after falling oil prices and easing pressure from the bond market helped Wall Street reverse many of its moves from the day prior. The S&P/ASX 200 was up 30.7 points, or 0.4 per cent, to 8763.1 in early trade. The ASX added 0.4 per cent on Thursday. The Australian dollar was stronger at US71.11¢. Wall Street’s benchmark index recorded just its second gain in the past nine sessions. Bloomberg RBA chief Michele Bullock said in her opening statement to a parliamentary panel on Friday that Australia’s central bank board needs to decide later this month whether its benchmark interest rate is at a level sufficient to restrain price pressures and return inflation to target. “A key question is whether the tightening in monetary policy to date will be sufficient to bring inflation back to target in a reasonable time,” she said.



Related Article Aviation Qantas ground staff set to strike over ‘Joyce-era’ bargaining agreements “I recognise that higher interest rates are difficult for Australians with mortgages who are also facing cost-of-living pressures. But reducing inflation is essential.” The remarks are Bullock’s first significant public comments since the RBA’s August policy decision, when it held the key interest rate unchanged at 4.35 per cent for a second straight meeting. Officials have been signalling mounting concerns that inflation has been too high for too long and are worried about additional price pressures. Mining stocks are mixed, with BHP up 0.3 per cent and Rio Tinto 0.8 per cent, but Fortescue lost 0.3 per cent. Gold rallied alongside Treasuries as a slump in oil prices helped ease concerns about inflation, following the Federal Reserve’s first interest-rate hike since 2023. Bullion rose as much as 2.8 per cent to exceed $US4380 ($6150) an ounce, snapping a three-day drop. Gold miners advanced, with Northern Star up 1.9 per cent and Evolution Mining 2.7 per cent in early trade. Energy stocks lost ground as oil dropped for a third day, as supply concerns eased and traders looked to the next round of diplomacy that’ll shape the US-Iran war. West Texas Intermediate fell towards $US101 a barrel after losing almost 4 per cent over the two previous sessions, while Brent ended below $US105. In the Middle East, Saudi Arabia has moved to restore the damaged East-West pipeline to its Red Sea coast, aiming to return about half its capacity within days. At the same time, some tankers continue to traverse the contested Strait of Hormuz. Woodside Energy shed 0.5 per cent and Santos, 0.2 per cent. Among the refiners, Ampol dipped 0.1 per cent and Viva Energy, 0.2 per cent.



Financial stocks are steady, with Commonwealth Bank up 0.1 per cent, Westpac 0.2 per cent and ANZ Bank 0.2 per cent, while National Australia Bank retreated 0.1 per cent. Technology stocks are steady, with WiseTech and Xero flat in early trade, while Technology One edged up 0.1 per cent. NEXTDC and Codan each advanced 1.9 per cent. The Australian dollar was trading at US71.15¢ at 10.28am AEST. Overnight the S&P 500 jumped 1.1 per cent for just its second rise in the past nine days. The Dow Jones Industrial Average added 316 points, or 0.6 per cent, and the Nasdaq composite, 1.7 per cent. World.title: Why this indie rock star says turning off your phone is a political act
World.content:
CultureMusicStage shows Why this indie rock star says turning off your phone is a political act Matthew Westwood September 18, 2026 — 9:02am Save You have reached your maximum number of saved items. Remove items from your saved list to add more. Share A A A

Turning off your phone before the music begins at a symphony orchestra concert may be more than good etiquette – for musician and composer Bryce Dessner, it’s a political act. Best known as guitarist and songwriter with US indie band The National, Dessner is also a composer of classical music whose output includes works for orchestra, string quartet and solo instruments. Bryce Dessner and Anastasia Kobekina ahead of the first Australian performances of Trembling Earth. Steven Siewert “I’m not someone who stays out of politics – I get involved in a lot of causes and things – but I think the music often is doing other things, it speaks for itself,” he says. “The experience of coming into the concert hall – to get off your phone, and just be in the room with music, and to feel those things – in a way is a kind of activism.”



At a rehearsal with the Sydney Symphony Orchestra this week, Dessner – dressed in triple-denim with jacket, jeans and cap – paces the front of the Opera House stage. In his hands is the oversized orchestral score for his new cello concerto, Trembling Earth. The cello soloist, Anastasia Kobekina, is a picture of poise, her bare feet rooted to the floor, even as her bow threatens to throw off sparks in a tightly wound rhythmic passage. Co-commissioned by the Sydney Symphony Orchestra, and having its first Australian performances on Saturday and Sunday, Trembling Earth was written especially for Kobekina and already has been heard in Dublin, Berlin and Prague. Members of The National (from back left): Matt Berninger, Aaron Dessner, Bryce Dessner, Bryan Devendorf and Scott Devendorf. The Washington Post via Getty Images The title takes its name from a painting of an oak forest by Norwegian expressionist Edvard Munch that Dessner recalls seeing in Oslo. He says his musical composition, by turns lyrical and rhythmically intense, is intended to convey the natural world and be a reflection on human folly and destruction.



“It’s not a political piece but it’s an awareness of the tremendous instability and conflict in the world – that nature bears witness to human calamity and catastrophe and mismanagement and bad politics,” he says. “What is the experience of the earth through all of this?” Related Article Sydney councils ‘In Sydney this is a rarity’: The hidden music haven caught in a bitter council spat While his band The National is active in US politics – they backed the presidential campaigns of Democratic candidates Barack Obama and Hillary Clinton – Dessner says he is less overtly partisan in his classical music. An exception was his piece Skrik Trio, which he describes as a scream at Donald Trump’s 2016 election win. While Kobekina is making her first visit to Australia, Dessner is no stranger to these shores, having previously toured with The National, and partnered on earlier projects with Sydney Dance Company, the Australian String Quartet and the Australian Chamber Orchestra. He will appear in two separate programs with the Sydney Symphony Orchestra. The first, with full orchestra conducted by Umberto Clerici, will see the local premiere of Trembling Earth and Dessner’s earlier work, St Carolyn by the Sea – a double concerto for electric guitars featuring Dessner and Australian guitarist Zane Banks.



The second program, at Sydney’s City Recital Hall and repeated at Melbourne Recital Centre, includes excerpts from his film score for Train Dreams, and instrumental works Aheym, Impermanence and Garcia Counterpoint, Dessner’s solo guitar tribute to the Grateful Dead’s Jerry Garcia. Kobekina, who was born in Russia and lives in Germany, has earned accolades for her performances of concertos by Dvorak and Elgar, and last year released a recording of Bach’s monumental cello suites. The piece was written specifically for Kobekina. Steven Siewert She says Dessner’s new concerto, written for her, expresses the lyrical side of the instrument, which is like the human voice, but also “this earthy, primal energy”. “I love both sides, because we all have this in us,” she says. “I like how in this concerto you can experience constantly these contrasts – hot and cold, rhythmic and lyrical … I really feel that this world of sound that Bryce created will embrace everyone in the room.”



Trembling Earth, she adds, will continue to be performed into the future. “I do believe that this piece will be played in 30 years – it’s just so well written for the instrument, and just expands the repertoire that already exists for cello,” she says. “It’s not a usual thing that happens to every contemporary piece. I have so many times been asked by my colleagues, ‘Can I have the score, it’s so exciting’.” Dessner says that while Trembling Earth does not wear its politics on its sleeve, he wants Kobekina’s performance to speak to the audience. “The experience of coming to the concert hall to hear live music, to hear musicians like Anastasia – who has spent her life perfecting what she does, and to hear the Sydney Symphony Orchestra – it’s a very human form,” he says.

World.title: How an NBA legend’s ‘superpower’ has shaped Melbourne United’s new coach
World.content:
SportBasketballNBL How an NBA legend’s ‘superpower’ has shaped Melbourne United’s new coach Jon Pierik September 18, 2026 — 8:00am Save You have reached your maximum number of saved items. Remove items from your saved list to add more. Share A A A

When it comes to coaching, there have been few better in NBA history than San Antonio Spurs legend Gregg Popovich. “Pop”, as he is affectionately known, won five NBA titles – the last in 2014 – with the legendary Tim Duncan as his on-court pilot, and Australian great Patty Mills sharing in that final victory lap. So, when it came to the opportunity to lean into Popovich’s so-called “superpower”, new Melbourne United coach Jacob Chance was all ears. Here’s how we do it: Melbourne United coach Jacob Chance helped lead his club to the NBL Blitz title in Bendigo this month. Getty Images for NBL Chance was coaching the Spurs’ G League affiliate, the Austin Spurs, this year when Popovich – no longer coaching but still a key, even mystical, figure – visited the change room.



“He spoke to our team before one of the games. He also spoke to the main team before the play-offs,” Chance said of the San Antonio Spurs, who returned to the NBA Finals under new coach Mitch Johnson, falling to the New York Knicks. Related Article NBL ‘Have you not seen what I have made?’ Why Joe Ingles gave up $5.1 million to play in the NBL “You hear different things, but again, I think his superpower is just how clear he keeps it with the expectations of what it means to be a Spur, and it really just comes back to that – play really hard, play the right way, and be really coachable and a great teammate – and he just holds them to account for that.” Basketball can be turned into complex game of strategy, but Chance, just 32 and the youngest head coach in the NBL since Shawn Dennis led the now defunct Newcastle Falcons in 1997, has the ability to simplify in-depth analysis, ensuring players and fellow coaches understand what’s needed. It’s not hard to see why United owners Travis Knipe and Aaron Sansoni, and chief executive Nick Truelson, hold Chance in such high esteem, and legendary coach Brian Goorjian describes him as “elite”.



“It was good and refreshing to see. Like, yeah, as much as this is the most heightened sense of basketball in the world, you know, [the] NBA Finals, you’re still talking about the same things,” Chance said of Popovich’s chat to the NBA Spurs. The Spurs Way: Legendary NBA coach Gregg Popovich has had an influence on new Melbourne United coach Jacob Chance. Getty Images “Everyone asked me when I was over there, like, ‘What have you learnt coming over here?’ “It’s the same way you lose basketball games in under-10 Perth games – your Perth girls’ game you’re coaching, or another under-14 boys game in Melbourne you’re coaching, or the Spurs in the NBA Finals or Melbourne United – you will lose for the same reasons. You didn’t get back in transition. You didn’t help each other. You didn’t play the right way. You didn’t play hard enough, and so it was just refreshing to be on the biggest stage, yet we’re still talking about the same thing ... [It was] a good learning moment for me.” ‘I think his superpower is just how clear he keeps it with the expectations of what it means to be a Spur ... play really hard, play the right way, and be really coachable and a great teammate.’ United coach Jacob Chance on NBA legend Gregg Popovich



Chance’s mantra of “playing the right way” was also reinforced through watching Spurs superstar Victor Wembanyama, and the way he prepares, searching for that “one per cent improvement”. “The talent’s one thing, but just his demeanour and how he approaches the game is pretty special,” Chance said, chatting in his office at Hoops City in Cheltenham. Related Article NBA Giddey leaks: Bulls superstar breaks the news of gun NBL recruit “Like today, for example, we finish practice at 1 o’clock in the afternoon. We don’t practice again until 10 o’clock on Thursday morning. What are you doing between now and then? “I think [with] Vic [Wembanyama], the curiosity and the willingness he shows to try and find ways to improve his body and use that time well, I think it really separates him from other guys, so it’s a good one for us.”



Chance, a Perth native, has taken these “learnings” to United, the famous “Spurs Way” clearly strong in his thinking, and even in sight, with Brett Brown, the former NBL championship and Boomers coach and long-time Spurs assistant, dropping by training last month. The chance to replace three-time NBL championship coach Dean Vickerman as head coach of a marquee NBL club was too good to refuse for Chance, who initially rejected United’s advances before club chiefs circled back with a bigger offer, including the role of head of basketball operations. Ready to go: NBA veteran Joe Ingles and fellow United recruit Sam Waardenburg were a part of United’s off-season rebuild. Eddie Jim Having progressed as a highly respected assistant alongside Trevor Gleeson in Perth, beginning with the Wildcats as an intern in the video room, before joining Scott Roth in Tasmania, then Vickerman at United, and becoming a deputy head coach with the Boomers, Chance, complete with a four-year contract, and fiancée Bree opted to return to Melbourne. Bree, however, has yet to arrive, the couple having welcomed Beaux, an Aussie Shepherd, into their home before the opportunity to return to Melbourne was presented. Beaux needs to pass testing and quarantine measures before being allowed to get on a plane, and that won’t happen until closer to Christmas.



“It’s a nasty little process, but it’s worth it once we get everyone here,” Chance said. Meanwhile, there is plenty of work for Chance to do, beginning with the home opener against six-time league most valuable player Bryce Cotton and the Adelaide 36ers on Saturday night. United have built a championship-level roster – former NBA players Joe Ingles, Cole Anthony, Luke Travers and Josh Oduro joining blue-chip New Zealand big man Sam Waardenburg (from Cairns) in ensuring veteran star Chris Goulding has a chance for another ring. Despite early injury issues, the signs are promising, with United claiming the NBL Blitz pre-season tournament title. Goulding, entering his 12th season with the franchise, said Chance had impressed through building relationships and his game craft.



“I don’t want to say surprised me, but what’s been really great has been his attention to detail, his intent to get clarity, and how steadfast he is in what he believes in, and what he wants us to do and how he thinks we can be successful in that. He’s steadfast in that,” Goulding said. San Antonio Spurs superstar Victor Wembanyama. Getty Images Ingles, the NBA and Boomers veteran, is ready after a pre-season calf issue, and has delivered with his intangibles off the court in showing the younger players what is required to succeed at the top level. Anthony, a former teammate of Ingles with the Orlando Magic, will provide speed and shooting. Perth-product Travers, a former Cleveland Cavalier, will again play multiple roles in his return to the club. Oduro was with the New Orleans Pelicans last season, while Waardenburg is an athletic forward who can shoot from outside. Loading

Best known as guitarist and songwriter with US indie band The National, Dessner is also a composer of classical music whose output includes works for orchestra, string quartet and solo instruments. Bryce Dessner and Anastasia Kobekina ahead of the first Australian performances of Trembling Earth. Steven Siewert “I’m not someone who stays out of politics – I get involved in a lot of causes and things – but I think the music often is doing other things, it speaks for itself,” he says. “The experience of coming into the concert hall – to get off your phone, and just be in the room with music, and to feel those things – in a way is a kind of activism.”



At a rehearsal with the Sydney Symphony Orchestra this week, Dessner – dressed in triple-denim with jacket, jeans and cap – paces the front of the Opera House stage. In his hands is the oversized orchestral score for his new cello concerto, Trembling Earth. The cello soloist, Anastasia Kobekina, is a picture of poise, her bare feet rooted to the floor, even as her bow threatens to throw off sparks in a tightly wound rhythmic passage. Co-commissioned by the Sydney Symphony Orchestra, and having its first Australian performances on Saturday and Sunday, Trembling Earth was written especially for Kobekina and already has been heard in Dublin, Berlin and Prague. Members of The National (from back left): Matt Berninger, Aaron Dessner, Bryce Dessner, Bryan Devendorf and Scott Devendorf. The Washington Post via Getty Images The title takes its name from a painting of an oak forest by Norwegian expressionist Edvard Munch that Dessner recalls seeing in Oslo. He says his musical composition, by turns lyrical and rhythmically intense, is intended to convey the natural world and be a reflection on human folly and destruction.



“It’s not a political piece but it’s an awareness of the tremendous instability and conflict in the world – that nature bears witness to human calamity and catastrophe and mismanagement and bad politics,” he says. “What is the experience of the earth through all of this?” Related Article Sydney councils ‘In Sydney this is a rarity’: The hidden music haven caught in a bitter council spat While his band The National is active in US politics – they backed the presidential campaigns of Democratic candidates Barack Obama and Hillary Clinton – Dessner says he is less overtly partisan in his classical music. An exception was his piece Skrik Trio, which he describes as a scream at Donald Trump’s 2016 election win. While Kobekina is making her first visit to Australia, Dessner is no stranger to these shores, having previously toured with The National, and partnered on earlier projects with Sydney Dance Company, the Australian String Quartet and the Australian Chamber Orchestra. He will appear in two separate programs with the Sydney Symphony Orchestra. The first, with full orchestra conducted by Umberto Clerici, will see the local premiere of Trembling Earth and Dessner’s earlier work, St Carolyn by the Sea – a double concerto for electric guitars featuring Dessner and Australian guitarist Zane Banks.



The second program, at Sydney’s City Recital Hall and repeated at Melbourne Recital Centre, includes excerpts from his film score for Train Dreams, and instrumental works Aheym, Impermanence and Garcia Counterpoint, Dessner’s solo guitar tribute to the Grateful Dead’s Jerry Garcia. Kobekina, who was born in Russia and lives in Germany, has earned accolades for her performances of concertos by Dvorak and Elgar, and last year released a recording of Bach’s monumental cello suites. The piece was written specifically for Kobekina. Steven Siewert She says Dessner’s new concerto, written for her, expresses the lyrical side of the instrument, which is like the human voice, but also “this earthy, primal energy”. “I love both sides, because we all have this in us,” she says. “I like how in this concerto you can experience constantly these contrasts – hot and cold, rhythmic and lyrical … I really feel that this world of sound that Bryce created will embrace everyone in the room.”



Trembling Earth, she adds, will continue to be performed into the future. “I do believe that this piece will be played in 30 years – it’s just so well written for the instrument, and just expands the repertoire that already exists for cello,” she says. “It’s not a usual thing that happens to every contemporary piece. I have so many times been asked by my colleagues, ‘Can I have the score, it’s so exciting’.” Dessner says that while Trembling Earth does not wear its politics on its sleeve, he wants Kobekina’s performance to speak to the audience. “The experience of coming to the concert hall to hear live music, to hear musicians like Anastasia – who has spent her life perfecting what she does, and to hear the Sydney Symphony Orchestra – it’s a very human form,” he says.

World.title: How an NBA legend’s ‘superpower’ has shaped Melbourne United’s new coach
World.content:
SportBasketballNBL How an NBA legend’s ‘superpower’ has shaped Melbourne United’s new coach Jon Pierik September 18, 2026 — 8:00am Save You have reached your maximum number of saved items. Remove items from your saved list to add more. Share A A A

When it comes to coaching, there have been few better in NBA history than San Antonio Spurs legend Gregg Popovich. “Pop”, as he is affectionately known, won five NBA titles – the last in 2014 – with the legendary Tim Duncan as his on-court pilot, and Australian great Patty Mills sharing in that final victory lap. So, when it came to the opportunity to lean into Popovich’s so-called “superpower”, new Melbourne United coach Jacob Chance was all ears. Here’s how we do it: Melbourne United coach Jacob Chance helped lead his club to the NBL Blitz title in Bendigo this month. Getty Images for NBL Chance was coaching the Spurs’ G League affiliate, the Austin Spurs, this year when Popovich – no longer coaching but still a key, even mystical, figure – visited the change room.



“He spoke to our team before one of the games. He also spoke to the main team before the play-offs,” Chance said of the San Antonio Spurs, who returned to the NBA Finals under new coach Mitch Johnson, falling to the New York Knicks. Related Article NBL ‘Have you not seen what I have made?’ Why Joe Ingles gave up $5.1 million to play in the NBL “You hear different things, but again, I think his superpower is just how clear he keeps it with the expectations of what it means to be a Spur, and it really just comes back to that – play really hard, play the right way, and be really coachable and a great teammate – and he just holds them to account for that.” Basketball can be turned into complex game of strategy, but Chance, just 32 and the youngest head coach in the NBL since Shawn Dennis led the now defunct Newcastle Falcons in 1997, has the ability to simplify in-depth analysis, ensuring players and fellow coaches understand what’s needed. It’s not hard to see why United owners Travis Knipe and Aaron Sansoni, and chief executive Nick Truelson, hold Chance in such high esteem, and legendary coach Brian Goorjian describes him as “elite”.



“It was good and refreshing to see. Like, yeah, as much as this is the most heightened sense of basketball in the world, you know, [the] NBA Finals, you’re still talking about the same things,” Chance said of Popovich’s chat to the NBA Spurs. The Spurs Way: Legendary NBA coach Gregg Popovich has had an influence on new Melbourne United coach Jacob Chance. Getty Images “Everyone asked me when I was over there, like, ‘What have you learnt coming over here?’ “It’s the same way you lose basketball games in under-10 Perth games – your Perth girls’ game you’re coaching, or another under-14 boys game in Melbourne you’re coaching, or the Spurs in the NBA Finals or Melbourne United – you will lose for the same reasons. You didn’t get back in transition. You didn’t help each other. You didn’t play the right way. You didn’t play hard enough, and so it was just refreshing to be on the biggest stage, yet we’re still talking about the same thing ... [It was] a good learning moment for me.” ‘I think his superpower is just how clear he keeps it with the expectations of what it means to be a Spur ... play really hard, play the right way, and be really coachable and a great teammate.’ United coach Jacob Chance on NBA legend Gregg Popovich



Chance’s mantra of “playing the right way” was also reinforced through watching Spurs superstar Victor Wembanyama, and the way he prepares, searching for that “one per cent improvement”. “The talent’s one thing, but just his demeanour and how he approaches the game is pretty special,” Chance said, chatting in his office at Hoops City in Cheltenham. Related Article NBA Giddey leaks: Bulls superstar breaks the news of gun NBL recruit “Like today, for example, we finish practice at 1 o’clock in the afternoon. We don’t practice again until 10 o’clock on Thursday morning. What are you doing between now and then? “I think [with] Vic [Wembanyama], the curiosity and the willingness he shows to try and find ways to improve his body and use that time well, I think it really separates him from other guys, so it’s a good one for us.”



Chance, a Perth native, has taken these “learnings” to United, the famous “Spurs Way” clearly strong in his thinking, and even in sight, with Brett Brown, the former NBL championship and Boomers coach and long-time Spurs assistant, dropping by training last month. The chance to replace three-time NBL championship coach Dean Vickerman as head coach of a marquee NBL club was too good to refuse for Chance, who initially rejected United’s advances before club chiefs circled back with a bigger offer, including the role of head of basketball operations. Ready to go: NBA veteran Joe Ingles and fellow United recruit Sam Waardenburg were a part of United’s off-season rebuild. Eddie Jim Having progressed as a highly respected assistant alongside Trevor Gleeson in Perth, beginning with the Wildcats as an intern in the video room, before joining Scott Roth in Tasmania, then Vickerman at United, and becoming a deputy head coach with the Boomers, Chance, complete with a four-year contract, and fiancée Bree opted to return to Melbourne. Bree, however, has yet to arrive, the couple having welcomed Beaux, an Aussie Shepherd, into their home before the opportunity to return to Melbourne was presented. Beaux needs to pass testing and quarantine measures before being allowed to get on a plane, and that won’t happen until closer to Christmas.



“It’s a nasty little process, but it’s worth it once we get everyone here,” Chance said. Meanwhile, there is plenty of work for Chance to do, beginning with the home opener against six-time league most valuable player Bryce Cotton and the Adelaide 36ers on Saturday night. United have built a championship-level roster – former NBA players Joe Ingles, Cole Anthony, Luke Travers and Josh Oduro joining blue-chip New Zealand big man Sam Waardenburg (from Cairns) in ensuring veteran star Chris Goulding has a chance for another ring. Despite early injury issues, the signs are promising, with United claiming the NBL Blitz pre-season tournament title. Goulding, entering his 12th season with the franchise, said Chance had impressed through building relationships and his game craft.



“I don’t want to say surprised me, but what’s been really great has been his attention to detail, his intent to get clarity, and how steadfast he is in what he believes in, and what he wants us to do and how he thinks we can be successful in that. He’s steadfast in that,” Goulding said. San Antonio Spurs superstar Victor Wembanyama. Getty Images Ingles, the NBA and Boomers veteran, is ready after a pre-season calf issue, and has delivered with his intangibles off the court in showing the younger players what is required to succeed at the top level. Anthony, a former teammate of Ingles with the Orlando Magic, will provide speed and shooting. Perth-product Travers, a former Cleveland Cavalier, will again play multiple roles in his return to the club. Oduro was with the New Orleans Pelicans last season, while Waardenburg is an athletic forward who can shoot from outside. Loading

World.title: 'Get on board':Te reo Māori offers a deeper understanding of Aotearoa
World.content:
The evolving education of te reo Māori in Aotearoa Morning Report Download MP3 4m

Te reo Māori is being learnt by more people across Aotearoa, as the language continues to be revitalised across generations.

This year's Te Wiki o Te Reo Māori theme, Ake, Ake, Ake - A Forever Language, reflects that intergenerational journey and the role each generation plays in keeping the reo alive and passing it on.

Māori Language Commissioner Professor Rawinia Higgins describes it as a three-generation kaupapa, where every step towards learning and using te reo contributes to the next generation.

At Selwyn Community Education in Tāmaki Makaurau, those journeys are coming together in one classroom.

For fifth-generation Pākehā Rebecca Jerram, learning te reo Māori is about understanding the relationship between Māori and Pākehā and what that means for future generations.

"I think we actually owe it to our future New Zealanders, to be honest," she said.

"If you've been here a long time, then maybe the onus is on us even more to make sure that, hey, we've been hanging out here for quite a while, and we really need to understand te ao Māori and te taiao, and all the concepts that come with being a partner with Māori."

Jerram has been learning te reo Māori for around five or six years. She teaches landscape architecture at Unitec and said she wants future generations of Pākehā and tauiwi to better understand the partnership between Māori and Pākehā.

"We are in a partnership, and some might say it's a forced marriage, or it's an arranged marriage. But it's a marriage nonetheless.

"We're married, and I guess you've got to get to know your partner. So in my mind, it's about really getting to know that partnership and understanding what we bring to it together. And we shouldn't be flying blind."

Pākehā akonga Rebecca Jerram says te ao Māori can offer a way towards greater understanding in times of division. RNZ / Layla Bailey-McDowell

Jerram said Māori have also created space for Pākehā to learn and engage with te ao Māori.

"Māori have been very patient with Pākehā in that they've actually opened their world to us. It's up to us to reciprocate," she said.

"It's never been, or not in my lifetime, has it been thrown at us. It's not been taunted for not speaking the tongue of the whenua.

"We've been coached and manaaki-ed through with a lot of awhi, and how lucky are we that Māori are prepared to take a long walk.

"It's a long, long walk, it's generational, and I still encourage Pākehā to join that walk."

Jerram said she sees learning te reo as part of that long-term commitment to the relationship between Māori and Pākehā.

"I just think it's on our generation, as much as it has been to our tūpuna that have gone, to actually ensure that the people coming through do understand this partnership as well."

For Argentinian ākonga Facu Cuello learning te reo Māori was one of the first things he did after moving to Aotearoa three years ago. Supplied / Facu Cuello

Argentinian ākonga Facu Cuello said learning te reo Māori was one of the first things he did after moving to Aotearoa three years ago.

"I moved to a new country, I need to learn the language of the country. I already spoke English, but from my perspective, Māori is the native language of the country, so for me moving from overseas into the country, the least I can do is to make an effort to learn the language."

He hoped that more people shared that whakaaro.

"I wish more people had the same perspective, that you're moving to a country that speaks Māori, and you should make an effort at least to pick up the basics, or do as much as you can, and it's within your reach in your day-to-day, to honour the language, honour the people, and contribute to the revitalisation of a language that needs it."

Cuello said learning te reo has changed the way he experiences the country around him.

"When you start learning about all those stories and those perspectives and ways of thinking, it really gives it a different meaning."

Aidan Te Whata says learning te reo is about reconnecting with a language that was not passed down through his whānau. RNZ / Layla Bailey-McDowell

For Māori ākonga Aidan Te Whata, learning te reo is about reconnecting with a language that was not passed down through his whānau.

Te Whata, who has whakapapa to Ngāti Porou, Te Whānau-ā-Apanui, Rongowhakaata and Ngāpuhi, grew up in te ao Pākehā, speaking English.

He said the attitudes he encountered towards te reo when he was younger became internalised.

"You hear, 'oh, what's that language? Oh, it's a dead language.' It's like, you kind of just bury it within you and you believe it yourself. It starts to manifest as a belief."

Now in his 30s, Te Whata said his relationship with the language has changed.

"I no longer believe that. And I'm finding ways to reconnect with my whakapapa, my language."

The te reo Māori class brings together people from all backgrounds. RNZ / Layla Bailey-McDowell

His reo journey has also brought him closer to his whānau and tūrangawaewae.

"Your whakapapa and your ancestors are looking down and going, you know, look at you go. You're carrying that with you. You carry your whānau with you."

He said being part of a generation helping revitalise te reo is something to be proud of.

"I was going to say it's been lost. It's not been lost. It's been revitalised.

"And we're the ones that are to bring it back. And it's exciting. And something to be proud of."

For many, learning te reo Māori has opened up a deeper understanding of the place they call home. RNZ / Layla Bailey-McDowell

Te Whata said having Pākehā and tauiwi alongside him in the classroom also shows the language is being embraced by people from across the world.

"I think it's beautiful...it shows us, the love will always overcome hate."

Te Whata wants to continue learning until speaking te reo Māori becomes second nature.

"I want to do this more, and I ain't going to stop until I begin thinking in Māori. That's when I'm like, 'ooh, I've made it'.

For many, learning te reo is a way to deeper understand the place they call home.

Jerram said the country has felt increasingly divided in the last few years and believes te ao Māori can offer a way towards greater understanding.

"I think the sea has been choppy in the last two to three years particularly. There's been storms coming through, and they are still coming.

Rebecca Jerram's kurī Daisy also attends the te reo Māori class. RNZ / Layla Bailey-McDowell

"I think we need to look to a place where Tangaroa is calm.

"We need the seas to just settle. We need people to understand why it's so important to have that settling, because we're a country that's at peace in a really mixed-up world."

Jerram believes it's on the generation that she belongs to, to see themselves as part of continuing the change.

"I was going to say proponents of change, but Māori themselves have driven that."

World.title: Future of banking could bring more choice, but also risk - RBNZ
World.content:
A Reserve Bank study says banking could become more like the apps people use every day, but the shift comes with risks.

Banking could become as quick, easy and personalised as services such as Netflix, Amazon and Uber over the next decade, with financial services increasingly built into the digital platforms New Zealanders use every day, according to a new study by the Reserve Bank.

Its Future of Banking 2035 report examines how banking might change over time, what it could mean for the resilience and stability of the financial system, and whether regulation can evolve quickly enough to cover future risks.

Director of financial system assessment Kerry Watt said "banking is changing and that change seems to be accelerating", driven by artificial intelligence, cloud computing, new entrants and changing consumer preferences.

For consumers, Watt said that could mean changes to the cost, effectiveness and tailoring of the banking products and services they use, as well as the risks they and their money could be exposed to.

The report identifies potential benefits including increased competition and innovation, better products, more tailored, cheaper and more effective services, easier access to credit for some customers, and better risk management.

Those benefits had the potential to drive increased productivity and better economic outcomes, Watt said, but the changes also came with risks.

They included operational risk, cyber risks, increased dependence on third-party technology providers such as cloud infrastructure and AI service providers, and risks associated with AI, including fraud and scams.

For regulators, Watt said a key risk was that regulation may not be able to keep up with the changes.

The future of banking mattered because it would affect almost everyone, Watt said.

"Banking is critical to most of our daily lives. It is how we spend, it's how we save, and it's how we borrow," he said.

Consumers would ultimately feel the effects through the banking products and services they use, their cost and effectiveness, how tailored they are, and the risks they and their money may be exposed to, he said.

Watt said open banking could significantly increase competition, but only if customers trusted the services and were willing to switch products and providers.

World.title: Controversial move on orders pass third reading, under urgency
World.content:
The government's controversial move on orders legislation has passed its third reading in Parliament, under urgency.

It means police will soon have the power to order people to move elsewhere if they are being disorderly, begging or rough sleeping.

Anyone disobeying the order will face a fine or possible jail sentence.

Parliament's Justice Select Committee - which includes MPs from most parties - had been considering the legislation for months, hearing submissions from the likes of police, social service organisations and legal experts.

Its recent report recommended a change so people under 18 years old could not be subjected to a move on order.

The first iteration of the law applied to people as young as 14.

More than 98 percent of those who submitted on the legislation were against it, describing it as morally indefensible, unnecessary and a breach of the Bill of Rights.

Some said it criminalised homelessness.

One of the very few submitters in support said the system currently had no teeth to deal with aggressive and non compliant behaviour.

Justice Minister Paul Goldsmith said move on orders would "reclaim our streets and town squares for the enjoyment of those who visit, work and live there".

They would not criminalise homelessness, he said.

"They simply provide Police with an additional tool to deal with people displaying disorderly behaviour in public places.

"Only people who refuse those orders will face prosecution. A move-on order is not a criminal charge."

During the final debate in Parliament on Friday, Goldsmith said public places belonged to everyone, and should be welcoming, accessible and safe.

"Yet for too many New Zealanders, that has not been the case for a while," he said.

"This legislation represents part of this government's efforts to turn that around."

'Shameful day' - Opposition

Labour's Camilla Belich said the bill targeted the country's most vulnerable people and did not give them the help they needed.

"This is a very, very shameful day for our Parliament," she said.

The Greens' Tamatha Paul agreed, labelling the law cruel and disgusting.

She argued the law did criminalise homelessness.

"[The government] did not even attempt to address the root factors of why there is record level homelessness in this country," she said.

"If only this House would not be so ignorant, and would listen to the actual people who are working on the front line, and what they have told us will work."

The Greens put forward a change requiring the Ministry of Social Development to provide assistance to everyone who was issued a move on order, but it was voted down.

ACT MP Todd Stephenson supported the bill.

"We inherited a mess in law and order, and this is yet another tool that we're putting in place to deal with antisocial behaviour," he said.

Stephenson claimed ACT secured changes to the bill, including the age change.

New Zealand First's Casey Costello said similar concerns that the law would not work were aired over the government's gang patch ban.

"Actually, as we see in the streets, it has worked perfectly," she said.

"This bill takes our streets back, it gives an opportunity to put some commonsense tools in the hands of police."

Te Pāti Māori MP Oriini Kaipara said her heart was heavy, and she had on Friday morning received messages from street whānau.

"[They said] please, save us, if this Bill goes through our lives will be ten times worse."

World.title: Dead Petone seal tests negative for bird flu
World.content:
A leopard seal found dead in the Hutt River died of natural causes and not bird flu, the Department of Conservation (DOC) says.

The seal drew crowds on Petone Beach earlier this month, with reports that some members of the public harassed the protected animal.

Ranger biodiversity David Moss said bird flu testing came back negative, and the seal did not appear to be infected with any other disease.

"The test results show the leopard seal was relatively old, and not infected with [high pathogenicity avian influenza] or any other obvious disease. From this, we can infer she died of natural causes."

World.title: Could a flexible superannuation cost taxpayers less?
World.content:
Could a flexible Super be cheaper Nine To Noon Download MP3 12m

The head of chartered accountants' organisation New Zealand says letting people choose to defer receiving superannuation could lead to savings of nearly $100 billion over 20 years.

Chartered Accountants Australia and New Zealand modelled letting people choose to take super between ages 66 and 70.

Chartered Accountants New Zealand head Peter Vial told Nine to Noon in their preferred scenario 40 percent of eligible retirees would defer receiving super until age 70, in order to get a higher payment.

That would lead to savings of $98 billion over 20 years, and in 2048 it would be saving $7.8 billion a year.

The current cost of superannuation to the government was $26 billion a year which was 5 percent of gross domestic product (GDP) and about 19 percent of all New Zealand tax collected was spent on superannuation, he said.

There would be a three-fold increase in the cost of super by 2048 to $73b a year and it would then be up to 8 percent of GDP and it would equate to 30 percent of all tax collected, he said.

"So the problem is stark and the numbers are scary."

In the 1960s New Zealand had seven working age people to every one pensioner, currently there are four and by 2065 there would only be two working aged people to every national superannuitant, he said.

"So we've got over 900,000 on super now and in 10 years time I think we'll have over 1.3 million."

Vial said although the superannuation fund would be helpful it would not go anywhere near solving the problem.

Raising the age at which people could receive superannuation would help but it would "only push the problem out", he said.

"What we're suggesting is that people have an option of taking super either at 65 or at ages right through from 66 to 70, so some people will defer and that reduces the cost."

One of the scenarios modelled was for people to still get superannuation at 65 but that meant they would only receive 95 percent of the current rate, he said.

"Or push it through out to 70 and each year they'd get 107.5 percent of the current rate - that would save $98 billion over 20 years."

He did say it was a harsher model for those who had no choice but to retire at 65, because they would receive 95 percent of the current entitlement.

The alternative was that the age you could receive superannuation would go up for everyone, he said.

"And it may go up to 67 as some of the parties are currently suggesting but the numbers are looking so serious and so scary that the numbers could go up to 68, 69 or 70.

"So in our view this is a much fairer approach, it gives people choice."

Ideally 40 percent of people would defer receiving superannuation but even if only 20 percent deferred it would still result in saving $64b over 20 years, he said.

Other models made smaller changes but would raise less for the government overall.

One was a scenario where people could get 100 percent of super aged 65, he said.

If you deferred taking super under that model you would get an increased amount depending on how long you deferred it, he said.

"So if you deferred to 67 you would get you'd get 105 percent, the curb is not so steep so the saving is less. The saving over the 20 years would only be $72 billion as opposed to $100 billion [in the first scenario]."

He said despite the lesser savings it was a fairer model where no one would be worse off.

"There is a third model which has a much steeper curve, so people take 90 percent at 60 and if they defer to 70 they get 130 percent which is a very big sum and that doesn't save quite as much as the first model."

It still provided a decent saving but it was much less fair, he said.

Vial said in doing the modelling they aimed to spark political debate on the issue.

"We want the next government, whatever it looks like, to have some cross party discussions and deep analysis here. Treasury and IRD [Inland Revenue] have done a lot of work here and politicians seem to be kicking the can down the road."
