World.title: Opportunity proposes methane trading scheme, $5b climate adaptation plan
World.content:
Opportunity wants to explore an emissions cap-and-trade scheme for methane and will commit $5 billion to climate adaptation, it says.

The party has released its full climate policy ahead of the 2026 general election, saying it is time to restore the cross-party consensus that led to New Zealand's zero carbon laws.

Its pledges include a $1 billion transition fund for industrial gas and coal users, and a $5 billion climate resilience fund to strengthen transport, energy and water networks against extreme weather.

Similar funds existed under the previous government but were scrapped by the National-led coalition, which says it is still funding climate resilience through transport and other budgets, rather than an earmarked fund.

The resilience fund would tag $500 million for "nature-based solutions" like restoring wetlands, while community groups and marae would also receive some of the funding for local projects.

The party said it would also introduce tax write-offs for home and business energy improvements like EVs, batteries and rooftop solar.

It confirmed its support for low-interest green loans administered by local councils - a policy proposed by Local Government New Zealand that has also been adopted by National, Labour and the Greens.

Opportunity leader Qiulae Wong said the party rejected the "false choice between cutting emissions and keeping the lights on".

"A low-carbon future isn't about doing without," she said.

"It's about making our homes cheaper to run, our businesses more resilient, and our country immune to volatile global fossil fuel prices."

The Zero Carbon Act - which passed in 2019 with near-universal parliamentary support - had provided businesses and communities with long-term certainty.

"We lost that certainty when the Coalition gutted the Act last year," Wong said.

New Zealand's agriculture industry produces large amounts of methane. RNZ/Alexander Robertson

The current Government has made multiple changes to the law without cross-party consensus, including weakening the targets for methane emissions and no longer requiring domestic climate policy to align with New Zealand's Paris Agreement pledges.

The coalition also ruled out any future methane tax last year.

Nearly half of New Zealand's total emissions come from agricultural methane - a short-lived but potent greenhouse gas that farming lobby groups argue should be treated differently to long-lived emissions like carbon dioxide.

Labour has also recently ruled out a methane tax, saying it would instead encourage farmers to adopt methane-busting technologies that are being developed in New Zealand and overseas.

Opportunity said it wanted to back farmers to cut their emissions through technology, but would explore a "cap-and-trade market or levy structure" to reduce biogenic methane emissions.

Asked whether that would entail a tax or levy on farmers and other producers of methane emissions, an Opportunity spokesperson said the design of such a scheme was "complicated and would need to be worked through".

However, it would likely include some "fair allocations to existing methane emitters".

Other likely characteristics included preventing emitters from saving their credits to use in future years, or trading them across to carbon credits or on a secondary market, the spokesperson said.

Climate spokesperson Kayla Kingdon-Bebb said the party was "deliberately open-minded about the design".

"Getting the incentives right for farmers and the wider food and fibre sector is critical," she said.

"We want to work through those questions with climate and agricultural experts, farmers, processors and industry rather than imposing a model before the evidence is clear."

The party is also proposing changes to the existing emissions trading scheme, to prioritise cutting emissions at their source rather than offsetting them through forestry.

World.title: Retirement village repayment period to shrink under new plan
World.content:
A leaked document shows the Government would require retirement villages to repay residents within nine months, and 10 percent of the owed amount within four weeks.

That 10 percent early repayment would replace the interest gains for residents who had not been repaid, which the government had previously announced.

With the legislation not set to be passed until after the election, it's as good as a National Party policy - although the changes also come as a result of a review of the Retirement Villages Act secured as a commitment in the National-NZ First coalition agreement.

Currently operators must repay residents, or their families, within 12 months of them leaving the village.

Some have complained that is too long to wait.

The document obtained by RNZ - which looks to be a press release - quotes Associate Housing Minister Tama Potaka saying the Government had listened.

"Older Kiwis told us the balance needed to shift further towards residents," Potaka said.

"They told us 12 months was still too long and that interest after six months would not provide meaningful help when money was needed most. We listened and strengthened the package."

Tama Potaka. Alyse Wright

It follows Labour in August announcing it would within 100 days of being elected pass a bill that would require full repayment within three months, based on a member's bill from its spokesperson for Seniors, Ingrid Leary.

That bill includes a similar initial repayment requirement for 10 percent within five working days, rather than four weeks.

Leary said National was "moving the deck chairs while locking in the unfairness".

"Nine months is still far too long, and 56,000 current residents will still miss out. Operators could still hold on to almost all of a resident's money until the nine-month deadline.

"Labour requires the 10 percent payment much more quickly within five working days and the full balance within three months."

Leary's member's bill has been in the ballot since May 2025.

The leaked document said the Government also considered a three-month repayment deadline, but official modelling had found that could require the sector to hold or access between $3.2 billion and $4.1 billion, and add up to $118,000 to the cost of entering a village if all costs were passed on to residents.

Both the Retirement Villages Association - which represents owners - and the Retirement Village Residents' Association which represents residents were opposed to the government's proposal.

Potaka said nine months would strike a fair and responsible balance.

"You can't keep everybody happy all of the time ... we think we've struck the right approach ... we've listened to operators, we've listened to residents, we've listened to the retirement commissioner and a range of other stakeholder groups and entities."

"It gets residents their money sooner while protecting the affordability and viability of retirement village living," he said.

Operators would still be required to sell units as fast as possible, at the best price possible, the document said.

They would also be required to provide regular updates to residents and their families, and obtain a valuation if the unit had not been relicensed after six months.

"A more efficient and effective dispute resolution system will be introduced for cases where operators are not meeting their obligations."

The changes would be made next Parliamentary term.

With the review having been published a year ago, Potaka said the time taken to get the policy across the line was because the government wanted to get it right.

"What we're not going to do is we're not going to break the industry with some quite unreasonable quite speculative proposals a la three months."

He rejected the suggestion a year was a long time for residents to wait.

"Not really ... it takes many many years to get some policies right, so I could refer to Te Turi Whenua, the Māori Land Act, that took 15 years ... we want to make sure we get to a sustainable and enduring solution."

Govt 'caved' to owners' lobbying - Consumer NZ

Consumer NZ, which has been campaigning for a three-month deadline in line with Labour's policy, said the decision to shift to a nine-month deadline "shows it has caved to business lobbying".

"The retirement village sector is a multi-billion-dollar industry. The government has effectively ignored the voice of the people in favour of big business," chief executive John Duffy said.

"This is equivalent to putting a ribbon on a donkey and calling it a stallion."

"Currently, most exiting residents are repaid within seven to eight months, which shows the sector can move quicker than what the government is proposing."

Duffy said Labour had "laid down the gauntlet and the current government failed to pick it up".

Change would hike residents' costs - retirement village sector

Retirement Villages Association executive director Michelle Palmer said the deadlines would backfire by forcing villages to hold capital for repayments rather than invest in villages, services and care beds.

"The Government may think this policy will help residents, but it will do the opposite," she said.

"Residents will pay more, fewer care beds will be built and more older New Zealanders will have to rely on an already stretched hospital system."

Palmer agreed residents and families should not face unnecessary delays, and said the sector supported the 12-month repayment window as well as ending weekly fees on exit, clearer disclosure, fairer treatment of chattels, stronger complaints pathways and early access for genuine hardship.

She said just as a homeowner is paid when their house settles, a former resident or their estate is repaid once the unit has been refurbished, sold and settled.

"In a weaker property market, that can take longer," she said.

World.title: Fuel prices see first rise in four months amid renewed US-Iran conflict
World.content:
Fuel prices rise in August amid US-Iran war flare-ups

Fuel prices still much higher than year ago

Food prices edge higher as meat, groceries, takeaways offset cheaper fruit/veg

Commercial accommodation, domestic airfares cheaper; rents, energy prices mostly flat

Items account for about half of consumer price inflation

Higher fuel and some food prices have kept the pressure on household costs in a partial measure of inflation for August.

Stats NZ figures showed petrol prices rose 2 percent in July and diesel prices were up nearly 9 percent, as global energy prices turned higher amid renewed US-Iran hostilities, and pressure on fuel supplies.

It was the first rise in fuel prices in four months.

Petrol was nearly 18 percent higher than a year ago and diesel was 46 percent more expensive over 12 months.

Fuel prices make up about 4 percent of the broad inflation measure, the consumer price index (CPI).

Food prices steady

Food prices rose 0.3 percent for the month, to be 1.9 percent higher than a year ago, the lowest annual rate since December 2024.

Fruit and vegetables were flat for the month, but 1.6 percent cheaper than a year ago.

"This is the largest annual price decrease in the fruit and vegetables group since March 2025," Stats NZ spokesperson Nicola Growden said.

Food bills were lifted by rises in meat, groceries, and restaurant meals.

Food prices make up about 19 percent of the broad inflation measure, the CPI.

Electricity, and rents were flat or marginally cheaper, with marked falls in domestic airfares, and local commercial accommodation as school holidays ended.

International airfares rose 4 percent on July, driven by higher fares to Europe and Asia, with the annual increase of 21.5 percent the highest in more than three years.

"Because we collect some international airfare prices around four months in advance, price changes that occurred earlier in the year for travel in August are now being reflected," Growden said

The items measured make up about half of the CPI, which quickened to a two year high of 4.1 percent in the year ended June.

World.title: First Nations netballers driving change, bringing cultural safety
World.content:
Tell us about your experience.

While netball may be Australian girls' and women's top participation team sport, it has long fallen short of producing — or at least nurturing — elite Indigenous talent.

Just three Indigenous Australian women have represented the Diamonds: Marcia Ella-Duncan, Sharon Finnan-White and, after a 22-year gap, Donnell Wallam.

In 2024, Wallam left Australia for New Zealand, taking a swipe at her former club, the Firebirds, on the way out.

At the time, she wrote that the New Zealand clubs' "respect for inclusion and culture" was a key factor in her decision to leave, while she eventually returned to the Sunshine Coast Lightning this year.

Netball Australia was not idly watching.

As accusations of a 'toxic culture' at the Firebirds were aired, the governing body launched an investigation and kickstarted a series of measures to enshrine 'cultural safety' for First Nations athletes in the sport.

This included the introduction of Australia's inaugural First Nations team, the Black Swans, following the appointment of Ali Tucker-Munro, Netball Australia's General Manager First Nations and former Diamonds squad member.

This is the third year the First Nations Tournament has run. (Getty Images: Daniel Pockett)

Tucker-Munro was also influential in establishing the First Nations Tournament, a yearly national championship currently being held in Melbourne, and the Spirit Series, which launched in 2026 and saw the Black Swans go undefeated against Australia's Pacific neighbours.

Speaking from the State Netball and Hockey Centre, Tucker-Munro, alongside players Gabby Coffey and Scarlet Jauncey, said the measures had begun to address the lack of visible role models for First Nations netballers, with more work to be done.

Embraced in Alice Springs

Twenty-six-year-old Coffey, representing the Northern Territory, is one of several First Nations netballers who have been stuck at the cusp of national competition.

Gabby Coffey says it means a lot to bring Indigenous netballers together for the tournament. (ABC News: Kyle Harley)

The defender spent four years as a Melbourne Vixens training partner before eventually making the decision to move to the UK to further her netball career.

She represented Birmingham over two seasons, and has since returned to Alice Springs.

Coffey had seen the writing on the wall at the Vixens.

"I knew there wasn't much movement in their defensive end, and the same with a lot of defensive ends around Australia," Coffey told ABC Sport.

While she has not given up on a professional career, she is also at peace with the idea that her role may be to support other First Nations athletes with their sporting aspirations.

The Wiradjuri woman grew up in Alice Springs, away from mob and country, but remembers being embraced by the community in Arrente.

Coffey (left) played for Birmingham in England's top competition. (Getty Images: Morgan Harlow)

"When you grow up on other Indigenous land and tell people you're Indigenous, they pull you into their culture, so [my family and I] were super lucky and blessed to grow up in the centre of Australia where arguably their Indigenous culture is very sacred and traditional," she said.

Determined to pursue netball, she was advised by coach Gillian Lee to move down south, and remembers the transition to Melbourne as a difficult one.

"It was really hard being away from home," Coffey said.

"I was really lucky with the team I entered [the Vixens] and the support I did have, but it's not the same for everyone. There's a lot of girls who do get those opportunities to move and then don't last because there's just not that support in place."

Hailing from the Northern Territory, Coffey said, was an additional barrier.

"Even with competitions like these, we don't get together until we're here, and we're training away from each other, so it can be quite a challenge."

Visible Indigenous role models key

Asked what more could be done to help First Nations netballers make it to the elite level, Coffey said role models were key.

"If you can't see it, you can't be it," she said, pointing out that there are only two Indigenous players currently in Super Netball.

Coffey says it is important to have visible role models. (Getty Images: Daniel Pockett)

Coffey said her own experience of spending multiple years as a train-on player, without breaking into the elite environment, showed how difficult it was to make it into a professional team in Australia.

"We get a number of internationals [coming to Super Netball], which I think makes the game better and more exciting, and I don't think [that] should be restricted," she said.

"But I do think there should be more focus on bringing Indigenous girls into the elite level."

She pointed to Netball Australia's plans to introduce two new teams into the competition, saying this would open further list spots.

A New Zealand team, she added, may take pressure away from the Australian players vying for contracts.

Scarlet Jauncey has spent the last year as a training partner for the West Coast Fever, pinching herself to line up on names like Jhaniele Fowler-Nembhard at training.

Scarlet Jauncey is representing Western Australia, and has captained the Black Swans. (ABC News: Kyle Harley)

A Yaruwu woman from Rubibi/Broome in Western Australia, Jauncey agreed with Coffey that cutting international talent was not a solution.

"We're happy to be playing against the best in the world, that's what we want," the defender said.

Like many of her teammates, Jauncey grew up idolising Wallam.

"I think it just gives us something to strive towards, knowing that we can be in that space," she said.

In 2025, Jauncey captained the Black Swans, in turn becoming a role model to other First Nations players.

"It was the best tournament I've played in, the best teams I've been with," she said.

"I think just being able to come to First Nations tournaments and having that connection with each other has been really great."

Jauncey in action during this year's tournament. (Getty Images: Daniel Pockett)

Coffey agreed, saying the experience had given her "goosebumps".

"I think it gives not only myself, but a lot of players so much power and push to keep going and play at the highest level," she said.

Cultural safety means listening to community

Tucker-Munro smiles when hearing the players' responses to playing for the Black Swans.

It has been one of her signature initiatives, alongside the First Nations Tournament and Spirit Series.

Ali Tucker-Munro is Netball Australia's general manager for First Nations. (ABC News: Kyle Harley)

"These tournaments are aspirational in terms of trying to inspire the next generation of our kids — who we know love sport and netball in particular — to trial for their respective state and territory," she said.

"It's about the kids that are here this week wanting to aspire to take that next step into the big leagues in terms of Super Netball and Australian representation as well."

Tucker-Munro acknowledged that while it was important to bring First Nations netballers into elite environments, those environments had to be culturally safe.

"First Nations people come into these spaces with our culture and community on our back, as well as cheering us on, so you want to do them proud," she said.

"It's also a tough journey, especially for the kids who have to relocate, so it's about thinking strategically about how we can support them."

Players have enjoyed coming together in Melbourne for this year's tournament. (Getty Images: Daniel Pockett)

Since her appointment, the code has put in place a First Nations Cultural Council, and last year ran a cultural safety review in collaboration with community.

The review considered the perspectives of the wider netball workforce, including coaches and umpires as well as athletes

Tucker-Munro conceded there are "multi-faceted" barriers to having more elite Indigenous netballers, including financial constraints and geographical barriers to access.

"For too long our voice has been very silent," Tucker-Munro said.

"We're not a homogenous people, so it's really important that we make sure we're hearing the voices of many.

"One thing we're really big on in our community is not to do things for us or to us, you've got to do it with us.

"There's real intent and good will to actually drive some of this change across the sporting landscape of netball in Australia."

World.title: From African shepherd to Australia's marathon record holder
World.content:
Tell us about your experience.

Australia's men's marathon record holder, Haftu Strintzos, thrives on hard work but still finds it hard to believe where life has taken him.

Born in eastern Tigray in northern Ethiopia, he grew up standing barefoot in fields for hours, helping provide for his family from dawn to dusk.

"I feel as though I have lived a double life in a way," he said after celebrating his 27th birthday in Melbourne.

"I consider myself very privileged to live this life.

" I spent my early days as a shepherd, herding goats and sheep through the mountains of my local village. I grew up without a TV or running water. "

In his remote community, 2,300 metres above sea level, the only source of information he had until age 10 was a mobile phone.

Haftu lost both biological parents by the time he was six, and was taken in by his maternal grandmother, living with his aunt and cousins.

A Greek Australian aid worker by the name of Maria Strintzos came calling, meeting Haftu in 2007 at the age of eight.

Aid worker Maria Strintzos adopted Haftu Strintzos in Ethiopia. (Supplied: Maria Strintzos)

After decades working across Ethiopia, she asked him if he'd like to be her son, adopted him and helped him migrate to Melbourne in 2011 — more than 12,000 kilometres from the mountains of Tigray.

Today, Haftu speaks five languages (Tigrinya, Amharic, Greek, Japanese and English), holds a Master of Electrical Engineering from Villanova University in the USA and recently broke the national marathon record.

Feeling the 'weight of the world'

Maria always felt compelled to help others. Growing up in South Melbourne in the 1960s, she found strength in the local Greek community, even while migrant families faced racism.

"We had absolutely everybody there. As much as I loved growing up there, it built a strength in me," she said.

Haftu Strintzos would walk barefoot from the mountains of eastern Tigray to the village with his blind grandmother, Shifta, to meet his future mother, Maria. (Supplied: Maria Strintzos)

"I grew up knowing what social injustice and inequality looked like."

Her aid work took her through Indonesia, Ethiopia, Eritrea and Sudan, supporting famine relief, water schemes, food security, women's empowerment and communities affected by conflict, spending 35 years around wars and disease, but also hope, in the Horn of Africa.

But something different about young Haftu stood out.

He would walk barefoot through dry riverbeds, guiding his almost blind grandmother, Shifta, through the mountains to meet Maria.

"He was very respectful," she said.

"And he would sit there really quietly … didn't muck around like the other kids.

"He always had this sort of sad and serious look about him. It's like he had the weight of the world on his shoulders.

Haftu Strintzos took every opportunity and excelled at school, with his mother Maria Strintzos helping him go on to the US college system and graduate with a Masters of Electrical Engineering. (Supplied: Maria Strintzos)

"But the way he looked after his grandmother and the way the grandmother would talk about him was very moving at the time too."

With the pull of family ties in Australia, Maria found herself at a crossroads.

"I was challenged at that time because I didn't particularly want to leave Ethiopia," she said.

"I loved my life. I loved what I did … I felt like I was achieving something."

Embracing the challenge of two different worlds

Excelling at school and winning education awards, Haftu embraced every opportunity.

When he migrated to Australia in 2011, he took nothing for granted in his new environment.

Can a marathon help you beat addiction? The science says yes From addiction recovery to mental health, science is revealing why running a marathon can feel so good.

Growing up without electricity, he became fascinated by anything electrical.

Maria bought Haftu toy cars that he would unpack and dismantle.

"He literally pulled them apart with the motors, everything, and reassembled them," she said.

Having never seen a TV, he would sit on the couch for hours waiting for people to appear outside the screen.

"Sometimes I'd catch him sort of looking behind the TV because he thought there was people in there," she said.

"I still can't believe it. It was quite incredible that given his background, that he had this innate gift, something about electricity."

A reward for excelling at school, Haftu Strintzos would relish the chance to earn new stationery and school supplies in Ethiopia. (Supplied: Maria Strintzos)

Maria said she's most proud of how Haftu had risen above adversity in his life.

"Where he's come from it was a rock hut, and they would sleep on the floor and the animals were next to them," she said.

" The uniqueness of Haftu is that he's managed to retain the positive qualities of his experience. I'm in awe of him. "

But the culture shock wasn't easy; different foods, subtle racism and grappling with Western values were also some of Haftu's greatest tests.

Warming climate forcing marathon changes to keep runners cool Marathon organisers across the United States are rethinking when they hold events due to warmer temperatures.

"My biggest challenges in assimilating to Australian culture were learning the English language and motion sickness while riding in cars," he said.

"I remember a time in my early days where the only way I would not throw up while Mum drove the car was if I sat in the front passenger seat and kept my eyes on the road in front."

From a school oval to an athlete with no fear

It wasn't until he moved to Australia that Haftu realised his potential in athletics, having grown up in Tigray not knowing it was even a sport or profession.

"My PE teacher at school encouraged me to pursue it when he saw me run a cross-country race at the school oval," he said.

Adding more strings to his bow, Haftu Strintzos won the 2026 Australian Athletics Cross Country Championships in Ballarat, Victoria. (Supplied: Australian Athletics)

In that school race, he just kept running and didn't stop after the finish line, such was his determination for long-distance.

"I have grown up through this sport and learned my most valuable life lessons through it," he said.

"Running helped me connect with my local community, just getting out and about and meeting like-minded people."

His talent soon attracted attention, including from Cathy Freeman, who became like a mentor and even attended his birthday party during his teens.

Training up to 190 kilometres a week under coach Adam Didyk, Haftu broke the Australian men's marathon record in two hours, six minutes and 20 seconds at the Gold Coast Marathon in July.

He became the first Australian winner in 20 years, smashed the course record and set a new Oceania record — all on his fourth attempt at the distance.

Haftu Strintzos regularly trains in Melbourne around Albert Park Lake as he prepares for global events. (ABC Sport: Damien Peck)

Didyk, who also coaches Australian women's marathon record holder Jessica Stenson, has guided Haftu remotely from Adelaide for two years.

"He's a fairly no-fuss kind of individual. He'll just take the work and get it done," Didyk said.

"He's obviously very capable when it comes to longer distances and feels confident running at the pace he needs to for the marathon; quite extraordinarily, mind you."

Didyk said Haftu's college experience and early development give him a strong understanding of racing, matched by mental strength.

"He backs himself. He has a lot of confidence in his ability, and he believes in what he can do.

"He's one of those no-fear athletes who sets a goal that looks pretty daunting, but it excites him more and more the scarier he makes it."

Having broken the Australian marathon record in July, Haftu Strintzos (third from left) is aiming for a podium at the Olympics in future years. (Supplied: Australian Athletics)

Australian records are just the beginning

Haftu's talent comes as a package. Didyk said the physical ability, mental strength and calmness on race day were all put together to make good decisions, ultimately which led to the record-breaking performance at the Gold Coast Marathon.

"He's just a sensible, quite an intelligent young guy, and that all comes together to match what he can physically do as well," he said.

Haftu's calmness and patience on the Gold Coast reinforced Didyk's belief that he had world-class potential.

"There's so many positives about Haftu that he can go and achieve what no Australian has before in the marathon," Didyk said.

"He's very determined to be successful in international level … it was a phenomenally strong close.

"I think what's probably most important to us now with seeing that is if he's going to be competitive at an Olympic or World Championships level, he's going to need that ability to be able to close really fast over those last 10 kilometres.

Robert de Castella (right) held the national marathon record for 36 years until 2022. (Supplied: Australian Athletics)

"He's shown he's got the foundations to do something like that."

"Off the back of that, it started to give us the knowledge of him to go, 'that's the game he can play when he goes to a major championship, he can put himself in there and he can put himself in a competitive situation late in the race'.

"And that's ideally what we're aiming to do with him over the coming years."

From his humble beginnings in Ethiopia, Haftu's dreams of standing on an Olympic podium remain his driving force for motivation for the 2027 World Championships in China, and Los Angeles Olympics in 2028.

Australia hasn't had an Olympic marathon medallist since Lisa Ondieki won silver in 1988.

"I am very fortunate to have the support systems I need to help me to achieve my goals — something that not every athlete gets to have," he said.

"I want to continue to break records. After all, records are there to be broken."

World.title: How Swans rebuilt their midfield to challenge for premiership
World.content:
Tell us about your experience.

Rome wasn't built in a day, and neither is an AFL midfield.

But instant construction seemed to be the task for the Sydney Swans after suspending five key players following last month's post-match incident at the Pullman Hotel in Melbourne.

While the suspensions were the catalyst for major change, smaller moves had been afoot in the weeks and months beforehand.

No midfield has been hotter than the Swans over the past five games. Sydney has gone from a league-average side across the middle to perhaps being the best.

This is despite losing three-time All-Australian Isaac Heeney, fellow superstar Chad Warner and premiership player James Jordon.

Two weeks ago, Sydney surprised the AFL by comprehensively beating reigning premiers Brisbane.

That victory was largely driven by this makeshift force in the middle dynamically (and aggressively) moving the ball while protecting their defence.

Instead of star power, the Swans are relying on structure and balance to drive them deeper into the finals.

System against talent

There's long been a debate in the footy world about system against talent. The Swans have placed themselves firmly in the camp of the former.

In their first game after the suspensions, Sydney tried new combinations, testing them in real footy.

It indicated coach Dean Cox was exploring how the available talent would fit the much-vaunted system, a message he had been preaching all year.

"One thing we want to make sure is that we are a system-based team and role-focused team," Cox said of covering injuries to Heeney and Gulden in March.

The changes to the frontline are the most visible. Sydney relied heavily on Heeney, Warner and Jordon to drive their midfield engine.

Those three accounted for about half of their midfield centre-bounce contributions, let alone their impact around the ground.

But that role focus may have made it easier to replace the suspended stars and, along the way, find a better balance.

Pieces of the puzzle

Midfield balance is often a delicate beast.

If a team is too aggressive, it can be beaten back the other way in transition.

Too passive or defensive, and you can struggle for territory and scoreboard pressure.

As a result, replacing Heeney, Warner and Jordon required some lateral thinking.

Excluding ruck Brodie Grundy, arguably the most important player is James Rowbottom.

Shuffled in and out of different roles, Rowbottom's flexibility within and between games has become a strength.

"I just do what the team needs," Rowbottom told reporters ahead of the qualifying final against the Lions.

"I sort of have done that for the last eight years or so. My role's been ever-changing this year.

"I've played a lot of half-forward, a lot of midfield, a bit of wing."

However, Rowbottom does his best work hunting the ball and his opponent at the bottom of packs and contests.

Rowbottom sits sixth all-time for tackles per game.

In the past fortnight, he has applied the clamps with 56 pressure acts over the two games, which is a league-leading rate.

He's unafraid to do the dirty work to make his teammates look better.

The reignited star

Two years ago, there were few more valuable young players in the league than Errol Gulden.

However, two injury-struck years dulled his star. It took just a month and a half for that supernova to reignite.

Since their round-20 win over cross-town rivals GWS, Gulden has quickly re-emerged as Sydney's attacking focal point.

Few see angles and hit potential kicks on the field better than Gulden.

As a result, the Swans look to get the ball into Gulden's hands more often than any other player in the league.

Gulden doesn't just blaze away. He's second among midfielders and sixth overall for retained metres gained, normally the specialty of defenders landing safer kicks.

In every way, Gulden finds ways to advance the ball with threat.

Without Heeney and Warner, Gulden is getting even more opportunity with ball in hand. This has improved their overall ball use and added more danger to their impressive attack.

Like all players, Gulden does have flaws.

While his attacking side is nearly unmatched, he is far from a defensive powerhouse.

At just 175 centimetres tall, he can be muscled out and pushed off balance when unable to use his speed.

It means his impact is best realised next to bigger bodies willing to do the hard yards.

The converted defender

While Jai Serong made last year's VFL Team of the Year at Hawthorn, he was unable to crack the stellar Hawks defence or in a wing role.

Given this, few expected Serong to be thrown into the heart of the contest.

But, needing a defensive boost around contest and given his aerobic ability, the Swans decided to explore using Serong as an inside midfielder.

His arrival at stoppage in round 22 accompanied a heavier dose of Gulden at the middle, with Serong further protecting the elite ball-user.

With Serong in the heat of battle, the Swans have become a dominant stoppage force.

He not only provides a safety blanket but has done damage off his own boot, much like Rowbottom.

Young gun

Like many young players in good teams, former first-round pick Angus Sheldrick had to bide his time with short stints on the edges of the midfield rotation.

Sheldrick has firmly established himself as an impact player, both as a regular sub last year and on limited time this season.

But he has made that time count, focusing those minutes on high-impact, stoppage play.

He is able to cover the gaps of the other three with minimal drop-off so far.

The second layer

Often the pinch isn't felt in the front line when changes are made. Instead, it's beyond the main group where depth is really tested.

The Swans are suddenly fielding a slew of names only briefly seen at the top level. Billy Cootee, Tom Hanily, Jesse Dattoli and Caiden Cleary have made leaps in relatively unsung roles around the outside midfield and high half-forward.

Pressure, holding position and supporting structures have been the order of the day. These players, hungry and well-educated, are tasked with forming the outside layer and impacting post clearance.

Alongside more senior figures such as Tom Papley, Jake Lloyd, Braeden Campbell and the potentially returning Justin McInerney, they have helped control the middle of the ground.

Formidable Dockers

In the Swans' path to the grand final stands self-proclaimed minor premier "underdogs" Fremantle.

The Dockers, with a midfield led by Serong's brother Caleb, can pile on points and defend with aplomb.

Winning territory through the middle is critical for the Swans' chances of staying alive one more week. But it's an area that the Dockers have been susceptible to in the past.

The Swans may have had an advantage in the element of surprise against Brisbane. Few knew exactly how Sydney would set up.

But Fremantle may have more of an idea now, unless Cox and the Swans have yet another surprise up their sleeves.

World.title: HYROX athlete hands back points after soiling herself during race
World.content:
Tell us about your experience.

Australian athlete Joanna Wietrzyk has apologised for continuing to compete in a HYROX competition in China having soiled herself.

Wietrzyk experienced the medical episode during the contest last weekend in Beijing, and went on to win, but has now retroactively withdrawn from the race and handed back all points earned.

The incident went viral on social media, with videos of her continuing the race shared widely.

HYROX, a popular fitness competition launched in Germany in 2017, sees competitors combine running with multiple workout station challenges, including sandbag lunges, burpees, sled pushes and rowing using shared equipment.

The athletics brand, which came under fire over health and safety standards, has since apologised for "not reacting immediately" over the incident.

Wietrzyk, who has faced questions over her decision to continue, has now issued a social media statement.

Joanna Wietrzyk shared an apology online on Thursday, withdrawing and handing back points from the race she won. (Instagram: @joannawietrzyk)

"I want to offer my sincere apology to the people of China, my fellow competitors, the spectators and the HYROX organisers for what happened during the race in Beijing," she said in a post on Instagram.

"I felt completely fit and healthy at the start of the race, with no reason to expect any illness,

" Looking back, I regret the decision to not have stepped off the track. I recognise that I should have made a different choice. "

In the statement, Wietrzyk said she had chosen to retroactively withdraw from the race and hand back the points she earned from competing.

Loading...

Within the HYROX elite framework, athletes accumulate ranking points based on their placement and finishing time. The points contribute to national and global ranking systems.

"I know my actions had an impact beyond myself, and I am genuinely sorry to everyone who was affected," she said.

"I am learning from this experience and will carry those lessons with me, including remembering that there is more to life than racing and knowing when it is right to step away.

"On reflection, I have decided to retroactively withdraw from the race and forfeit the points I earned."

Joanna Wietrzyk (middle in black top) has issued an apology. (Instagram: joannawietrzyk)

Rules changed after backlash

The incident attracted intense criticism of HYROX's health and safety standards.

HYROX co-founder Moritz Fürste had earlier taken to Instagram to apologise "to all who were directly or indirectly involved".

Social media posts about the incident during the HYROX race in Beijing. (Weibo, RedNote and Douyin)

"HYROX made a mistake by not reacting immediately during the race," he added in a statement on Instagram.

"In the end it is my job to foresee these potential incidents — and I did not."

HYROX apologises after athlete soiling The apology comes after different arms of the organisation tried to explain how the situation was managed after the competition went viral online.

He said new event procedures and rules were being drawn up to "prevent situations like this from happening again".

The rules now state that if a "racer's blood, vomit, urine, or faeces poses a welfare or contamination risk to the racer or to other racers, a Race Director may withdraw the racer from the race on medical grounds".

Before the rule change, competitors were penalised for littering, spitting, or clearing their nostrils onto the race course, which some online described as a double standard.

World.title: Court battle looms for Socceroos star after drug test
World.content:
Tell us about your experience.

Cristian Volpato is set for a court battle with the Socceroos star's lawyer confirming he will challenge charges that he was driving with cocaine in his system.

The 22-year-old returned a positive roadside reading for cocaine after he was pulled over by police on Sydney's Anzac Bridge on July 24.

He had been driving at 109 kilometres per hour in a 60km/h zone.

He later underwent independent testing at a private clinic, where it was claimed he returned a negative reading.

However, Volpato was then sent for a secondary oral fluid test by police, which again confirmed a positive result for cocaine.

He copped a $722 fine as a result of the second positive test, but on Thursday his lawyer Paul McGirr confirmed to AAP that he had elected to take the matter to court.

Volpato has maintained his innocence, insisting he never knowingly ingested the substance.

He also undertook a test when he returned to Italy, which was negative, his club side Sassuolo said.

The Sydney-born player was a late inclusion for the Socceroos' World Cup campaign after switching his international allegiance from Italy to Australia on the eve of the tournament.

In a statement provided to AAP, a Football Australia spokesperson confirmed the organisation was aware of reports concerning Volpato and a "traffic matter currently subject to a police process".

"As the matter is ongoing, it would not be appropriate for Football Australia to comment further at this time," the spokesperson said.

Regardless, the positive reading on Volpato's secondary police test could have major ramifications for his availability heading into January's Asian Cup.

Sources have previously told AAP that Volpato could be hauled before FA's disciplinary and ethics committee, where the sport's governing body has the power to suspend him from national team action.

The 22-year-old is currently playing in Serie A with Sassuolo but is sidelined with a right leg injury sustained against Bologna this month.

AAP

World.title: 'Cinema' expected as rival wingers go to battle one last time
World.content:
Tell us about your experience.

Robert Toia will have a front-row seat to the last instalment of the battle between teammate Mark Nawaqanitawase and Ronaldo Mulitalo, and the Sydney Roosters centre is bracing himself for more box-office entertainment.

"Cinema, that's what I expect — [another chapter in] an ongoing battle and I think if we get the win that will top it off," Toia said.

Saturday's sudden-death semifinal could be Nawaqanitawase's last in the NRL, with the 26-year-old former Wallabies star switching back to the 15-man code with Japanese side Saitama Wild Knights.

Few could have imagined the impact Nawaqanitawase would have had in rugby league when he crossed codes after the Paris Olympics.

There have been highlights in just about every game — be it his grubber ahead and tip toe down the sideline against Canterbury last season that was named try of the year, or last weekend's tap-ahead intercept before climbing off the deck and racing away to score against Penrith.

"It's pretty hard to stay alert because you don't know what's going to happen," Toia said.

"I didn't expect him to do what he's been doing, I think he has shocked everyone."

Nawaqanitawase's long-running on-field feud with the sledge-happy Mulitalo — the pair of wingers openly admire each other off it — has made Roosters-Sharks games fixtures to savour.

"There's a bit of competitiveness there but I think that is what makes the game so great — it's the best of the best going at it with each other," said Roosters forward Siua Wong.

Toia's opposite number KL Iro said of Mulitalo: "He can get personal at times but after the game he always makes sure he clears it up straight away and shakes his hand.

"He loves getting in the mix, he's a huge competitor."

Nawaqanitawase has made the switch to rugby league look easy, having won caps for the Kangaroos, played State of Origin for NSW and scored 41 tries in 44 games for the Roosters.

The Roosters and Sharks battle on Saturday night from the Sydney Football Stadium.

AAP

World.title: Canberra is the greatest mystery of the NRLW finals
World.content:
Of all the teams in the fight for the NRLW premiership, Canberra shapes as the ultimate wildcard.

Ahead of the first finals series in club history, the Raiders are a difficult puzzle to solve; for themselves and opponents alike.

Darrin Borthwick's side enter the finals in fifth place with a 6-5 record that belies a strange tendency that developed over the season: more than any other team in the league, they play to their opponent's level.

Can anyone stop the Roosters in the NRLW? After completing the most dominant regular season in NRLW history, the big question around the Sydney Roosters is simple: can anyone hope to stop them?

The Raiders have a winning record against fellow top six teams, highlighted by a 28-4 win over third-placed Broncos, comfortably the Brisbane team's biggest ever NRLW loss.

They even put the gloves up against powerhouses Gold Coast and Sydney Roosters, losing to the two competition heavyweights by a combined 10 points, finishing close enough in both games that they would fancy their chances in a rematch.

But as easily as the Raiders can be inspired by the challenge of taking on the big dogs, they can be complacent when facing teams they should handle easily.

Canberra dropped games to stragglers Parramatta, North Queensland and Cronulla throughout the season, costing them a home final.

As they prepare to head to Campbelltown to take on Wests Tigers in tomorrow night's sudden-death final, they are still trying to work themselves out as they head into the deep waters.

"I've found we've lifted for those bigger teams. We've spoken about that, that we need to believe we can win because if we get that down, our effort and our fight will come," said captain Zahara Temara.

"For some of the other teams who aren't as high on the ladder, we've matched them in terms of effort, and that's disappointing. But we know we can lift for the big teams."

It is an unorthodox way for Canberra to live, but now that only big teams are left, the Raiders' record against the top sides makes them perhaps the best candidate to break open the Roosters-Titans hegemony at the top.

Canberra will lean heavily on Zahara Temara's experience through the finals. (Getty Images: Scott Gardiner )

Temara's experience will be crucial for Canberra, with the clever halfback one of the few Raiders with an extensive finals pedigree, having won a premiership with the Roosters in 2022.

That was the 29-year-old's third grand final, and she admits she took the team's success for granted in the earlier years, something she is desperate to ensure does not happen to her Raiders teammates this time around.

"Something I wish someone told me in those early years at the Roosters was how hard it is to have regrets. I took it seriously, but not as seriously as I could have," said Temara.

"It's hard to make the finals. It's extremely hard to win a grand final, and with the position we're in now, I want them to have no regrets, to realise how we can make history."

That perspective was reinforced by former Roosters teammate and current Canberra co-captain Simaima Taufa, especially after their losing effort in the 2020 grand final.

The Raiders will be without gun lock forward Simaima Taufa tomorrow night. (Getty Images: Mark Nolan)

The sight of the whole-hearted Taufa after the match has never left Temara, and inspires her to this day.

"She gave it her everything, and I didn't feel like I did," said Temara.

"We were all disappointed, but I tell her all the time now I couldn't look at her because I knew I hadn't done everything I could for her and the team.

"I still took it seriously. I just wish I took it as far as she did."

With Taufa sidelined due to suspension, there will be even more responsibility on Temara's shoulders tomorrow night.

The Tigers are polar opposites of the Raiders: they beat every side that missed the finals, but went 1-4 against the other play-off teams, with their sole success coming via a one-point win over Newcastle.

But there are similarities too. The joint venture is also playing in its first finals match, and given Raecene McGregor's form at halfback, the team will also lean heavily on an experienced playmaker to show the way.

Inside Tigers remarkable NRLW turnaround Few expected much from Wests Tigers in this year's NRLW competition, but after winning as many games this season as the rest of their history combined they've proved the doubters wrong ahead of a maiden finals push.

To add to the intrigue, this is a rematch only seven days in the making. The two sides met last Friday night at Leichhardt with the Raiders grinding out a 22-10 victory.

Winger Mackenzie Wiki and centre Leianne Tufuga, who was crowned the club's player of the year, both played blinders as Canberra's strike out wide carried the day.

It ensured the Tigers would enter the finals on the back of consecutive losses, but Temara understands how dangerous they still can be when the stakes are highest.

"Their fight stood out," said Temara

"They were down on the scoreboard, but their fight and hunger to keep coming at us was hard to manage. We got lucky with some errors and penalties that kept the momentum for us."

World.title: Croc-inhabited Fitzroy River gets green light for 2032 Olympic rowing
World.content:
Tell us about your experience.

After months of fierce debate, the International Olympic Committee (IOC) has approved rowing and canoe sprint events on Rockhampton's Fitzroy River for the 2032 Brisbane Olympic and Paralympic Games.

The central Queensland river will host the events despite concerns over its suitability, including its crocodile inhabitants.

Premier David Crisafulli said the doubters had been proven wrong with today's announcement.

"The IOC assessment for the site is complete," Mr Crisafulli said.

" The Fitzroy has passed with flying colours. It's official. Signed, sealed and delivered. "

International rowing bodies had questioned the location's suitability for competition. (Supplied: Rockhampton Regional Council)

It comes after World Rowing and Paddle Worldwide also backed an independent technical assessment of the Rockhampton flatwater course.

The Games Independent Infrastructure and Coordination Authority (GIICA) and internationally renowned marine engineering experts WaterProof Marine Consultancy and Services B.V. (WaterProof) completed a comprehensive, independent technical assessment of the Fitzroy River.

The assessment included extensive on-water investigations and modelling to understand how the course would perform under a range of conditions, weather patterns, water levels and flood risk at both Games time and throughout the period leading into the event.

Loading...

Having reviewed the assessment, World Rowing president Jean-Christophe Rolland and Paddle Worldwide president Thomas Konietzko endorsed the central Queensland waterway.

Mr Rolland said it could provide a safe, fair and consistent field of play suitable for Olympic and Paralympic rowing and canoe sprint competitions.

"Based on the extensive analysis undertaken, we now know that the Fitzroy River is capable of providing fair competition conditions during the period of the Games, consistent with the requirements of Olympic and Paralympic rowing," he said.

A future Olympic dream is taking shape on the Fitzroy River, where young rowers could one day compete for their country on their hometown course. (Supplied: Rockhampton Regional Council)

Deputy Premier Jarrod Bleije told state parliament "it's a win for regional Queensland".

"The experts have confirmed it. World Rowing and Paddle Worldwide have endorsed it," he said.

" Rockhampton is good for rowing and rowing is good for 2032 and beyond. "

Rowing Australia and Paddle Australia today acknowledged the completion of the independent technical assessment of the field of play for the Rockhampton flatwater course.

The assessment included detailed surveys of the riverbed and competition course. (Supplied: Rockhampton Regional Council)

"This assessment forms part of the full project validation report," a Rowing Australia spokesperson said.

"Rowing Australia looks forward to the completion of this full report and will continue to support key stakeholders involved in the venue planning process for the Brisbane 2032 Olympic and Paralympic Games."

Brisbane 2032 president Andrew Liveris said "thorough and robust" assessments had been undertaken on the Fitzroy River before it was given the tick of approval.

Game on Rocky

Rockhampton Mayor Tony Williams welcomed the confirmation of the Fitzroy River as the venue for rowing at the 2032 Olympic and Paralympic Games.

Tony Williams has thanked the state government for its support of Olympic rowing in the city. (ABC Capricornia: Jacob Gamble)

"This endorsement proves what we've always known. That Rockhampton's Fitzroy River will be the perfect venue for rowing at the 2032 Games," he said.

"Rockhampton is ready for the world stage. Now it's time to get to work and secure the infrastructure and opportunities that will benefit our community long after the Games have ended."

Queensland senator and National Party leader Matt Canavan, who first championed the Fitzroy River as an Olympic venue, said it was a great day for central Queensland.

The Fitzroy River has faced intense scrutiny since it was selected as a venue for the Brisbane 2032 Olympics. (Supplied: Rockhampton Regional Council)

"The Fitzroy River is one of the most beautiful parts of our country. It's an iconic Australian river," he said.

" It's been a tough fight, and some people had not wanted rowing to be outside of south-east Queensland. "

But Tom Sharp, mayor of rival rowing location Scenic Rim, dismissed today's announcement, and said there was still a long way to go for Rockhampton as a host city.

"You've got the financial assessments, you've got the overlays for the visitors, spectators, you've got the accommodation assessments, you've got the rowers themselves," he said.

"We're only at the starting blocks and Rocky's only starting to catch up to Scenic Rim."

The Rockhampton rowing facility will host the Queensland Schools' Championship regatta this weekend. (Supplied: Rockhampton Fitzroy Rowing Club)

The Queensland premier said GIICA would now proceed with the detailed planning, design and construction of the Rockhampton site.

He also told state parliament there would be no widening or dredging and that the Fitzroy Barrage was Rockhampton's "secret weapon".

While the river has passed an independent technical assessment, the region will require more accommodation to support an influx of athletes and visitors in 2032.

"Rockhampton knows how to host major events. It already hosts tens of thousands of people for Beef Week and Rockynats, and the Games will deliver extra accommodation for the future," Mr Crisafulli said.

The Fitzroy River has been used as a venue for Australian rowing team training camps over the years. (ABC Capricornia: Alice Roberts)

Rowing Queensland chief executive Anthea O'Loughlin also welcomed the outcome of the technical assessment, as the Rockhampton venue prepared to host more than 800 young rowers for the Queensland Schools' Championship Regatta this weekend.

"This is an important step to provide certainty to our athletes and community as we progress towards 2032," Ms O'Loughlin said.

"We note the references in the statement to legacy and investment in the sport and look forward to further information on this as it develops."

Sarah Black says the Olympics will bring a great legacy. (ABC Capricornia: Katrina Beavan)

President of the Rockhampton Fitzroy Rowing Club, Sarah Black, was ecstatic when the ABC broke the news to her that Rockhampton had been given the final seal of approval from the IOC.

"We've known that the course here is fantastic, but to have that international endorsement for the technical assessment is just fantastic news for us here in Rockhampton," she said.

Capricorn Enterprise chief executive Mary Carroll said today's announcement was a major milestone for central Queensland and an opportunity to deliver lasting economic, tourism and community benefits for the region.

"Commercial in confidence discussions have been proceeding positively with major investors to this region who I strongly believe will be able to deliver new hotel accommodation, an athletes' village and legacy infrastructure including world-class rowing and canoeing facilities," she said.

Tech.title: The AI Superintelligence Slowdown
Tech.content:
Remember when tech leaders would tell their employees to “move fast and break things”? It seemed that would be the way of AI too. But after a summer where rogue AI agents became reality, and researchers warned that AI could kill us all, a number of leading US AI companies are publicly suggesting it’s time to pump the brakes and “pace the frontier” of bleeding-edge AI development.

Their motivations are suspect, but leaders at major AI companies — including Anthropic, OpenAI, Google, Microsoft, and X — are at least paying lip service to the idea of a superintelligence slowdown.

Will these AI companies actually slow down? Will anyone step in to regulate these companies like they claim to have wanted for years? Will they manage to convince world leaders that the US must “beat China” to superintelligence and go even faster?

Each thread can further split its delegated work into pieces using subagents, loops, and workflows when needed so large assignments finish faster.

Tech.title: Xbox’s clever disc-to-digital feature was 15 years in the making
Tech.content:
Posts from this author will be added to your daily email digest and your homepage feed.

When Xbox announced a new feature last month that lets you digitize existing physical game collections, I immediately thought of the Xbox One. Disc-to-digital seems like a clever new feature for Xbox, perfectly timed as a response to Sony killing PlayStation discs. But the reality is that it has been 15 years in the making and is now a big part of Xbox’s ongoing game preservation efforts.

Ahead of the launch of the Xbox One in 2013, Microsoft made a key decision to uniquely identify discs. Sources familiar with Microsoft’s plans tell me the company was exploring the idea of true Xbox digital ownership in 2011, including digital gifting, recycling digital games, and the ability to swap discs at retail stores in exchange for a digital version. Some of those original Xbox One plans leaked out online, and many others have remained secret for more than a decade.

Microsoft’s Xbox One launch hinted at some of these ideas, too. The console was originally supposed to be always online, to enable Microsoft’s vision of digital game sharing, and more. Microsoft walked back those plans after a messy and confusing Xbox One launch created a backlash to the always-online requirement. But some of those original digital ideas are now starting to come to life in different ways.

Microsoft’s decision to essentially embed a serial number on the discs that Xbox consoles can read has allowed it to launch disc-to-digital, a method that lets you turn a physical Xbox One disc into a digital copy simply by slotting it into a disc drive. A decision made 15 years ago has resulted in this useful feature and may well lead to true digital ownership in the coming years.

It’s not something Sony can copy, either. Unless the PlayStation maker has been quietly adding metadata to its discs over the years, it will have to find another method to help PS5 owners move their physical collections over to the digital era.

Microsoft thought ahead, not necessarily to disc-to-digital, but just about identifying discs so it was ready for when console games moved into an all-digital era. That era looks like it’s right around the corner, especially now that Sony has announced it’s killing PlayStation discs in 2028. Both Microsoft and Sony also ship digital-only variants of their consoles, and it’s clear from game sales numbers that most titles are purchased digitally these days.

I fully expect Microsoft to follow Sony and eventually scrap Xbox discs, especially as the number of authorized manufacturers capable of producing physical media continues to shrink. That’s largely because almost every other form of media, from music to movies, has moved on from optical discs. The big difference with Xbox, though, is that Microsoft has always been obsessed with game preservation.

In the same year that disc-to-digital is launching, Microsoft is also bringing original Xbox and Xbox 360 games to PC. The company has also spent years working on its backward compatibility program, to get as many games from the Xbox and Xbox 360 eras working on modern Xbox consoles. Game preservation is a central part of Project Helix, the next Xbox that could play every Xbox game ever made.

It’s not an easy task to pull off game preservation, either. There are the complex technical challenges that need to be overcome, alongside licensing issues and the business challenges from publishers that decide how a game should be sold.

Some of those technical challenges mean that not every single Xbox One disc will work with this new disc-to-digital feature. That could be because some early discs simply didn’t get pressed with the unique identifier. Microsoft warned its internal Xbox testers that “it all depends on how and when the disc was manufactured and it may not have the features we need for this program.”

Discs that are slightly damaged might also not work with disc-to-digital, but run just fine otherwise. That’s why it’s important that Xbox is launching this right now — physical media decays over time.

The licensing and business challenges are far more complicated. Publishers need to agree to disc-to-digital, and some could hold back. It appears that most are on board, and even Ubisoft games started showing up recently. We’ve seen a number of other games come online since Microsoft’s announcement, and the company has been clear that more will follow.

The next challenge beyond disc-to-digital is solving digital ownership. If all we really own of a digital game is a license, I hope that one day those licenses can move freely across devices and platforms. I want to buy a single copy of a game and have that license follow me across Xbox, PlayStation, Nintendo, and PC. I also want to be able to gift or sell that license on different marketplaces, just as we’ve been able to do with physical discs at retailers for decades.

Microsoft envisioned this true digital ownership future 15 years ago, and it has gradually taken steps toward making it a reality. I hope Xbox can eventually pull it off, but the solution will require publishers and platform owners to agree on a shared system for how game licenses are bought, transferred, gifted, and resold. That’s a much bigger challenge than simply getting rid of the disc.

The pad
